Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff face redundancy risk as the telecoms firm looks to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition.

The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000 workforce, the BBC understands.

VMO2 has billions of debt on its balance sheet and is tackling competition from both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, a move which VMO2 has firmly opposed.

VMO2 declined to comment. The Prospect union, which represents VMO2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling".

Deputy general secretary Noel McClean said it is "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected".

The majority of the affected staff will be in non-customer facing roles and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told.

VMO2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts that were first reported by Sky News.

As of 30 June, VMO2's total debt stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts.

Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear, and YouFibre.

VMO2's had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by VMO2's owners.

However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal, with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from VMO2.

At the time, VMO2 called the BT takeover a "stitch-up", which allowed its rival "tighten its grip" over the market.

BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover.

VMO2 was minded to go ahead with the plans after halting upgrades and expansion of its own infrastructure to ease concerns over its debt pile, the paper reported.

How Dart revived career with help of Wimbledon champion

This video can not be played

Dart reacts to her first WTA title after 'incredible week'

In the hour following her first WTA title win, Britain's Harriet Dart had little time to respond to the stream of congratulatory messages flashing up on her phone.

Most pressing was making a call to her proud parents, Nick and Susie, who had been watching the final with friends at their local tennis club in north London, and her sister Phoebe.

The next person she spoke to was 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli.

Dart has been coached by the French former world number seven since the start of the season on a part-time basis, and she credits Bartoli for helping her achieve what some thought was beyond her.

On Sunday, with Bartoli watching from home, the world number 115 won the Guangzhou Open in China by beating rising Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger.

"It's been quite incredible to work with Marion, and I was really fortunate she was open to working with me," Dart, 30, told BBC Sport in a video call from Guangzhou.

"I'm obviously at a very different stage of my career to someone who is, say, 20. But I still feel I have a lot to improve and there are gains to be made.

"She really believes in me - that means the world to me. Seeing a Grand Slam champion having that belief has made me believe a lot more in myself."

Britain's Dart wins first WTA title in 'wild week'

When Dart started working with Bartoli, she was ranked outside the top 160. The pair live close to each other in Dubai and spend training blocks together there when Dart is not on the road.

Dart and Bartoli, who has a young family, are not travelling full-time together on tour, but there have been opportunities for them to work on the ground, particularly during this year's Grand Slam tournaments.

Dart says 42-year-old Bartoli still hitting the ball "really well" in practice is another benefit of the partnership.

In Guangzhou, Dart was accompanied by her fitness trainer Dario Gonfiantini and boyfriend Stephen Falck. Without her coach, Dart had to largely rely on figuring things out herself - with the help of Bartoli sending over observational notes.

Dart is projected to rise to 83rd on Monday after lifting the Guangzhou trophy to cap a stunning second half of the season.

Dart has won 19 of her 24 tour-level matches on the hard courts since Wimbledon, taking her overall record on the WTA Tour this season to 23 victories from 34 matches - the highest winning percentage of her career.

"More than anything, Marion is just a great person. She cares about me as a person first and foremost, as well as improving me as a tennis player, of course," Dart said.

"It's been invaluable and amazing for her to share her experiences to make me better.

"I've learned a lot from her and look forward to continuing to learn more. I hope we will be able to spend more weeks together next year."

Bartoli, 42, has coached several WTA players since retiring, including 2017 French Open champion Jelena Ostapenko

Dart reached a career high of 70th in the world in 2024, having made the Wimbledon third round and US Open second round, but has languished outside the top 100 for most of the past two seasons.

During this period there have been clear vulnerabilities with her game, with opponents learning they could take advantage of a slow second serve that tended to produce double faults.

There have also been questions about her on-court mentality and whether she could handle the pressure moments.

In Guangzhou, she answered those doubts with a series of gutsy wins where she needed to fight back from behind.

"She's always had a fantastic work ethic and has always set the bar high with her professionalism," Anne Keothavong, Britain's women's team captain, told BBC Sport.

"But there is certainly more belief and confidence now. She's in a very good place.

"She's been grinding away on the tour for a long time and it's great to see someone who has put in a lot of time to succeed and win a big title."

Keothavong named Dart in her squad for September's Billie Jean King Cup Finals and although she did not select Dart to play in the tie, she was impressed by her ball-striking during practice.

Taking that level back on tour has helped Dart continue what has been an encouraging few weeks for British women in the Asian hard-court swing.

Sonay Kartal reached the final of a WTA 1000 event in Wuhan, Katie Boulter made the semi-finals at a WTA 250 in Osaka and now Dart has won her maiden title at WTA 250 level.

Last week, teenager Hannah Klugman won the biggest title of her career at the Wrexham Open - a W100 event on the second-tier Challenger tour.

Green Party at 'crossroads', says former co-leader

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 15:52:51 GMT

The Green Party is at a "crossroads" and needs to focus on its "core values", a former party co-leader has told the BBC, weeks after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

Adrian Ramsay suggested the Greens need their policies to appeal to a majority of British voters if they want to bring the "environmental changes that we need" and advised against taking an approach that risks being "quite divisive".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski responded by saying there was "no environmental justice without social, racial and economic justice".

The motion, which Polanski did not take part in or vote upon, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.

It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month.

It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.

Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski, who is Jewish, from entering the country.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission also wrote to the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.

Labour later said it would end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy.

Speaking to Newscast, Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".

The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.

Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.

He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.

Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.

"One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."

Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".

He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."

Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".

He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".

Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.

He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pair losing to Polanski in the leadership contest.

Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.

However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

A police force has said it is reviewing a video which shows one of its officers punching a boy.

The footage circulated on social media shows a Merseyside Police officer punching what appears to be teenage boy three times while holding a pair of metal handcuffs in the hand he is striking him with.

The force said officers had been responding on Friday to reports of about 20 youths in the Alder Wood Avenue area of Speke, Liverpool, blocking roads with wheelie bins and "aiming fireworks at anyone who tried to remove them".

"We would like to stress that a short clip doesn't always show the full context," a Merseyside Police spokesman said.

The footage being circulated on social media - which has been viewed more than 40,000 times - begins moments before the officer strikes the boy.

It does not show anything that happened in the run-up to the incident.

After a complaint was made on Saturday, the force said its professional standards team would look into the incident.

"While we look to establish the full circumstances of what happened, we would urge people not to speculate and avoid sharing rumours or misinformation," the force said in a statement published on its website.

"We have a contempt for criminality and a commitment to cracking down on people committing serious offences in Merseyside," a force spokesman added.

More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 13:41:00 GMT

More than 300 people have been arrested during a protest supporting the banned Palestine Action group outside the US embassy, police have said.

Hundreds of people gathered at Nine Elms in London on Saturday, with many holding signs reading phrases such as: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."

The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that 325 arrests were made. The force added on social media that 320 of them were for "expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act".

At least 4,000 arrests have been made in relation to the group, which was proscribed in July 2025.

The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's ban under terrorism legislation, after the group's co-founder was granted permission to appeal it.

The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.

Officers on Saturday made arrests into the evening, taking people to police vans for transfer, to the applause of many protesters, some of whom chanted: "Free, free Palestine."

In some instances, officers had to carry demonstrators who refused to walk.

Retired lawyer Charles Allison - who was taken by police in the afternoon - had travelled from Cumbria to participate. He said he feared for people's civil liberties, which he said were "being devalued and watered down".

"I hope the Supreme Court justices - they won't necessarily be influenced by it [the protest] - but I hope that they will take a long-term view of what is happening in this country and decide that the proscription was unlawful, as I believe it was," the 75-year-old said.

David Bolden, another protester awaiting arrest called the ban an "absurd law".

Defend Our Juries, which has been co-ordinating a series of protests over the ban, said the number of people detained this weekend took the total over 4,000 arrests since the group was proscribed, calling it "truly dystopian".

According to Home Office figures seen by the BBC, 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026. Along with the 134 people arrested outside Westminster Magistrates Court earlier this year and those on Saturday brings the total up to 4,089.

The BBC has contacted the Met to confirm any figures it might hold.

Amnesty International UK has criticised the arrests and called for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action.

Defend Our Juries called the arrests "unjust" and an assault on free speech.

Sir Tom Jones mentors Welsh singer to victory on The Voice UK

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:46:17 GMT

A singer who began her career as a teenager busking on the streets of Cardiff has been crowned winner of The Voice UK.

Cate McHugh, from Llantwit Major in the Vale of Glamorgan, appeared stunned when she heard her name announced on the ITV show, telling viewers "I did it" when asked how she was feeling.

The performer, who has a degenerative sight condition which has left her registered blind, was given a congratulatory hug by her coach Sir Tom Jones on his final appearance on the show after previously announcing he had been "fired".

Speaking after the show, McHugh, 31, said: "I won The Voice! I'm entirely gobsmacked and absolutely haven't fully processed this information just yet."

Footage shared by McHugh on social media showed her laughing and smiling with family and friends screaming in delight as they celebrated her victory at a watch party in Cardiff.

McHugh's prizes include a £50,000 cash prize and a recording contract, with her first ever single, a cover of The Beatles classic Blackbird, now released.

Posting on social media, she said: "From the bottom of my heart I want to say THANK YOU for following my journey, and joining my world! This is where it's going to REALLY get fun!"

In an interview with BBC Radio Wales Breakfast in September, McHugh said being chosen to be on Team Tom at the blind audition on The Voice UK was "absolutely undescribable".

Her rendition of Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars song Die With A Smile prompted Sir Tom to hit the button to turn his chair around after hearing her.

McHugh said she began singing "before I was talking" and started singing lessons aged six, turning professional when she was about 15.

At 22 she was diagnosed with degenerative sight condition Stargardt disease during her second year at music school and is registered blind.

As it affects the centre of her vision, it meant the singer was not sure if anyone had turned around at her audition until she heard Sir Tom's voice, she added.

"I just waited because I didn't know that anything had happened and then Tom Jones started talking," McHugh said.

She said her "fantastic mother" has the same condition and has been an inspiration to her over the years, "working around anything that might be affecting her physically or mentally".

McHugh said when she phoned her parents to tell them she was on Team Tom "there was this massive roar".

McHugh performed a duet of John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads during the final.

Some of her family members could be seen celebrating in the audience during the show.

It was also a poignant night for Sir Tom as he made his final appearance on the show, having been a coach on and off since it first aired in 2012.

The It's Not Unusual and What's New Pussycat? singer made headlines after revealing that ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from the show's coaching panel.

Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:05:40 GMT

The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.

In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.

Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

In a BBC interview broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?

"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.

It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.

Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.

"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.

"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."

"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling.

The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come.

The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week.

But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."

Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year."

"But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".

She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."

Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".

Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference.

"So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:47:03 GMT

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".

In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.

At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.

But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.

The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.

In the Sunday Times, Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."

She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".

Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.

She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.

Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.

In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.

She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she "can't even believe we are reopening" the Brexit debate.

She told BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "This is not something that is needed in order to cut welfare, in order to spend money on defence.

"We are having yet another Westminster bubble argument about the EU when it is time for us to actually start using the opportunities, fix mistakes that have been made and go into the future."

Badenoch added: "I do not want to indulge Andy Burnham's fantasies about redoing the referendum because he doesn't have a plan for what to do today."

Burnham told Badenoch during the most recent session of Prime Minister's Questions that he was focused on "getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility".

The next UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.

No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 00:17:05 GMT

When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.

Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.

But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.

She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.

But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.

The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.

Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."

While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal.

"It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."

Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".

During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area.

"I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.

For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".

Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.

While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says.

"If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."

Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.

His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".

He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals.

"It's common sense and common decency," he says.

His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI.

Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.

Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

"Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.

The announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.

Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."

Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system.

"If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."

He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect.

"Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."

Who are the real winners of Celebrity Traitors?

BBC News Sun, 01 Nov 2026 00:06:01 GMT

Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final

In some ways, all the players on The Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.

They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.

But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.

Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.

We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.

After a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.

There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.

When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.

"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.

When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.

For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.

And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.

The BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.

But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.

The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.

And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.

Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms.

Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.

When it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.

Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.

But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.

Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny.

"He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.

Fellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.

Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week.

What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.

But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors.

"Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.

Of all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.

But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final.

"And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.

The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.

But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.

Just a few days ago, it was announced that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".

And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.

Culture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.

Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.

But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men.

"There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.

In the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.

Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.

He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.

He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.

His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.

What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.

Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.

On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.

But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.

And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?

Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home

BBC News Sat, 31 Oct 2026 23:06:13 GMT

When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.

The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".

Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.

After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.

Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.

Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.

As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.

"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.

"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."

Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.

Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.

In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.

She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.

But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.

That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.

So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.

It turned out to be a disastrous decision.

She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.

Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".

"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."

But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.

Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.

In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.

Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.

"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.

On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.

She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.

One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.

"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.

But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.

Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.

"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.

She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.

The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.

McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.

New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.

To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."

Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".

When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.

Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".

Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."

But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried.

"Her mental state is not good," he tells BBC Sinhala.

"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."

Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna Khan

If you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide.

Fish pay attention to one influential neighbour in virtual reality

New Scientist November 01, 2026

A virtual reality tailored to fish reveals that each animal may be paying attention to only a single, most influential neighbour. This finding may shed light on how animals move as groups without becoming overwhelmed by all the activity and interactions around them.

Fish form schools, milling about seamlessly and acting as a collective. But how does a single fish know what to do? Guy Theraulaz at the University of Toulouse in France and his colleagues attempted to answer the question by using virtual reality (VR) to better study interactions between five rummy-nose tetra fish (Hemigrammus rhodostomus).

“A fish in a group can perceive, simultaneously, many, many individuals, but perception is not equivalent to influence,” he says. “Does a real fish use all this information at once, or does it just focus on a few neighbours?”

Advertisement

Swimming in a school may help fish hear dolphins’ ultrasound clicks

The researchers put a single tetra fish in a hemispherical bowl and tracked its swimming with a camera while projecting four virtual tetra fish onto the bowl’s interior in such a way that they appeared real to the tetra. The projections and the camera were connected into a feedback loop, allowing the virtual tetras to react and adjust to the real fish. Theraulaz says that he and his colleagues previously studied tetras in observational experiments and developed a mathematical model for how they might interact. The virtual reality setup allowed them to test that model.

Specifically, they tested three hypotheses: that a single fish would have the most influence on the real tetra’s behaviour; that two tetras would jointly be the most influential fish; and that the real tetra would pay attention to all four virtual fish. The team found clear evidence favouring the first case: as far as the real tetra was concerned, there was only one most influential fish at a time. This may be the case simply because it is easier on the fish, says Theraulaz. “By focusing on just one neighbour, the fish reduce their sensory and cognitive demand,” he says.

Researchers trained a hawk outfitted with microphones to fly through a swarm of 600,000 bats, revealing how they can hear their own voice in a crowd

Iain Couzin at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany says that the new study confirms past ideas about tetra behaviour, which were largely pioneered by Theraulaz and his colleagues. It also underscores how powerful VR could be for eventually getting into the heads of animals as they make decisions, he says.

Studies of collective animal behaviour are difficult to perform because an individual animal in a group can’t be isolated without disturbing group behaviours that the researchers want to study, which makes it tricky to test specific hypotheses. But making some animals virtual and fully under researchers’ control sidesteps this problem. Overall, VR leads to endless opportunities for experimenting, says Guy Amichay at Northwestern University in Illinois.“You could technically design any virtual world you want,” he says. Couzin says that it would be exciting to apply the new method to other species of fish for whom no mathematical models exist.

Therauluz and his colleagues now want to advance their experiment by making some of the virtual fish act stressed, as if they were facing a predator, and then see whether this would affect the real tetra through their interactions.

PRX Life DOI: 10.1103/18qw-sfyd

The best new science-fiction novels of November 2026

New Scientist November 01, 2026

I am currently deeply engrossed in the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, a piece of classic science fiction (well, from 2012) from Chris Beckett, Dark Eden. But I’m also in the mood for some fresh writing, and the new sci-fi on offer this month is an exciting and eclectic range. I’m keen to check out Benjamin Percy’s audio drama Exoplanet, produced by none other than Andy Weir, as well as books from some old favourites: Michael Moorcock, Carole Hailey, John Scalzi and Andrew Hunter Murray. And for all those still in the mood for scares after Halloween, there’s some space horror from SA Barnes in the deliciously named Cold Eternity.

The best new science-fiction books of October 2026

This is something a little different – produced by Andy Weir, author of The Martian and Project Hail Mary, and written by Benjamin Percy, this sci-fi thriller is a full-cast audio drama from Audible, and it sounds really exciting. It follows the fallout when a quantum anomaly tears a starship apart, leaving its crew in different eras on the same deadly exoplanet – one in a machine-ruled future, for example, another in a past peopled by hostile aliens. I’m a recent (only this year) audiobook adopter, and this sounds right up my street.

I really enjoyed Andrew Hunter Murray’s speculative novel The Last Day, in which the world stops turning, leaving half the planet in scorching sunlight and the other half permanently dark. This latest book sounds equally interesting. A young woman, Esme, escapes her dull job by taking tiny potions known as The Elsewheres, which allow her to visit alternate versions of herself. But then an “incident” turns her into the most important person in this, or possibly any, universe. How will she handle it?

Advertisement

I always appreciate a good “asteroid hitting Earth” story (my recent-ish reads include Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle’s Lucifer’s Hammer, a classic from 1977, and Not With A Bang by Temi Oh, a twist on the tale). Carole Hailey’s previous book, The Silence Project, was great, so I’m looking forward to her take on this story. It follows Cassie, who grew up with a father obsessed with an impending apocalypse. Now she’s middle-aged and discovers that his teachings might have some use after all when an asteroid is found in the solar system, heading for northern Europe.

There aren’t many names in science fiction and fantasy bigger than Michael Moorcock, and this is the final part of his “fictional autobiography”. It sees, if I understand the blurb correctly, the author tell the story of both his real life (from the impact of his science fiction to the music of the sixties) and of a fantasy world only he can see (the example given: “the Carmelite Monks must protect their latest multiverse-spanning invention”). Intriguingly weird, as you’d expect from this wonderful writer – I’m keen to see how, as we’re promised, “Moorcock meets ‘Moorcock’ and together they produce a remedy for the world’s pain!”.

If I were SA Barnes, I would be pretty pleased with the moniker laid on me by my publisher: she is, apparently, “the queen of space horror”. In this latest, Halley Zwick (who is on the run) boards the spaceship Elysian Fields. This was sold to the super-rich as a place to enter cryo-sleep until their immortality could be assured, but it has been silent and dark for decades… although is it really?

Allergic reactions after sex should be listed as an antibiotic risk, experts say

New Scientist October 31, 2026

Clinicians are calling for patient information leaflets to be updated after a woman had a life-threatening allergic reaction to an antibiotic in her partner’s semen. They also want healthcare workers to be made aware of such risks during their medical training.

“If you read any drug leaflet, they list a whole bunch of super-rare risks, so it’s not unreasonable to also include this risk on those leaflets to boost awareness,” says Cassim Akhoon at King’s College Hospital in London.

Slashing sugar intake before antibiotics may save your microbiome

The woman developed anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, due to probable exposure to the antibiotic amoxicillin via her partner’s semen. He took the drug to treat a sinus infection 6 hours before they had penetrative vaginal sex without a condom.

Advertisement

The partner of the woman asked his doctor whether it was safe for the couple to have unprotected sex because she had a history of allergic reactions to penicillins, a group of antibiotics, of which amoxicillin is one of the most commonly prescribed. “He was explicitly reassured by his doctor that she would not be at risk of allergic reactions,” says Akhoon, who is part of a team that examined the case after the event.

But 5 minutes after ejaculation, the woman developed symptoms of anaphylaxis. “Everything started to swell. I couldn’t breathe,” she told New Scientist. “Obviously, nearly dying is quite a terrifying experience.”

Free newsletter

The woman self-administered an EpiPen, a device that injects a shot of the hormone adrenaline into the body to halt anaphylaxis. Paramedics then arrived and treated her with further adrenaline. She was taken to hospital and was discharged 6 hours later.

The healthcare workers who treated her seemed to be unaware that exposure to amoxicillin via semen is possible, the woman says, and some of them assumed she must have taken the drug. “I wasn’t taught about this in medical school,” says Akhoon. “I definitely think we should make this part of formal medical training.”

About a year after the incident, Akhoon and his colleagues confirmed the woman’s allergy to amoxicillin via a skin test. This has led them to conclude that exposure via semen was the most likely cause. Around 1 per cent of people have allergies to penicillins, as confirmed via skin-prick tests, but anaphylaxis as a result of exposure to these drugs is extremely rare.

Antibiotics enter the bloodstream and can then reach the prostate and the seminal vesicles, a pair of pouch-like glands situated behind the bladder, which produce most of the fluid that makes up semen, says Akhoon. Prior studies have also found that amoxicillin is excreted in urine, suggesting it can persist in the urethra – a thin tube that transports urine and semen – until it is flushed out during ejaculation, he says.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the microbe responsible for gonorrhoea, is developing resistance to most antibiotics, which means we need new drugs to treat the condition. An antibiotic called zoliflodacin might be part of a solution

Earlier case reports have described similar incidences, with one woman developing anaphylaxis after exposure to amoxicillin during oral sex. The team thinks the evidence that such transmission routes are a risk is strong enough to list it on the patient information leaflets provided alongside medications.

Amoxicillin’s leaflet already lists a rare side effect called aseptic meningitis, says Akhoon, which occurs when tissue around the brain and spinal cord become inflamed. “We don’t have any mechanistic proof that amoxicillin was absolutely, definitely the cause [of related meningitis cases], yet because of [the] high likelihood of causality, it’s mentioned on the leaflet.”

There isn’t sufficient evidence to list a risk of transmission via semen for other antibiotics or drugs, but this may emerge in future case reports, says Ahkoon. “As people consider this route of transmission more, we might start to get a bigger collection of cases to determine which drug classes are implicated.” There is also no evidence that transfer of antibiotics via vaginal fluid could lead to allergic reactions in sexual partners, he says.

As the world warms, antibiotic-resistant bacteria are escaping from frozen sediments. But with new monitoring tools, we can identify problem genes and develop treatments before our pathogens acquire them

The team has submitted the findings to the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency, which will decide whether updates to amoxicillin leaflets are needed. It couldn’t respond to a request for comment before this article was published.

Once informed, “people can then wear condoms or avoid sex until the antibiotics course is over”, says Patrick Yong at Frimley Park Hospital in Surrey, UK, who also examined the case.

Consultant allergist Chris Rutkowski in London thinks the most effective way of avoiding such transmissions is for the risk to taught during medical training. “Not because it’s common, but because the cost of missing it is high,” he says.

BMJ Case Reports DOI: 10.1136/bcr-2025-271777

Rusty crust made Mars warm and wet

New Scientist October 30, 2026

Mars once had a climate that kept it warm enough for water to flow on the surface. But scientists haven’t been able to agree on an atmospheric recipe with enough warming potential. A new proposal says that hot water circulating underground produced a missing ingredient.

Water reacting with iron in Mars’s crust may have delivered a steady supply of hydrogen to the atmosphere for millions of years, says Cin-Ty Lee at Rice University in Texas.

While not a greenhouse gas itself, hydrogen can have a planet-warming effect through its interactions with atmospheric carbon dioxide. Collisions between the H2 and CO2 molecules deform both of them, and this makes them absorb wavelengths of infrared radiation that CO2 by itself doesn’t block, so the molecule pairs enhance the greenhouse effect.

Advertisement

Did NASA’s Viking landers find life on Mars after all, asks new book

Depending on the total amount of CO2 in the Martian atmosphere, even a few per cent of hydrogen in the atmosphere could be enough to bring the average global temperature above freezing. “I think there’s enough CO2 even now to do it,” says Lee.

The underground hydrogen production plant that Lee proposes is the extremely thick crust, thought to extend as far as 80 kilometres below ground, that underlies Mars’s southern highlands. “Like an iceberg floating on water, the higher the mountain, the thicker the root,” he says.

Just as on Earth, the crust will contain radioactive elements, such as uranium, thorium and potassium, which produce heat as they decay. Thicker crust contains a greater total quantity of these elements, while the surface area available for cooling remains the same. In 2024, Lee published calculations showing that, with sufficiently thick crust, ice in its upper few kilometres would melt and create aquifers.

Free newsletter

Once those aquifers exist, Lee told the annual conference of the Geological Society of America in Denver, Colorado, earlier this month, the water will start shedding its heat by circulating up and down through the porous upper layers of the crust. These layers mostly consist of basalt, which is rich in iron. The water would make the iron rust, a process that frees up its constituent hydrogen molecules, which would then find their way up into the atmosphere.

The hydrothermal pump eventually died, leaving Mars the cold desert it is today, because it ran out of both water and power. “For the water, this was a one-way ticket,” says Lee. “And also the radioactivity diminished.”

Ramses Ramirez of the University of Central Florida, who has studied volcanoes as potential sources of hydrogen for the warming of Mars, says that until he has seen a full paper about the idea, he is sceptical the idea can explain Mars’s formerly warm surface “without invoking some extremely favourable circumstances”.

The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century

Ramirez also notes that the possibility of water releasing hydrogen from rocks was proposed over a decade ago. But, according to Lee, while earlier studies just supposed that water somehow would be involved, his work shows “how it’s almost inevitable that this has to happen” with a thick enough crust.

He says his idea is testable by looking deep into the Martian crust. “If we find that it is oxidised down to several kilometres, this is the only way it can happen.”

As scientific bycatch, this would then also provide an explanation for the redness of Mars. Meteoroid impacts or other processes would expose some of the rusted rock on the surface. “With the erosion by wind, you are going to generate a lot of dust and it coats everything,” says Lee.

How did the biggest crypto heist in history just happen?

New Scientist October 30, 2026

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance has been hit with the biggest ever cryptocurrency heist, in which billions of dollars of reserves were drained in just 20 minutes.

From 8:05pm on 29 October, $6.36 billion in cryptocurrencies were shifted from wallets in a coordinated attack believed to have originated from a North Korean-linked hacking unit called TraderTraitor. This group was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit crypto exchange in February 2025.

The US Treasury has previously said that such stolen funds are used to finance North Korea’s nuclear missile programme.

Advertisement

Despite cryptocurrency’s founding idea of decentralisation, meaning no one has singular control over the money flowing through the network, there are some large single points of failure. It is thought one of these was the cause of the Binance hack, which gave access to a system the exchange uses to authorise transfers out of customers’ accounts.

Quantum computer quickly mines cryptocurrency while using less energy

In a statement, Binance said its early investigations indicate the security incident may stem from a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. TRM Labs, a cybersecurity firm, suggests that preparations for the attack may have begun several days ago.

Binance claims it has found no evidence that the private cryptographic keys used to authorise transactions were stolen. Instead, the attackers appear to have gained access to the software that requests withdrawals, potentially allowing them to instruct Binance’s own systems to approve the transfers. However, the investigation is continuing and the firm has said in a subsequent statement there may have been “additional points of breach”.

“It shouldn’t be possible for a single [developer] PC to be compromised and somehow for that to allow the entire exchange to be compromised,” says Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK. “I don’t understand how that can happen.”

If that is the case, it highlights how precarious major financial hubs in the crypto world can be to single points of failure.

Free newsletter

“You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened,” says Clive Summerfield at FARx, a cybersecurity company. “Most crypto platforms are as centralised as any bank, with a small number of privileged individuals controlling billions. The difference is that once crypto is transferred, it’s gone.”

That centralisation can be a blessing as well as a curse, though: cryptocurrencies Tether and Circle have been able to freeze billions of dollars of stolen coins, stymying the hackers in attempts to transfer about half the stolen funds any further.

Woodward says the Binance incident potentially strikes a distinction between crypto security and more traditional finance. “You would hope there’d be things like two-man rules [where two separate people have to approve a change] or things that banks have for changing critical systems, but it doesn’t look like those were in place.”

Scientists confirm fruit and vegetable skin really is good for you

New Scientist October 30, 2026

Some people are convinced that fruit and vegetable skin is particularly nutritious, and now scientists have confirmed the idea. They have discovered that these parts of fruits and vegetables often contain far more fibre than the flesh we normally consume.

The finding suggests cooks are unwittingly discarding fibre-rich food by chucking out the seeds, skins and stems of fruits and vegetables when preparing a meal.

Home cooks and caterers should adopt “root to tip” eating and start cooking with squash peel, watermelon rind and pepper stalks to improve the public’s intake of dietary fibre, the team says.

Advertisement

Our food system is vulnerable to El Niño, warns UK climate minister

“We’ve really got to shift our purchasing habits to buy whole fruits and vegetables, and then use all of the fruits and vegetables in dishes,” says Rachel Gibson at King’s College London.

Gibson and her colleagues tested the fibre content of 12 fruits and vegetables, including butternut squash, kiwi fruit, watermelon, broccoli and bell pepper. The team measured the fibre content both in the parts typically consumed and the parts that usually go to waste.

They found that, in 10 of the 12 produce types, the normally wasted components contain more fibre than the commonly consumed parts. Butternut squash seeds and skin, for example, contained 9.25 grams of fibre per 100 grams, compared with 2 g of fibre per 100 g of squash flesh. Meanwhile, the skin and core of a pineapple core contains 450 per cent more fibre than the flesh. These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable.

Free newsletter

Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day.

Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says.

King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind.

Rejigging the meal choices on offer in a canteen can prompt people to make healthier, climate-friendlier decisions

Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks, says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.”

Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting investigation”. But he points out that the most carbon-intensive food waste is meat and dairy products. Reducing fruit and vegetable waste is therefore “part of the solution, but it’s not the only thing we need to do”, he says.

In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet

New Scientist October 30, 2026

I came up with the idea of the planet Eden in 1992 for a short story called The Circle of Stones. At that time, I had no idea that there really were such things as planets without suns, but it seemed likely to me. It also seemed possible to me that life might arise on such a planet, since, even here on Earth, whole ecologies thrive without sunlight around thermal vents in the deep ocean. Life on Earth may have even have begun in such places.

Quite often, if something seems likely, it does indeed happen. (In another book, I predicted that a US president would one day seek to take over Greenland and Canada.) Having written that story, I learned that free-floating planets did indeed exist. Being dark, they’re hard to spot, but a number have been detected using gravitational lensing. And I gather it’s not particularly controversial to think that some of them might support life (though not quite in the form that I chose to imagine it – but I’ll come to that).

When creating a world for a story, I don’t usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent. I didn’t build Eden by doing a lot of research, but I did put a lot of thought into how it might all work. This wasn’t so I could put it all in the book – no one in Eden knows this stuff and the story is told entirely by its characters! – but so that I had something to guide my imagination and make my invented world feel coherent.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

My idea was that Eden had once been covered in ice, but its hot core meant there was liquid water below the ice in which life could come into existence. One particular kind of life form appeared, somewhat resembling tree roots, that was able to obtain additional energy by pushing deep down into hot rocks, pumping its sap through them to heat it, and then pumping it back up again, like a geothermal power station. One of the ways these organisms used this heat was to push upwards into the planet’s shell of ice, melting parts of it, feeding on the nutrients it contained, and creating more living space – and they carried on doing so until much of the surface of Eden was ice-free, and had an atmosphere that would turn out to be breathable by humans.

Millions of years later, this thawed-out surface, now populated by a multitude of different life forms, became the stage on which my drama could unfold: first that early story, then another story and then the novel Dark Eden and its two sequels. In Dark Eden, a tiny community of humans, descended from stranded visitors from Earth, eke out a living using tools made of stone and wood, and try to make sense of their life as exiles from a sunlit world that lives on in folk memory, but which they can only very shakily imagine. (In the biblical story of Eden, humans are exiled from Eden – my Eden is the place of exile.) Their stories tell them that Earth people could fly through the air, that there was a thing there called leckytrickity, that Earth animals had eyes that you could look into and see their minds looking back out at you, not like the flat, blank eyes of Eden creatures.

Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time

On the surface of Eden, those root-like life forms put up structures that Eden’s humans call “trees”. A whole ecosystem has evolved around them, including “starflowers” that parasitise their roots. (These, as it happens, turn out to be a rich source of Vitamin D. Phew! What a stroke of luck!) And there are many animals – or quote-unquote “animals”, strictly speaking, since they’re not related to the animal kingdom of Earth. There’s no sunlight in Eden (and therefore no alternation of day and night) but, like organisms that live in the ocean depths of Earth, Eden’s life has developed bioluminescence. The “trees” have luminous “lanternflowers”; the starflowers glitter. Imagine a leafless forest on a moonless night, lit by thousands of Chinese lanterns. Then add in twinkling fairy lights at ground level. With your eyes half-closed, the forests of Eden would look something like that.

Just as life on Earth depends on plants that turn sunlight into chemical energy, so the life of Eden depends on geothermal trees. They bring heat to the surface to power their metabolisms, they keep the air warm and, if you live on Eden, the steady “Hmmmph hmmmph hmmmph” of their constant pumping is the background of your waking and sleeping life, merging in the distance to a steady hum. All the trees are hot, and some of them are so hot that you’d burn yourself if you touched their trunks. If you cut down a tree, you have to watch out for the spurt of scalding liquid that bursts out.

When I read stories set on alien planets, I’m sometimes disappointed in the “animals” (I’ll drop the inverted commas now). Writers often seem to dream up a motley collection of bizarre creatures without much regard for how they might actually survive or how they are related to one another. I tried to design my animals on evolutionary principles, giving thought to how they were adapted to their environment, the role they played in the ecosystem and how they might plausibly have evolved. Animals on Earth fall into a large but finite number of basic body plans. For example, monkeys, cows, crocodiles and seagulls all have four limbs and, though some descendants of quadrupeds have lost their limbs (snakes, whales), there are no examples of quadrupeds developing extra ones. In the same way, large animals on Eden all have a six-limbed body plan. There are other animals that don’t conform to this, just as there are arthropods, et cetera on Earth, but the large animals are all based on this six-limbed pattern.

From drowned worlds to virtual utopias via deep space, wild ideas abound in Emily H. Wilson’s picks for her favourite sci-fi reads of the year

I’ve already mentioned how different Eden eyes are from the eyes of terrestrial animals. They have evolved alongside the evolution of bioluminescence, rather in the way that colourful flowers and nectar-eating insects have evolved alongside one another on Earth. Eden trees use luminous lanternflowers to attract the creatures that help them reproduce, just as flowering plants on Earth use colour and scent.

I gave a lot of thought to the biology of Eden, but I have to admit that, in strictly scientific terms, my imaginary world isn’t entirely viable. Free-floating planets with warm cores? Yes! Not just possible, but a certainty! But free-floating planets with warm surfaces? Sadly no. More than one astronomer has told me they just couldn’t happen. No matter how many radiator-like trees there might be, I’ve been told, it still wouldn’t be enough to maintain liquid water or a warm atmosphere.

Let’s call it “fiction science”, science made up for a story, which works in some places and in others allows itself poetic licence. Almost all science fiction uses fiction science and Dark Eden contains several other examples. I took some liberties with human genetics, for instance. And then there’s the question of how people got to Eden in the first place. (It’s many light years away from Earth.) Like the writers of pretty much all stories set in interstellar space, I pretended that faster-than-light travel was possible and went with that, although it most probably isn’t.

(I think that’s OK. It allows us to visit, in our imaginations at least, parts of the universe we could never otherwise hope to reach.)

What I wanted from Eden was for it to be a world that hung together well enough to be a satisfying setting for my story, one in which I and my readers could immerse ourselves. The story is about exile and loss. The perpetually dark sky, and the animals with their blank unreadable eyes, serve as reminders that Eden folk are exiles. At the beginning of Dark Eden, every human being in Eden lives around a circle of stones that marks the place where their ancestors first touched down. And this circle represents to Eden folk the hope for return and redemption, which is central to their whole world view.

The fact that I took some liberties when constructing Eden doesn’t mean it wouldn’t be interesting also to write about a real free-floating planet. And, as it happens, I’ve had the opportunity recently to do just that. In a project initiated by Comma Press, I was one of a number of writers who paired up with astronomers from Jodrell Bank to write stories for an anthology called Firmament. My astronomer collaborator, Ida Janiak, helped me build a scenario in which a free-floating planet called Lupus arrives in the solar system. Apart from being roughly Earth-sized, Lupus isn’t much like Eden, but somewhat like the Jovian moon Europa. Its surface is covered by a kilometres-thick shell of ice in no danger of melting, with a liquid ocean beneath and… well, read the story! The anthology will appear in November but there will also be a condensed version of mine and Ida’s story in the Christmas edition of New Scientist, out online on 16 December and in print on the 19th.

I hope, meanwhile, you will immerse yourself in the luminous forests of Eden with their pulsing trees. Possible or not, they are very beautiful, if I say so myself.

Dark Eden by Chris Beckett (Corvus) is the November read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.
