Read an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett

New Scientist October 30, 2026

We went out by a path that led through a big clump of flickering starflowers and then into Batwing. A whole bunch of Batwing grownups and newhairs were in their clearing banging away at a giant redlantern tree with their blackglass axes, working in the pink light of its flowers.

We walked round the edge of their clearing to Family Fence, dragged away the branches at the opening, and went out into open forest. No more shelters and campfires ahead of us now: nothing but shining trees.

Hmmmph, hmmmph, hmmmph, went the trees. Hmmmmmm, went forest. We walked for a waking under the light of the treelanterns, slashing down whatever birds and bats and fruit we could get as we went along, and finally stopped to rest at the big lump of rock called Lava Blob. Old Roger handed us out a gritty little seedcake each, made of ground-up starflower seeds, so we could have something in our bellies, and then we settled down with our backs against the rock, so we didn’t have to worry about leopards sneaking up behind us. There were lots of yellowlantern trees round there, which we didn’t get so much back in Family, and also yellow animals called hoppers that came bouncing out of forest on their back legs and wrung their four hands together while they looked at us with their big flat eyes and went Peep peep peep. But hoppers were no good to eat and their skins were no use either, so we just chucked stones at them to make them go away and let us sleep in peace.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

When we woke up, Starry Swirl was still bright bright in sky. We ate a bit of dry cake and off we went again, under redlanterns and whitelanterns and spiketrees, with flutterbyes darting and glittering all round us and bats chasing the flutterbyes and trees going hmmph, hmmph, hmmph like always, until it all blurred together into that hmmmmmmmmm that was the background of our lives.

After a few miles we came to a small pool full of shiny wavyweed and all us newhairs took off our wraps and dived into the warm water for crabfish and oysters to eat. All the boys watched Tina Spiketree diving in, and they all thought how graceful she was with her long legs, and how smooth her skin was, and how much they wanted to slip with her. But when she came up she swam straight to me, and gave me a dying oyster with the bright pink light still shining out of it.

“You know what they say about oysters, don’t you, John?” she said.

Tom’s neck, she was pretty pretty, the prettiest in whole of Family. And she knew it well well.

In another couple of hours we reached the place where Peckham Hills began to rise up out of forest of Circle Valley, and started to climb up through them by Monkey Path, which isn’t really a path, but just a way we know through the trees. The trees carried on up the slopes – redlanterns and whitelanterns and scalding hot spiketrees – and there were flickering starflowers growing beneath them, just like in the rest of forest. Streams ran through them down from darkness and ice, heading towards Greatpool, still cold cold but already bright and glittering with life. And small creatures called monkeys jumped from tree to tree. They had little thin bodies, and six long arms with a hand on the end of each. Handsome Fox shot one with an arrow, and was pleased pleased with himself, even though they were all bones and sinews and only give a mouthful of meat, because they move fast and are hard to aim at with those big blotches on their skin that flash on and off as they swing among the lanternflowers.

As we climbed up it got colder. The starflowers disappeared, the trees became smaller, and there weren’t any monkeys any more, only the occasional smallbuck darting away through the trees. And then the trees stopped and we came out from the top edge of forest onto bare ground. Pretty soon, when we’d climbed above the height of those last few little trees, we could see whole of Circle Valley spread out below us – whole of Eden that we knew, with thousands and thousands of lanterns shining all the way from where we stood on Peckham Hills to Dark shadow of Blue Mountains away in the distance, and from Rockies over the left, with the red glow of Mount Snellins smouldering in middle, to the deep darkness over to our right that was Alps. And above all of it the huge spiral of Starry Swirl was still shining down.

Of course, with no trees to give off light with their lanternflowers or to warm the air with their trunks, it was dark dark up there – you could only just barely make things out in the starlight and the light from the edge of forest – and it was cold cold, specially on our feet. But us newhairs dared each other to run up as far as the snow. The ice felt like it was burning, it was so cold, and most kids took ten twenty steps, yelled and came running down again. But I took Gerry right up to the ridge of the hill and then, ignoring Old Roger yelling at us to come back, went far enough down the other side so that the others couldn’t see us.

“We’ve made our point now, haven’t we, John?” Gerry said, shivering. We only had waistwraps on, and buckskins round our shoulders, and our feet were hurting like they’d been skinned. “Shall we go back down to rest of them now?”

Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time

My cousin Gerry was about a wombtime younger than me – his dad was giving his mum a slip, in other words, about the time that I was born – and he was devoted to me, he thought I was wonderful, he’d do just about anything I asked.

“No, wait a minute. Wait a minute. Be quiet and listen.”

“Listen to what?”

“To the silence, you idiot.”

There was no hmmmmmmmm of forest, no hmmph, hmmph, hmmph of pumping trees, no starbirds going hoom, hoom, hoom in the distance, no flutterbyes flapping and flicking, no whoosh of diving bats. There was no sound at all except a quiet little tinkle of water all around us coming out from under the snow in hundreds of little streams. And it was dark dark. No tree-light up there. The only light came from Starry Swirl.

We could barely make out each other’s faces. It made me think about that place called Earth where Tommy and Angela first came from, way back in the beginning with the Three Companions, and where one waking we would all return, if only we stayed in the right place and were good good good. There were no lanterntrees back there on Earth, no glittery flutterbyes or shiny flowers, but they had a big big light that we don’t have at all. It came from a giant star. And it was so bright that it would burn out your eyes if you stared at it.

“When people talk about Earth,” I said to Gerry, “they always talk about that huge bright star, don’t they, and all the lovely light it must have given? But Earth turned round and round, didn’t it, and half the time it wasn’t facing the star at all but was dark dark, without lanterns or anything, only the light the Earth people made for themselves.”

“What are you talking about, John?” Gerry said, with his teeth chattering. “And why can’t we go back down again if you just want to talk?”

“I was thinking about that darkness. They called it Night, didn’t they? I’m just thinking that it must have been like this. What you get up here on Snowy Dark: it’s what they would have called Night.”

‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds

New Scientist October 30, 2026

There’s a bit of an open secret in physics. Even when our theories work well – and some have been rigorously tested for centuries – we don’t always fully understand them. We start with experimental evidence, then build mathematical models and theories, test and update them with more experiments and hope that it all adds up. Often, it does. But were a mathematician to ask what a theory we built this way is – that is, what type of well-defined mathematical objects comprise it – that isn’t a question that researchers can always fully answer.

“The sense from a lot of physicists is these are maths details and that is not really physics, so it’s not their job to set them straight,” says Gabriele Carcassi at the University of Michigan. But if we are to tackle the biggest problems in physics, such as marrying quantum mechanics with general relativity to produce a theory of quantum gravity, we may have to take a different tack.

That’s where the “reverse physics” programme comes in. It is Carcassi’s passion project: he spends his days trying to put physics on accurate, rigorous and meaningful mathematical foundations. He is mapping out the bridge you must be able to walk to fully connect mathematics and physics. Carcassi puts it like this: “When the maths is derived from the right physical assumptions, the physical assumptions can be derived from the maths.”

Advertisement

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

Like most physicists, I didn’t learn to think this way. All the concepts that were taught to me came from physics, such as fields or forces or even slices of space-time, then I’d learn just enough about what they are mathematically to know which equations predict their behaviour. If you asked me to define a mathematical object called a Lorentzian manifold, I am really not sure that I could, yet I have a fairly good mental image of the physical thing it is representing: space-time as the fabric of reality. Reverse-engineering a theory of a changing space-time, essentially the theory of general relativity, from ideas like Lorentzian manifolds and other mathematical ingredients certainly hadn’t been put on my radar throughout my education.

But Carcassi and his colleagues at the Assumptions of Physics project want to establish these equivalent, two-way definitions for nothing less than all of physics. It’s an enormous undertaking, to say the least.

Trained as an engineer, Carcassi fell into this line of work because he married a physicist, Christine Aidala at the University of Michigan, who had a lot of physics books lying around. Reading them puzzled him, particularly those on quantum mechanics. Whereas most people get hung up on the matter of which interpretation of quantum mechanics is correct – if and how a theory captures the objective physical reality of our world, or if there even is an objective reality – Carcassi found that every idea was missing something.

Why no one can agree on what quantum physics really means

“To me, all these [theories, such as quantum mechanics] are models, and I need to understand when they’re applicable and when not, essentially what they’re supposed to describe and under what assumptions,” he says. While he was grappling with this, the situation got worse. “I realised that we don’t really understand classical mechanics,” he says. This isn’t to say that classical mechanics doesn’t work, but that some of its theoretical ingredients are ill-defined, in Carcassi’s view.

As we talked, I was reminded of my advanced mechanics courses where I learned about objects called the “action” and “Hamiltonian”. They are incredibly useful, and I can define them loosely in English, saying something about an object’s preferred path through space or about its energy, but I’d be offering intuition that I got through homework problems more than mathematical rigor.

Carcassi says his experience was similar. “You know how to use them. You know their properties, but what exactly are they describing? You don’t know. I basically started reverse engineering a lot of these things.” This is just one example of the kind of definitional work reverse physics could offer.

“The tagline is to find a minimal set of physical assumptions from which we can rigorously re-derive the laws,” he says. Ideally, this would resolve many existing physics paradoxes and puzzles, such as the role of measurements in quantum physics where objects seem to acquire a fixed reality only after being observed. If we understood the maths underpinning those scenarios better, we could ascertain whether the world is fundamentally fuzzy or if a solid reality exists after all.

In the past 11 years, the Assumptions of Physics team, primarily consisting of Carcassi and Aidala, has broken down essentially all of classical physics into a set of mathematical equivalencies that allow the researchers to run over that bridge between maths and physics in either direction. Notably, entropy – which quantifies whether a physical system must assume one very precisely ordered state, or can find itself in many more equally likely states – has emerged as a key player in their effort.

For instance, they have shown that restricting any change in the entropy of a system is equivalent to previously known rules for how such a system can evolve over time. Reverse physics has already illuminated connections between quantum and classical physics – according to the team’s list of mathematical concepts and assumptions that undergird all of physics, it seems that classical physics is akin to quantum physics, but with entropy made high.

Quantum theory is challenging long-standing ideas about entropy

Carcassi is currently working on a slew of quantum problems, and candidly notes that it will be difficult to tackle various features of quantum field theory (QFT), where quantum fields extend through all of space and infinitely large numbers are known to crop up. One of the central objects that physicists use for QFT computations – for instance, to predict outcomes of particle accelerator experiments – is the “path integral”, which even professors who teach it often admit is an poorly defined headache for mathematicians. I’ve personally been fascinated by this enough to have devoted to a chapter to the path integral in my book.

But Carcassi’s quantum hopes soar higher: he thinks reverse physics could help researchers marry quantum physics and Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity by providing sufficient clarity on how both can be built from a shared mathematical base. “How can we even proceed and try to get new theories of physics, if we don’t even understand exactly what we have in the current one,” says Carcassi. The quest for a theory of quantum gravity has been one of physics’ biggest and least fruitful efforts for decades, which makes any new approach welcome.

Intriguingly, the way reverse physics could interweave these two pillars is indifferent to many of the common quantum fights among physicists. Carcassi and his collaborators aren’t interested in whether the equations of quantum theory imply that we live in the multiverse or that, for example, everything in the cosmos is inextricably connected with everything else. They are interested in the commonalities between every possible mathematical framework for quantum physics, and whether any resultant theory that encompasses them all makes sense with how we can measure and observe the universe.

Trying to redo all of physics from the ground up in this manner isn’t for the faint of heart. But what intimidates Carcassi is mostly the lack of funding and broad interest into this type of nitty-gritty work in physics’ very foundations. With appropriate funding and a big enough team, the reverse physics programme could be completed within a decade, he says. It brings to mind a story from my college years.

Once, during office hours, I told a physics professor about all the maths courses I was taking in the hope that they’d make me a better physicist. “I just know there will be a moment when all the maths and physics come together, and I finally get it all,” I said. The professor chuckled. He said he’d been waiting for that moment for his whole career. I hope the wait will soon be over.

The 12 strangest science stories we can’t stop thinking about

New Scientist October 30, 2026

There are some stories that stay with you forever, the big scientific moments that change the course of history. These are not those moments – but we can’t stop thinking about them anyway.

Surgeon Stuart Meloy was performing a pain-relief operation on a woman’s spine when she started exclaiming emphatically. “You’re going to have to teach my husband to do that,” the woman said. This inspired Meloy to invent an implant to help women who are unable to achieve orgasms in the usual way. New Scientist broke the news in 2001, sparking a frenzy of worldwide media excitement. But 13 years later, Meloy was still struggling to raise funds for a full clinical trial, and the “orgasmatron” never reached a climax.

We aren’t the only primates capable of coming up with creative ways to pleasure ourselves. In a study of long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in Bali, Indonesia, Camilla Cenni at the University of Lethbridge in Alberta, Canada, and her colleagues filmed hundreds of examples of male and female monkeys using stone tools as sex toys, rubbing or tapping them on their genitals. According to Cyril Grueter at the University of Western Australia, the Balinese monkeys get plenty of food handouts from humans, and this frees up time for sexual experimentation. But some monkeys in other places have unusual kinks, too: another study reported a wild macaque in Japan rubbing its genitals on the back of a sika deer.

Advertisement

In 2015, surgeon Sergio Canavero announced plans to carry out the first human head transplant, intended to extend the lives of people with muscle and nerve degeneration or widespread cancer. He claimed his technique could overcome technical hurdles, including how to fuse the spinal cord and prevent the body’s immune system from rejecting the head. In the following two years, Canavero published animal experiments supposedly backing up his methods, but other surgeons remained highly sceptical. A human head transplant never did happen, but Canavero has reportedly moved on to an even bolder ambition: transplanting a brain into a non-sentient clone.

Have you ever wondered if a rat can drive a car? Kelly Lambert at the University of Richmond in Virginia has. She and her colleagues built a tiny car with three copper bars that would steer it left, forward or right. Sure enough, 18 rats learned to drive towards food rewards. They even found it relaxing, as measurements of their stress hormones indicated. Lambert proposed that driving challenges could replace traditional maze tests when using rat models to study neuropsychiatric conditions.

Humans are more similar to rats than we like to think. In a psychology experiment, Noam Sobel and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, surreptitiously filmed 153 volunteers. After shaking hands with someone of the same sex, people smelled their shaking hand more than twice as much as they did before the handshake. Puzzlingly, after shaking hands with someone of the opposite sex, people were more likely to sniff their non-shaking hand. The team suspected that humans use chemical signals all the time without being aware of it.

Communication through scent is, of course, widespread in mammals, but some never-before-seen behaviour in dolphins took biologists by surprise in 2025. While studying Amazon river dolphins (Inia geoffrensis), or botos, in Brazil, Claryana Araújo-Wang at CetAsia Research Group in Ontario, Canada, saw a male “flip his belly up out of the water, expose his penis and then proceed to urinate into the air”, she told New Scientist. They saw dolphins do this a total of 36 times, and most of the time another male was nearby and would pursue the stream of urine. The purpose of this behaviour hasn’t yet been established, but hormones in urine might signal a male’s social position or physical condition, said Araújo-Wang.

Orcas have begun wearing salmon hats again – and we may soon know why

As for human modes of communication, many of us struggle to put our smartphones down – so the last thing we’d want is for them to crawl across the table towards us. Nevertheless, Marc Teyssier at the University of Paris-Saclay in France and his colleagues gave phones this ability in 2018, with a robotic appendage dubbed the MobiLimb. It plugs into a device’s USB port and, for some reason, looks eerily like a human finger, giving it a spooky quality reminiscent of Thing from The Addams Family. The MobiLimb can stroke your wrist, wave, wag like a tail or, most disconcertingly, drag the phone around. Thankfully, the idea hasn’t taken off.

If you find the thought of a phone with a finger horrifying, wait until you hear about the nightmare-inducing hairy frog Trichobatrachus robustus. In 2008, researchers reported that these frogs can break their own bones to produce claws that burst through their skin. David Blackburn at Harvard University’s Museum of Comparative Zoology thought these weapons were for defence, but two years later, another team argued that they were used in fights between males – and that the frog’s unusual hairs were a kind of armour to protect its vulnerable parts from sharp claws.

In 1957, when New Scientist was 1 year old, we reported on a new method for shrinking an adult human body to the size of a baby. At an exhibition of inventors in Winnipeg, Canada, the unnamed inventor of this process claimed it would make disposing of dead bodies simpler, as they could be slid into underground tubes and take up less space. The method involved applying high pressure to the corpse and squeezing out fluids so its flesh could be compressed into a mould. “All this is, of course, highly ingenious but it is uncertain why the inventor thinks that his newly proposed form of burial is in any way better than the current and very popular method of cremation,” the writer mused.

The brain has its own microbiome. Here’s what it means for your health

We may take it for granted, but the anus, which allows food to pass through the body, was an evolutionary breakthrough, both figuratively and literally. The earliest animals, like jellyfish today, had only one gut opening, where food went in and waste came out. In 2019, scientists discovered that the warty comb jelly (Mnemiopsis leidyi, pictured top) forms an anal opening when it needs to defecate, but it vanishes straight afterwards. This, they suggested, could represent how the anus evolved in the first place.

Flatus – gas expelled from the anus – has been a topic of endless fascination for many readers (and journalists). In 2001, we featured the work of Michael Levitt at the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Minneapolis, a leading authority on the subject. He developed a “Toot Trapper” that reduces odours by trapping certain gases using activated charcoal. We also reported on a device for monitoring gas emissions from dogs, used to test dog snacks that were supposed to reduce flatulence. In 2016, researchers in Australia worked out which foods cause the smelliest farts by mixing faeces with different foods. They recommended eating less protein and more slow-release carbohydrates to minimise hydrogen sulphide production. In 2022, Nagarajan Kannan at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and his colleagues worked out that some poos float because of gas from gut microbes, confirming a hypothesis first put forward by Levitt 50 years earlier.

Even stranger things go on inside some people’s intestines, as we found out in 2019. A 46-year-old man started experiencing unexplained mental fogginess, dizziness and memory loss, and had to give up his job. Later, doctors found high levels of alcohol in his blood when he hadn’t been drinking. Eventually, they realised his gut contained high levels of Saccharomyces cerevisiae – brewer’s yeast – which got him drunk any time he ate a lot of carbohydrates. This rare condition, known as auto brewery syndrome, had been triggered when the man took antibiotics for a thumb injury, which disrupted his gut microbiome. This year, a study reported that another man with this condition fully recovered after getting a transplant of faeces from a healthy donor. Both articles were written by Alice Klein, who we also have to thank for the monkey sex toys, car-driving rats, smelly farts and floating poos. Thanks, Alice!

Election 2026 live updates: Luxon accused of misleading the public on vote splitting tactics

New Zealand Herald November 01, 2026

National Party leader Christopher Luxon speaks to the media. Photo / Michael Craig

Which MPs will likely be out of a job based on polling analysis? The careers on the line this election.

Speaking to media at a campaign stop in Auckland, National Party leader Christopher Luxon addressed a poll this morning that revealed voters back Labour over National on almost every major issue.

Labour has gained ground on several key matters, including increasing its lead over National on the issue of inflation.

The Ipsos Issues Monitor showed that of the top 20 issues to voters, National is ranked ahead of Labour on just one, “crime/law and order”, which is the ninth-most-important issue overall.

“There's a range of polls, you see it in any given week saying a lot of different things, what I'm interested in is the data,” the National leader said, flanked by finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis and Tāmaki candidate Mahesh Muralidhar.

He pointed to increased economic growth, manufacturing, tourism, and export figures, saying kiwis are staring to feel the benefits.

“That is the future that we have ahead of us and it's a pretty exciting future,” he said.

Questioned further on the poll, Luxon said he won’t get “bounced by polls and reckons and commentators, I very much drive things off a fact-base and I look at those [economic] numbers regularly”.

Asked to respond to the numbers that showed people think Labour is better placed to manage key issues, including the economy, Luxon took aim at the opposition party’s economic track record.

“It's a Labour Party that increased spending by 70%, it's a Labour Party that drove inflation to a 32 year high, it's a Labour Party that took interest rates up 12 times, it's a Labour Party that slowed down a New Zealand economy and people lost their jobs because of that mismanagement,” the National leader said.

The country's unemployment rate is expected to fall for the first time in five years in numbers released this Wednesday. It currently sits at 5.6%.

National’s finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis told Ryan Bridge TODAY the outlook was positive.

“The Treasury are confidently forecasting that we’re not creating more jobs than the workforce is growing by.

“We’re now growing faster than Australia and many countries we like to compare ourselves with.”

She said it had been a difficult five years post-Covid.

“We had elevated inflation, an interest rate spiral, a global tariff war, a global oil shock and despite that, this little economy is now so strong.

“We’re looking at an outlook in which international economists are saying, ‘New Zealand is the economy to watch’ we can’t take that for granted.”

Former Prime Minister and Labour leader Dame Jacinda Ardern did a speech on politics at the Sydney Opera House yesterday.

She talked about rebuilding trust by “rebuilding financial security”.

“It would have been nice if she hadn’t tripled the country’s debt, left us with an interest servicing bill of more than $9 billion … ” Willis said.

“She’s right we should focus on financial security. It’s a shame she didn’t do that while she had the chance.”

Appearing on Newtalk ZB's Leaders Breakfast, National Party leader Christopher Luxon was asked whether his leadership was to blame for National's low polling.

"Oh look, I take responsibility as a leader," Luxon said.

"I'm not a career politician, I don't think I've always got every media soundbite perfect.

"We've had a Prime Minister who did media soundbites beautifully and actually we got no delivery, and I don't think I'm there for that reason, I actually think I'm there to actually get the best out of my team, make sure I'm delivering, moving the show forward," he said.

Asked by Hosking whether he thought he was improving, Luxon said "I think I'm getting better".

“There's no doubt about it ... it's been a challenging time for the country and for the cycle that we're in.

“I'm doing a deep turnaround job and that's difficult, and it's hard, and not everybody's on board with that,” the National leader said.

“So why did they try to roll you twice?” Hosking asked, referring to the two confidence votes held within the National Party on Luxon’s leadership in April and August this year.

Luxon would not discuss what issues his MPs took with his leadership, saying “what happens in caucus stays in caucus”.

“I came into a National Party after a second worst result in 2020 I dealt with a situation where I had to bring a party together that had factionalised terribly, and those things, if they're left to fester and to go places, it's not a good place, and disunity's death in politics.”

Hosking put to Luxon a rumour that suggests he could be rolled as leader if on the numbers, National needed to work with Opportunity Party in order to form a Government after election day, which Luxon dismissed as a conspiracy theory.

“I've just dealt with ever since I came into politics endless conspiracy theories and thoughts about all sorts of things. So my job is just to truck on through and make sure I'm delivering.”

Act leader David Seymour says his party agreed to the vote-splitting ads because it would not want to stand in the way of encouraging people to give their vote to Act.

Ads recently appeared in the Herald, written in the name of Don Brash, the former National and Act leader, encouraging people to give their party vote to NZ First and Act.

Asked about the ads on Ryan Bridge TODAY, Seymour said the campaign was going to be run regardless of the party's approval.

"They needed our permission to mention party vote Act, and if somebody wants to go out and spend their money this week encouraging people to give their party vote to Act to re-elect the coalition, then we're not going to stand in their way doing that. But the rest of it, we have our own message."

Seymour said he believes people's electorate vote should go to the person they believe will best represent the community, and party vote to the party which represents their values.

"Our message is very clear. The voter is in charge, you have two votes, and you should be using your vote as you see fit.

"When it comes to an electorate, my advice no matter where you are from Cape Rēinga to the Bluff is vote for the person who answers your call on a Friday afternoon because local communities do actually deserve a person that will advocate for them. I don't believe that electorates are just there to be used as some sort of strategy. Strategy is something, but it's not everything."

National is fighting back on Don Brash’s claims not voting two ticks blue will help keep a centre-right government.

He is pledging to National voters that if they instead vote Act and NZ First, it will “mathematically” help in an overhang.

National’s finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis told Ryan Bridge TODAY he was making assumptions.

“What he’s presuming is that it’s a foregone conclusion that National doesn’t win enough party votes to return list MPs.

“It's not a foregone conclusion. Actually, we have everything to play for.”

Willis described the idea as “defeatist”.

Brash earlier told Ryan Bridge that Christopher Luxon was "misleading the public" when he told people split voting was damaging.

“His accusations that what we’re doing is damaging centre-right is simply incorrect," Brash said.

“Mathematically it’s incorrect and if he doesn’t know that I’m astonished its blatantly obvious.

“He’s simply wrong and he’s misleading the public.”

Speaking to Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking, National Party leader Christopher Luxon was asked questioned the role of the Waitangi Tribunal.

"Why do you continue to fund this when you at best ignore what they do," Hosking asked.

The National leader said the tribunal was a "long-standing feature" of New Zealand's Government, but said the country had to "ask the question of what's the role of the Waitangi Tribunal ... [it] could be no role, could be evolved role, adjusted role," he said.

Put to him that his Government had stalled on the issue, Luxon defended his record on Māori and treaty issues saying it had "sort[ed] through" things like disbanding the Māori Health Authority, ending co-governance of public services, and "put[ting] English into Government agency departments."

Of the tribunal, Luxon said there is "certainly going to be a plan to change it in some form or another" if re-elected.

"Whether it's gone could be an option," he said.

Both Act and NZ First want to disband the tribunal once all remaining historical Treaty claims are settled, but Luxon said the parties have not yet had a conversation with National over a plan.

"I appreciate those parties may have their views about that, what we all agreed is that there's got to be a question about what the role is, actually to be questioning the role is something we're all committed around doing.

"It could be that it gets disbanded, it could be that actually there's a different orientation or a different role for it, I don't know, but I want to look at that and go through that sensibly."

Country Life: Makahuri – from former boarding school to village

New Zealand Herald November 01, 2026

Drew Mackenzie in the former chapel at Makahuri. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By Sally Round of RNZ

A decade after Drew Mackenzie and Anthony Ryan bought a derelict Catholic convent on the Kāpiti Coast, a village is taking shape.

The sign on the gate says, “people and dogs running free”, but the project has not been without struggles.

Makahuri, in Te Horo, was once Marycrest, a boarding school for girls which closed in the early 1980s, leaving classrooms, a chapel, paddocks and dormitories to the pigeons and vandals until, in 2016, its new owners came along.

With people seeking accommodation and keen on a village lifestyle, the couple decided to invite others in, turning the buildings into homes and shared spaces, an idea developed in Denmark in the 1960s.

“If I could see this 10 years ago, would I have done it? I probably would have, you know, for all its battles,” Mackenzie told RNZ’s Country Life.

She said it had been a protracted process navigating regulations and council requirements.

“We kept trying to say we’re not a subdivision, that’s not what we’re about.”

The 14.6ha property at Te Horo, south of Ōtaki, includes a hotch-potch of former school buildings and a homestead, where Mackenzie and Ryan live, plus an ancient stand of native forest and paddocks which are being planted as part of the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project.

The buildings had lain empty for seven years before the couple and their family moved in.

“We’ve replaced, we think, probably around 2000 windows since we got here,” Mackenzie said.

“Most of the windows were broken. People have been coming in, ripping out the nice native timbers.”

Work is ongoing as consents allow and residents include students, retirees, fulltime workers and families, aged from under a year to 90.

The aim is to have about 14 households either buying their apartments under a body corporate system or renting, Mackenzie said.

“Makahuri is a sustainable, safe, creative and harmonious co-housing community. It is a place of beauty where the mauri, forest, land, people and animals are honoured and respected by all,” its vision statement reads.

“People often have asked if we’re a commune, which we’re so not, and even ‘community’ has a connotation that you’re living in each other’s pockets, and we don’t do that. We are a village,” Mackenzie said.

“I think of villages of old, and how they just lived in an area together, and they knew each other and supported each other, and they didn’t necessarily even get on all the time, but they had each other’s backs regardless, and that’s us, that’s how we are. We’re a village.”

Berylla Jones moved in during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020.

She grew up on a farm and liked the idea of being in the country as well as village-style living.

“There’s a diversity of people, so there’s a diversity of ideas,” she said.

“There’s like support around if you need support.

“When my partner died during Covid, it was really lovely to have villagers here to, you know, be here supporting.”

Jones’ quilts adorn the walls of the former chapel now used for community events, exercise classes and meetings.

Residents pay a co-housing fee to run the vegetable garden.

They pay for wheelbarrows of wood collected from the property as well as eggs from the chickens looked after by Makahuri’s oldest resident.

“We have our own recycling station, and John manages that. Anything you want fixed, you can take it to John.

“So, if you break a shovel handle, you just take it to John. He fixes it for you.

“And his wife, Blossom, who’s 82, I think, she just feeds everybody, and she’s a fabulous gardener.

“She’s one of our wise people of the village.”

Mackenzie said Makahuri had experienced significant tensions and difficult periods but has treated each problem as an opportunity to improve its clarity and processes.

“We’ve never got to the point that we looked like we were going to fall over, but there have been times when there have been huge issues going on.

“But every one of them we’ve learnt from; every one of them we thought it’s because we weren’t clear or we didn’t have a process, and so with every point of tension we develop better as human beings and as a village.”

Prospective residents were encouraged to join a working bee, Friday morning “café” or one of the other activities at Makahuri “to listen how we react to each other and understand more, not only the kaupapa, but also the whakapapa”.

Western Bay of Plenty officer-issued speeding offences surge 525% from 2021 to 2025

New Zealand Herald November 01, 2026

New police data shows a sharp increase in speeding offences across the Western Bay of Plenty.

Speeding offences across Western Bay of Plenty have surged more than fivefold in four years, according to recently released police data.

The figures show police officers issued 16,579 speeding infringements in 2025, up from 2652 in 2021, a rise of 525%.

Offences increased 40% between 2024 and 2025, climbing from 11,820 to 16,579.

Road policing district manager Inspector Brendon Keenan said the increase reflected a combination of population growth, changing driver behaviour and increased enforcement activity.

Stats NZ’s 2023 Census recorded an 8.3% increase in the Bay of Plenty’s usually resident population between 2018 and 2023.

Keenan said speed remained a major focus for police, particularly on rural and semi-rural roads and in locations with a history of crashes.

“It’s important to be targeting where the accidents are, but also where 80km/h posted speed limits are, because we’re seeing that people might be creeping well above the 80.”

He said police were also placing greater emphasis on drivers travelling less than 11km/h over the speed limit because even small increases in speed could significantly worsen crash outcomes.

“If there’s going to be a crash and the speed is greater, it’s always going to be a lot worse.

“What might have been a serious crash can become a fatality, and what could have been minor can result in injury.”

Police can issue fines ranging from $30 for speeds up to 10km/h above the limit to $630 for speeds between 46km/h and 50km/h over.

Drivers also receive between 10 and 50 demerit points depending on the offence. A total of 100 points within two years results in a three-month licence suspension.

Motorists caught travelling more than 40km/h over the limit can face an immediate 28-day suspension, while those exceeding 50km/h over may face careless, dangerous or reckless driving charges.

Keenan said speed was one of the four key risk factors identified in the police RIDS approach, alongside restraints, impairment and distraction.

With summer approaching, he said increasing traffic volumes heightened the risks.

“Over those summer periods, people are out and about more, people are on holiday more, especially out with families. It’s also a season when we see drink-driving and impairment.

“So you combine that with speed, then it’s going to be particularly more serious as well.”

Separate figures from the same police data set show mobile speed camera infringements in Western Bay nearly tripled between 2021 and 2024, rising from 8967 to 25,402. The largest increase occurred between 2022 and 2023, when infringements almost doubled from 9275 to 18,288. They rose a further 39% in 2024.

Mobile camera infringements totalled 3836 between January and June 2025, before responsibility for speed camera enforcement transferred from police to NZ Transport Agency.

As reported by RNZ in 2022, police lowered the activation threshold for fixed and mobile speed cameras, meaning more motorists were detected travelling only slightly above the speed limit. Police said the change was intended to improve road safety and resulted in a higher proportion of lower-level speeding infringements carrying smaller fines.

Students Against Dangerous Driving general manager Donna Govorko said the figures alone could not determine whether speeding had become more common, as enforcement levels, traffic volumes and police deployment could all influence offence numbers.

The organisation works with young people to help them understand road risks, make safer choices and speak up when they feel unsafe as passengers.

She said speeding remained a concern, particularly for young drivers who were still developing their experience and judgment.

“Speed leaves less time to recognise a hazard and respond, increases stopping distance, and makes the consequences of a crash more severe.

“We need to challenge the idea that travelling a little over the limit is harmless or that arriving sooner is worth the risk.”

New Zealand director of road safety charity Brake, Caroline Perry, said it was frustrating that people continued to risk their own lives and the lives of others by speeding.

“Whether or not speed is a factor in the cause of a crash, it’s a factor in determining the outcome.

“The higher the speed, the more likely it is that someone will be killed or seriously injured in a crash.”

Perry said enforcement was crucial for penalising offending drivers and discouraging others from speeding.

She called for speed limits that better reflected road conditions and an increase in speed cameras, reminding motorists that a speed limit was “a limit, not a target”.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post.

Disputes Tribunal’s release of murder victim’s address ‘significant factor’ in couple’s killings

New Zealand Herald November 01, 2026

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong were killed 2023. Photo / NZ Police

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

A police review has found the Disputes Tribunal’s release of a murder victim’s address against his wishes was a “significant factor” in the subsequent killing of him and his wife.

It also found police could have “possibly prevented the homicide” if they had acted on information one of the killers provided about a separate murder plot two months earlier.

In September, Lok Fung Lorrence Li was found guilty of murdering Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in 2023. He was also found guilty of plotting to murder his former landlord.

Li’s co-defendant, Shu Man Poon, earlier pleaded guilty to the charges.

During the trial, the jury heard Li obtained Kwok’s address from the Disputes Tribunal.

They also heard about an incident where Poon went to police and told them he was being pressured to take part in the murder of Li’s former landlord to clear a debt.

Police earlier said an internal review was done following the murders.

The review by Detective Senior Sergeant Craig Johnson, obtained by RNZ under the Official Information Act, examines both the disclosure by the Disputes Tribunal and Poon’s visit to police.

Li went to the Auckland City Police Hub public counter on December 30, 2022, to report a crash he had been involved in.

A Traffic Crash Report (TCR) taken by a police officer noted the driver of the other vehicle refused to give his details to Li. The identity of the driver was therefore unknown; however, it was thought likely to be the registered owner of the vehicle (Kwok), given Li’s description.

Li also told police he was uninsured.

The TCR said no further action was required.

Then, on January 4, 2023, AA Insurance emailed Auckland Police requesting the TCR on behalf of their client, Kwok.

Police released a redacted TCR to AA Insurance on January 7. The report redacted Li’s middle names, the details of his passenger and other information about him.

It did not redact any details in relation to Kwok, such as his address, phone number and email.

Johnson said AA Insurance then “entered into discussions” with Li in relation to the crash.

“The matter has been unresolved, and AA have sought resolution via the Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal.”

The matter was set down for a hearing on November 29, 2023.

As part of the process, AA Insurance asked Kwok if he had any security concerns regarding his personal details being disclosed to Li.

“He responded, ‘I have no objection to disclose my personal information if necessary but rather not having my address disclosed to the other driver as I never attempted to obtain his’,” Johnson said.

AA Insurance then referred the matter to the tribunal.

“Of note, AA deleted both Kwok and Li’s personal details including addresses from the TCR supplied by police. In the application, AA Insurance expressed Kwok’s request his address not be disclosed.”

The Disputes Tribunal application coversheet also noted confidential details were requested by Kwok, Johnson said.

“This has been noted as declined, stamped by Deputy Registrar [redacted],” he said.

“The comment recorded is ‘(A)’s request for confidentiality has been declined due to insufficient safety reasons’.”

Disputes Tribunal correspondence with both parties listed their home address.

The review said that in Poon’s interview with police, he referenced the address being provided to Li.

“Then at that time Lorrence (Li) was also laughing, he was laughing at the court being so stupid, why the court even showed the address [to] me.

“He told me for the first time that how about just getting rid of this guy, then I don’t need to appear in court.”

Johnson said it appeared the disclosure of Kwok’s address to Li “has been a significant factor in Li and Poon’s preparations for the murders”.

He said he was aware that the officer in charge of the police investigation, Detective Inspector Scott Beard, had spoken with the Ministry of Justice, “who are aware of the potential implications of this”.

About 11pm on September 3, 2023, Poon went to the public counter at the Auckland City Police Hub. He was accompanied by two support people.

Poon was primarily dealt with by frontline station support officer Simran Chadha, Johnson said.

“Poon disclosed he was being forced to clear a debt owing by helping to kill the two landlords of [redacted].

“He named Li as the person involved, and that the offence was planned for overnight 5-6/09/23.”

The motive was to “obtain cash flow cards and money”, the review said.

While at the station, Poon appeared to be in “increasing psychological distress”, and was crying in pain and clutching his head and said he wanted to kill himself.

The review said mental health and an ambulance were called. However, due to delay, it was agreed with Poon and his associates that they would travel to Auckland Hospital for treatment themselves, and they left the station.

Chadha sought advice from a police officer who advised her to report it, which she did, linking Li, Poon and other information to the file.

The file was automatically assigned to Northern Region 105. Chadha then immediately reassigned the file to herself and five hours later to her supervisor.

A staff member, whose name is redacted but is referred to as frontline station support team leader, was on leave at the time.

When she returned to work on September 9, she reviewed the file and electronically filed it.

The file was later identified during the initial stages of the homicide investigation.

Johnson said there were several matters of concern regarding Poon’s visit.

“Murder (in this case a conspiracy to murder) is arguably the most serious offence investigated by police. The disclosure of this information by Poon was correctly escalated by Chadha to an inquiry with CIB.

“However, clarity on what was intended by the direction given was either not expressed or not adequately recorded.”

A file relating to the planning of a murder “warranted further investigation”, he said.

“Poon’s account was credible, and he was able to provide accurate details of the other party and the location. These were verified in NIA (National Intelligence Application) when the matter was recorded.

“The fact that the collection of information was cut short by Poon’s mental/physical health concerns should have also raised the possibility that further corroborating evidence may be available.”

He said police should have gone back to him to obtain further information.

Police had “missed an opportunity to investigate the matter further”, Johnson said.

“Critically, had police acted on the original information presented by Poon in September 2023, it could have alerted police to and possibly prevented the homicide.”

Detective Inspector Scott Beard earlier told RNZ an internal review was done and several requirements were initiated for front-counter staff handling reports of serious or potential crime.

“When dealing with information that relates to violence or threat to property, this will immediately be assigned to the appropriate Criminal Investigation Branch team.

“There is also a requirement for front-counter staff to obtain the name of the person from the CIB they are speaking to so they can be identified moving forward.”

In response to questions from RNZ, Ministry of Justice chief operating officer Carl Crafar said the ministry acknowledged the “tragic sequence of events” that led to Kwok and Chong’s murders.

Since the tribunal was established, contact details including names and addresses had “routinely” been shared between parties involved in disputes.

Kwok’s request for confidentiality was not granted as it did not meet the threshold under the Disputes Tribunal Rules, Crafar said.

“Specifically, he did not raise any safety concerns and the statutory threshold was not met.”

In February 2024, the Chief District Court Judge wrote to the Secretary for Justice and invited him to review the claim form and consider whether applicants should continue to be required to provide a residential address, particularly where another means of contact was available, Crafar said.

The Secretary for Justice, in consultation with the Principal Disputes Tribunal Referee, has responsibility for the contents of Disputes Tribunal forms.

“As a direct result of this case, changes have been made to how personal information is shared. Physical and postal addresses are now kept confidential and are not shared with other parties. Only email addresses and telephone numbers are shared between parties.”

Asked whether the ministry stood by the decision to decline Kwok’s request for confidentiality, Crafar said it was a tribunal decision, which the ministry could not comment on.

He also said it would be “inappropriate” for the Ministry of Justice to comment on whether the ministry accepted the findings in the police review that the disclosure of Kwok’s address was a significant factor in the preparations for the murders.

Rotorua Eastgate intersection gets $3.46m Government funding

New Zealand Herald November 01, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Rotorua has “jumped the line” and got funding for what the Government says will make a busy road safer and open up land for new business and local jobs.

A $3.46 million grant from the Regional Infrastructure Fund, announced today, will fund traffic lights at a four-way intersection at Rotorua’s Eastgate Business Park, near Rotorua Airport.

The intersection will be at the junction of State Highway 30 and Wahanga-A-Rangi Cres.

The money has come from a different pot after a funding standoff between Rotorua Lakes Council and NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA).

NZTA preferred a dual-laned roundabout estimated to cost $10m, while the council had a tender for a $3.2m four-way signalised intersection.

NZTA wouldn’t pay for it any time soon, saying there was not enough traffic in the area to justify the investment and the council was forced to look at funding its preferred option through debt at ratepayers’ cost.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said Rotorua had asked for the roading upgrade for about 10 years. Thanks to advocacy by the council and Rotorua MP Todd McClay to the Regional Infrastructure Fund, it was able to get the money quicker in a different way.

“We have been able to jump the line ... We are lucky this Government has backed us to do that, like we said for jobs and the economy but also, very importantly, safety,” Tapsell said.

McClay said State Highway 30 was the main route to Tauranga and its port.

“Trucks, locals and visitors use it every day and getting in and out at the airport is not always safe,” he said.

“Opening up land around the airport for business also means new jobs for Rotorua people, close to home.

McClay said land on both sides of the road was suitable for light commercial and retail, with the potential for shops and a future supermarket.

The MP said the council “owns a lot of land at the airport that isn’t being used well. Good access means they can develop it and get a rental or other return for ratepayers”.

McClay said Tauranga was New Zealand’s busiest port, and the land could attract businesses to Rotorua that wanted quick and easy access to export markets.

McClay said the project sat low on NZTA’s priority list and leaving Rotorua Lakes Council to foot the bill would have put an unreasonable financial burden on ratepayers.

He said the Government had funded five major road projects and now every entrance to the city was upgraded.

“People coming into our city, from all directions, now get a safer road. That’s taken a lot of work and our city is the better for it.”

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Transport Minister Chris Bishop made the funding announcement today.

Jones said safe, suitable access to Eastgate would support development at the site and future-proof the wider area for more growth.

“This investment reflects the Regional Infrastructure Fund’s focus on backing practical regional infrastructure that unlocks economic opportunities.”

Bishop said building one road intersection to serve both business parks was the most practical approach.

“It will serve existing businesses while providing for the airport business park as it develops,” Bishop said.

Rotorua Business Chamber chief executive Melanie Short said this was “very good news” for Rotorua as this type of infrastructure was “pivotal” to improving traffic flow and productivity.

“This will open up land and opportunities for future development and investment, which is what Rotorua needs to continue to grow. Well done to all parties involved in getting to this point – I know there have been a lot of discussions over many years and that perseverance has paid off.”

Rotorua Airport chief executive Nicole Brewer said she was “thrilled” with news that highway developments alongside the airport would receive funding sooner rather than later.

“The four-way intersection is a critical priority for the growth and development of the Eastside community, as well as future site development plans at the airport.

“Enabling infrastructure like this must come ahead of development, as it gives public and private developers certainty and confidence about future investment.

“The first stage of the airport’s site development was planned specifically around the fact we did not have certainty regarding the intersection. However, the intersection is a key priority for our wider site development programme.”

She said the airport master plan unlocked several economic and social benefits for the entire city, including opportunities for the local community, economy and iwi, including the creation of new jobs.

“For all of these reasons, this funding development is welcome and exciting for the airport and wider Rotorua.”

The project will be managed by Rotorua Lakes Council. Construction is expected to begin in the next few months, subject to final confirmation and contractors being secured.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

My suburb is split between grotty sharehouses and ritzy family homes. That’s its charm

Sydney Morning Herald November 02, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

Every afternoon at 4pm, at the St Lucia and Taringa roundabout, a man sits on his balcony and waves at everyone who passes by.

His name is Franky, and the restaurant beneath him, Franky’s, has been closed for as long as I’ve lived here. I’m not quite sure it ever opened. Still, every afternoon, there he is.

Franky is one of St Lucia’s colourful local celebrities, and the sight of him up on his porch with his afternoon drink is one I got to know well while living at Union College at the University of Queensland. Like most at college, I was not from Brisbane, and I picked St Lucia as my base camp for four years without knowing how grateful I’d be that I did.

Living and studying at UQ meant my whole world existed inside a one-kilometre radius. Everyone talks about the European walkable city as if it only exists in Paris or Berlin or Amsterdam. But I found it in a suburb built on hills, where the only thing standing between me and the gym was a steep walk home.

St Lucia’s two halves are easy to map. On one side, UQ and a few thousand 18-year-olds living away from home for the first time. On the other, the St Lucia Golf Links and the leafy green streets around it, where people golf, marry and settle into middle age. But even the fairways weren’t off limits to us: we held college balls at The Hillstone, ran along its paths, and took our first dates on picnics on its grass.

If St Lucia is a suburb consisting of two generations then Hawken Drive Village is where the two intersect. You have college kids buying cartons of Great Northern from Liquorland, and Ironside State School parents buying steak and macadamia milk from the IGA.

My first-ever job was at A Salt & Battery Fish & Chips, located in the “Ville”, as everyone called it. And one of my housemates had the shortest commute in Brisbane: a three-minute walk down the road where she opened Yonder Espresso at 5am. Her customers: all students on weekdays, and all families on weekends. Then the college kids go home for summer, and the suburb finally exhales. No more drunk, rowdy students ravenous for late-night kebabs from the institution that is Mr Deno Kebab & Pizza.

My second job was at Wordsmiths Cafe on the UQ campus. For three years I served coffee to students who couldn’t really afford a triple-shot coffee but needed one, then lecturers at lunch who could. By then, most of my social circle worked and lived in St Lucia. I knew the bartenders at the uni bar, The Redroom, and the baristas at If You Say So and Saint Lucy. I don’t think I ever paid full price for an oat cappuccino or a pint of Stone & Wood in those four years of my degree.

My suburb is a bubble you never had to leave. Then the 2022 floods made it an island.

At first, it felt like a snow day: classes were cancelled, and most of us stayed in, watching movies, playing games and drinking, waiting it out. The Munro Soccer Fields became a mini-lake with kayakers and stand-up paddleboarders floating gracefully over the goalposts.

With catering staff cut off by the floods, students stepped up to cook and serve dinner for all 300 of us. The menu was the same comforting college classic: frozen veggies steamed in bulk, and tray after tray of chicken parmis popped into the oven. The mood was closer to a party than a disaster.

But the bubble popped on Coleridge Street when we saw cars sitting underwater, and ground-floor neighbours who had lost everything. We joined the community clean-up, hosing out garages and salvaging belongings. I recall one elderly man whose garage was full of random memorabilia. His eyes went misty as we played with his old cowboy bullwhip; I think it had been years since anyone had.

Moving from Union College into my first sharehouse was a hungover blur. My three friends and I hauled our things onto Hawken Drive and into a spacious house with front and backyards, and a sunroom that became the centre of our lives. We ate, cooked and hosted parties, always coming and going through our weird blue and off-yellow kitchen.

The grotty sharehouses of 19 and 20-year-olds are only a few streets from people who’ve owned their homes for decades. We walked dogs, house-sat and cleaned for the wealthy families nearby. One mansion paid so well that all three of us went shoe shopping the next day.

Contributor

Two years into living in our sharehouse, we learnt our landlord was the family in the mansion next door. The two sides of the suburb that never seemed to meet had been neighbours the whole time.

And Franky? He’s still at the roundabout, every day at 4pm, with seemingly all the time in the world.

Families on the after-school pick-up wave to him. Then in the evenings, college kids cruise past in their Ubers on the way to Fortitude Valley. Some still stick a hand out the window to wave at Franky’s balcony, even though he’s long gone inside by then.

Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 20:31:30 GMT

Endorsement was met with backlash from the party, condemning Stevens for her ‘betrayal’

Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.

Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’s endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.

The endorsement was met with immediate pushback from Democrats, who condemned Stevens for her “betrayal”.

Neera Tanden, the former senior adviser to president Joe Biden, wrote on X: “Standing with Mike Rogers is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career. It’s also a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her. I hope Abdul El-Sayed has a strong victory on Tuesday and that all Democrats and like-minded independents support vote for him.”

Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said: “Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.”

Some of the people who worked for Stevens’s campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers endorsement. Her long-time chief of staff, Justin German, and her communications director, Logan Basch, were among those who left, according to CNN correspondent Manu Raju.

German later released a statement on behalf of Stevens’ campaign team endorsing El-Sayed: “As Haley Stevens’ Chief of staff for eight years, I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate. This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines. We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”

In his first public comments since Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, El-Sayed told reporters at a press conference outside of a rally he held on Sunday, the very same rally that Stevens had earlier been disinvited from attending, “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.” He added, “I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.

“If you are somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said.

But Stevens’s political pivot earned her praise from Donald Trump, someone whose policies she has an entire page on her website dedicated to denouncing.

“Wow, this is BIG! Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a Highly Respected Democrat, who narrowly lost in the Primary to Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed, and who has been breathlessly wined and dined by the Dumocrats to help in their Michigan Campaign for the United States Senate against Mike Rogers, has just ENDORSED Mike Rogers for Senate!” the president wrote.

Stevens had lost by a close margin in this year’s primary, and for months had refused to openly campaign for El-Sayed, as had his other opponent Mallory McMorrow. But top Democrats had brokered the truce between El-Sayed and Stevens. After the two had sparred viciously in the primary campaign Stevens extended him a tepid endorsement, and this weekend was scheduled to join El-Sayed at a predominantly Black church in Detroit’s North End.

Those plans have quickly unraveled over an issue that divided Stevens and El-Sayed perhaps more than any other: Israel.

Later last week, Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, made clear that her appearance alongside El-Sayed was preconditioned on his denouncing of an outside group’s campaign ad that had blamed US support of Israel for the rising cost of living. El-Sayed declined the request, accusing Stevens of needlessly reopening debates from a settled primary.

As the feud escalated, El-Sayed’s campaign went further, formally disinviting Stevens from his campaign events in the closing days of the campaign. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan congresswoman, later told CNN she had been the one to tell Stevens “this isn’t working” when it came to Stevens’s appearance with El-Sayed on Sunday. Dingell added that the tensions between the two were a distraction and that “there’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place”.

Earlier on Sunday Stevens had put out a statement that said she expected El-Sayed to win and telling people to vote. But just hours later she appeared with Donald Trump’s Senate pick and in one comment said she supported Rogers’s purported future investment in Black businesses.

As the vicious political firestorm has unfolded, Democratic commentators have also pointed out that Stevens’s fiance, Jason Turkish, has been condemning El-Sayed publicly while supporting Rogers. Turkish, who is also vocally pro-Israel, has donated heavily to Democrats in the past, but this year also donated to Republican candidates including Susan Collins.

On Sunday, Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats.

“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans. These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.”

WSL roundup: Arsenal stall despite Russo strike; Chelsea’s James suffers injury

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 20:17:13 GMT

Arsenal salvage late 1-1 draw at home against Aston Villa

Chelsea beat Charlton 6-0 but England ace goes off early

One shot, on target and in the back of the net, was all it took for Aston Villa to reopen the wound that Arsenal had been carefully trying to stitch back up.

Despite almost 65% possession, 28 shots to one, and 56 touches in the opposition box to four, Alessia Russo’s 85th-minute goal meant Arsenal were only able to salvage a point against Villa after back-to-back wins in the league and Champions League had appeared to have kickstarted their season.

The worst possible scenario for a team that has struggled against low blocks arrived in the 25th minute, when Lynn Wilms found Chasity Grant, who fired low into the bottom corner. It was a hammer blow to the home team, with Villa knowing exactly what to do next: stick 11 players behind the ball and frustrate the Gunners.

Russo’s late goal spared Arsenal’s blushes a little, the forward flicking a header in at the far post from a Stina Blackstenius cross, but the reprieve delivered by Arsenal’s victories over Tottenham and Benfica has been rolled back.

The Gunners have an incredibly tricky run of fixtures coming up, with Liverpool away followed by Barcelona, London City and then Lyonnes. And, despite the back-to-back wins, they haven’t been able to resolve the problems in the final third that have plagued every performance.

The pressure will be back on head coach Renée Slegers and there are questions to be asked about some decision making. However, with similar problems present under Joe Montemurro and Jonas Eidevall before her, maybe it’s time to look beyond the head coach.

Elsewhere Lauren James was forced off with an injury in the first half of Chelsea’s 6-0 win at Charlton. The England forward was replaced by Erin Cuthbert in the 35th minute with the away team 4-0 up. There were five different goalscorers with Melvine Malard getting two. The coach, Sonia Bompastor, said: “It is too soon [to know] about Lauren’s injury. I spoke to her at half-time and it seems to be her hamstring so we will have to have a proper assessment tomorrow.”

Tottenham climbed to fourth in the table after a comprehensive 4-1 win at Birmingham City. The Spurs midfielder Drew Spence set a new all-time WSL appearance record with 2017 to move one above the former Chelsea defender Millie Bright. West Ham were also 4-1 winners, over Liverpool, in their third league win of the season, leapfrogging their opponents in the table to move up to 10th.

Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 20:10:27 GMT

Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ

A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.

Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.

The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot, which Republicans fear could take away votes from the incumbent and influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.

The justice department said it planned to appeal Sunday’s ruling: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.

Sullivan, in an interview with CNN on Sunday morning, said that he would accept the results of his upcoming election.

According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Peltola’s campaign recruited another man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent.

Since those revelations, Republicans, including Donald Trump, have called for Peltola to be disqualified from the race and criminally prosecuted. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign, recently telling a reporter at a campaign event that she had “no idea” if any of her staff were involved.

Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won, Sullivan responded: “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”

Earlier in his interview with Tapper, Sullivan also said he wasn’t focused on how Peltola’s campaign might be legally challenged. He was focused instead on winning the race outright. He nonetheless expressed doubt that Peltola had lacked any knowledge of the effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

“She’s continually lying to the Alaskan people,” Sullivan said. “And I guarantee you, she’s lying right now.”

Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported that Republicans tried to boost unviable Democratic candidates in the Alaska primaries as well. A Republican Super Pac boosted two candidates for Senate who did not live in Alaska, and praised them as “progressives” similar to Bernie Sanders.

UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 19:50:39 GMT

British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda

British officials initially insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.

Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.

Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.

“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.

“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”

Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.

“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.

He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”

Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.

He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”

There was no immediate comment from the British government.

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.

On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.

Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.

Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.

“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
