Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.

“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”

Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.

Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.

The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.

As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.

King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.

On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.

“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.

Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 19:47:35 GMT

MPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandal

Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.

Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

The government’s response to the consultation on the reforms, which will be put before MPs on Monday, is expected give some exemption to care workers already in the UK, though most other professions will face the lengthy waits for settlement.

Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system” or if they were earning higher incomes.

She is expected to meet union general secretaries on Monday – some of whom have raised alarm at the changes – to map out the final details.

The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector. The Home Office has granted about 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.

Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to proposed exemptions and reductions.

In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.

In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

The Windrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.

In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.

Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.

They warn that proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.

The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conducted by Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.

The Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.

The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”

The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed” and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.

The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, like radiography.

It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”

Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”

Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 19:36:46 GMT

Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology

An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.

Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.

The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.

In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”

It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.

Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.

“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her.

“Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did … “My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”

The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.

The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.

Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation.

Arsenal hold on for first league win at Liverpool since 2012 after Kai Havertz pounces early

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 18:44:48 GMT

It was a game when Arsenal showed their ruthless side and all of the champion knowhow that they ­accumulated over the course of last season. They headed back to London ­having made a statement. Irrespective of what ­happens to ­Manchester City over their financial rule breaches, Arsenal remain the Premier League’s team to beat.

Mikel Arteta was in the Arsenal midfield when the club ­last won a league fixture at Anfield; it was in September 2012, although his memories are a little hazy given the concussion that he sustained in a collision with Jordan Henderson.

Arteta has a clear-eyed focus on retaining the title and this was an occasion for his hopes to surge. Kai Havertz’s first goal in 10 appearances proved the difference but the victory was rooted in Arsenal’s capacity to control and frustrate.

It was a tough watch for the Liverpool crowd and they bayed ­throughout at what they perceived as Arsenal’s use of the dark arts. Arteta’s team won 18 free-kicks and there were some soft ones – each was the prompt for an eruption from the Kop. It said plenty that Virgil van Dijk responded to the full-time whistle by sarcastically applauding the ­referee, Andy Madley. The Liverpool ­captain was booked.

The home team had their grie­vances. Alexander Isak felt Jurriën Timber grab a handful of his shirt in the 21st minute as he tried to reach a Bradley Barcola cross in front of goal. It was a mystery as to why the video assistant referee did not alert Madley. Van Dijk could also be heard shouting in the tunnel afterwards at Noni Madueke, saying the Arsenal winger should have had a second yellow card.

Madueke, who was booked for a foul on Barcola, took a risk when he initiated a touch of foreheads with Alexis Mac Allister towards the end after a melee had broken out. It was sparked by Mac Allister’s ­furious ­reaction to Martin Ødegaard’s ­winning of a free-kick. Liverpool, however, lost any claim to the moral high ground when Mac Allister ­crumpled to the turf in an attempt to get Madueke sent off. The Arsenal player survived. It would have been a harsh dismissal.

In the final analysis, Liverpool did not do enough. They provided high‑energy enjoyment in the first half but they fizzled out, the invention drying up. They ­finished with no shots on target as their five-match winning run in all competitions ground to a halt. Goals remain a problem for them in the league and the truth was ­Arsenal kept them out with a measure of comfort. Arsenal’s previous trip to the north‑west had ended in ­Carabao Cup humiliation at Fleetwood on Tuesday night. This was much more like it.

Liverpool brought the intensity at the outset with Trey Nyoni snapping into challenges on his full league debut. The 19-year-old’s first action was to leave something on Ødegaard and, not long after that, he did the same to Havertz. Nyoni was fortunate to emerge without a yellow card.

The tone was set early, the Kop teeming with indignation at what they saw as Arsenal’s readiness to go down easily and stay down. The match was shaped by Havertz’s goal on 16 minutes and from a Liverpool point of view, it was a self-inflicted wound. Alisson tried to be too cute with a short pass out from his area for Jérémy Jacquet; the weight and direction of it was wrong. But when ­Ødegaard pounced, a stunning piece of interplay followed. Arsenal worked it over and up the right for Declan Rice to flash over the final ball, low and across the corridor of a six-yard box of uncertainty. Havertz, a player who needed an easy tap-in, got one.

Liverpool responded with more fire and they could have scored before the interval, Mac Allister ­blowing the big chance – a free header from Milos Kerkez’s cross in the 43rd minute. Moments earlier, Florian Wirtz had whipped a free-kick from the left‑hand side against the crossbar.

Arsenal flickered on the break. There were a few times in the first half when they flooded men ­forward and there were possibilities. This was a long way from being a smash‑and‑grab. Havertz narrowly failed to get a touch to a Bruno ­­Guimarães cross-cum-shot while Timber could not react in front of goal after Madueke volleyed a Christos Tzolis cross back from an acute angle.

Arsenal had the match where they wanted it. They backed themselves to keep Liverpool at bay. It was about their game management. They have become masters at drawing the sting and the longer the second half went on the more assured Arsenal looked. They stifled Liverpool and there remained the sense they could land something on the counter.

When Jacquet slipped in the 68th minute, Arsenal went left to Tzolis and he almost teed up ­Ødegaard. With Alisson out of position, ­Jacquet got back to make an important intervention. Tzolis also forced an excellent save with a first‑time shot for the far corner. ­Liverpool fought a losing battle to keep a lid on their emotions. They huffed and they puffed. Juan Atkins, pioneer of Detroit techno sound, dies aged 64

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 18:31:22 GMT

US artist known as Model 500 and as one half of the duo Cybotron had huge influence on dance music worldwide

Juan Atkins, one of the pioneers of Detroit techno and a huge influence on dance music more widely, has died aged 64.

His agency, Greensmith Artists, confirmed the news to the dance music website Resident Advisor, saying Atkins had been found unresponsive in a hotel room in Mexico City prior to a performance there, and was pronounced dead after being taken to hospital.

Atkins created a gleaming, mechanistic form of electronic music, first as part of the duo Cybotron and then under the alias Model 500, that could command a dancefloor while also evoking sci-fi fantasias. He was the first person to use the term “techno” in tandem with this hard electronic style, pre-empting an entire genre that now stands as one of the pillars of dance culture.

Born in Detroit in 1962, Atkins later moved with his family to the rural Michigan suburb of Belleville. “I just wasn’t used to going to school on a yellow bus and living on a dirt road,” he told the Guardian in 2024. But it was here that he met Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, two junior high schoolmates with whom he formed the Belleville Three, a trio of like-minded musicians sitting at the vanguard of electronic music.

Still in high school and utilising increasingly affordable hardware such as the Roland TR-808 drum machine and the Korg MS-10 synthesiser, Atkins formed Cybotron with Richard Davis. “I had a class called future studies, about the transition from an industrial society to a technological society,” Atkins told the Guardian in 2014. “I just applied a lot of those principles to my music-making.”

Equally in thrall to Kraftwerk and Jimi Hendrix, Cybotron’s propulsive yet psychedelic tracks, such as Cosmic Cars and Clear, became dancefloor staples. The duo split​ in 1985, with Davis drawn more towards rock music. “I think that was where he wanted to be, in that album-orientated rock [scene],” Atkins later said.

Atkins went solo as Model 500, creating other foundational dance tracks such as No UFO’s and The Chase. In 1985, he also founded his own record label, Metroplex, to release his work. Over the years, it also put out material by artists including Anthony Shakir and DJ Bone.

Throughout​ the 1980s and beyond, Atkins evoked not just techno-utopian visions, but also more troubling and politicised ones. “I make social statements. My lyrics are supposed to make you think about something other than shaking your booty on the dancefloor and falling in love,” he told the Guardian in 2024.

By the early 1990s, the techno scene he helped inspire had flourished, and Atkins further finessed his sound with the uptempo project Infiniti later in the decade.

The 2000s were less productive in terms of releases, but he formed the duo Borderland with another techno icon, Moritz Von Oswald, releasing two albums in 2013 and 2016.

In 2023, Atkins reformed Cybotron, releasing new music and performing live. By this point, Atkins’s influence had extended far beyond techno, with dozens of artists sampling Clear alone. Missy Elliott made it the backbone of her track Lose Control, which reached No 3 on the US Billboard chart in 2005.

Saunderson was among those paying tribute to Atkins on Sunday, calling him “a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included”.

Should Premier League strugglers stick or twist as pressure on managers mounts?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 18:00:30 GMT

Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far away

No Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change.

The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away.

Michael Carrick remains the favourite to be the next manager to leave his post. He is unsurprisingly followed by the managers of the clubs who occupy the relegation zone: Pierre Sage of Crystal Palace, Sunderland’s Régis Le Bris and Oliver Glasner at Nottingham Forest. It seems almost inevitable that Carrick will leave soon so the more interesting analysis lies among the bottom three.

Sunderland sit 20th and are predicted by Opta to finish there. However, they have had a testing start to the season. Le Bris’s side have faced five of the current top seven clubs, the joint-most along with Liverpool. The manager also has enormous reserves of goodwill after taking the club back to the Premier League and then into Europe.

Despite their tough schedule, Sunderland came into the weekend within one expected point of Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham before losing 3-1 at Coventry with the xG count 1.8 to 0.7 in their favour. It was a familiar outcome for a side that has scored 6.2 goals fewer than expected this season.

With Sunderland’s next five league opponents being Chelsea, Aston Villa, Tottenham, Liverpool and Newcastle, the challenge of staying up will not immediately get easier. At least their chance‑converting woes are not as bad as those of Nottingham Forest.

Their shots have been worth 14.7 expected goals, the fourth most in the division after the matches on Saturday. But not once in a game this season have the goals they scored at least equalled their xG, let alone surpassed it. It is a finishing issue, not a question of opposition goalkeepers having super-human performances against them.

The analytical step above standard expected goals is xG on target (xGOT). It measures the likelihood of an on-target shot becoming a goal based on chance quality and shot placement. Forest’s xGOT this season is 7.4, little more than half of their expected goal tally.

This inability to test goalkeepers severely enough explains why Glasner’s men have scored just six times. They are squandering almost one goal per game on average according to their expected goals, a significant shortfall. None of the 96 teams in Europe’s big five leagues were worse than 0.5 goals per match below xG last season, which suggests Forest’s luck should turn for the better.

Is Evangelos Marinakis patient enough for that to happen? Forest’s expected goal data is much stronger for Glasner than it was under any of the four managers their owner fired last season. Whether he pays attention to such numbers is a different issue.

Glasner hinted at a physical deficiency in the squad after defeat at Brentford. “We are outrun by the opposition in every single game. We have to change it,” he said. Distance covered data from Fotmob suggests that is not quite the case, albeit Forest have been outrun in their past five league games. Both the underlying xG data and physical statistics are worse at Glasner’s former club Crystal Palace though.

As expected goals have a far greater bearing on future performance or results than running stats, those numbers are the greater concern. Equally, Palace’s average of 96.9 sprints per match is the fewest in the Premier League (after Saturday’s matches).

The club have been through similar teething troubles with new managers before. Palace’s previous two appointments that occurred between seasons were Frank de Boer and Patrick Vieira. The former was sacked after only five matches in all competitions in 2017, the latter won just one of his first nine league games four years later before recovering to finish 12th.

While Palace are a little wasteful in attack, they have not been as bad as Forest or Sunderland. Their defence is a much bigger problem, which is unusual as Sage’s Lens conceded the fourth fewest expected goals in Ligue 1 last season. Palace are second worst for that metric in the Premier League in 2026‑27, rock bottom if penalties are excluded. Some of that may be down to starting seven combinations of players in the back three because of injuries and Axel Disasi’s three‑match ban, but it is imperative that a manager overcomes such inevitable difficulties.

Palace host Liverpool next weekend. They return after the international break with potentially winnable games against Coventry and Hull. Will those fixtures represent a good opportunity for Sage to kickstart his reign or an excellent chance for his replacement to hit the ground running? Only the chair, Steve Parish, will know the answer but Palace are the strugglers who look most in need of managerial change.

How Rachel Reeves has mapped out economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 17:47:42 GMT

On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her

Reeves says UK’s future is in the EU

Which senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”

It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, in a lecture six months ago.

Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.

A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until after John Healey’s first budget.

She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.

The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.

“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.

The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion under Keir Starmer.

Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.

Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.

It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”

Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.

Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.

That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.

But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.

That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.

The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.

“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.

She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.

Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.

There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.

Police have said they arrested 325 people on Saturday at a demonstration outside the US embassy in London against the proscription of Palestine Action.

The arrests came ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on Palestine Action – the first direct action group to be proscribed under the Terrorism Act – which came into effect on 5 July last year.

Defend Our Juries, which has organised the mass civil disobedience campaign against proscription, said Saturday’s detentions took the total number of people arrested for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since the ban to 4,200. Most arrests have been for holding placards reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

The overall number of detentions will probably feature in the hearing before the UK’s highest court, which was granted on the basis that it was arguable that the ban represents a disproportionate interference with the rights of freedom of speech and protest.

However, neither the high court, which ruled that the ban was unlawful, nor the court of appeal, which overturned the high court’s decision, gave much weight to the fate of the placard-holders.

About 2,500 of those arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action have been charged under the Terrorism Act but all trials have been postponed pending a definitive decision on whether or not the ban was lawful.

Saturday’s demonstrations – there was also a vigil in Edinburgh, although Police Scotland made no arrests – were the largest, against the ban, of Andy Burnham’s premiership.

In September, when quizzed by LBC radio’s Andrew Marr about the “elderly people, vicars and grannies” who have been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised. But obviously the supreme court has got to look at this issue and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as a government.”

The following week, in an interview with The Rest is Politics podcast, Shabana Mahmood said it had been “very uncomfortable” to see some protesters arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action. Mahmood, the home secretary, nevertheless defended the ban.

The supreme court hearing will conclude on Thursday, with judgment reserved until a later date.

The Guardian view on listening to people with learning disabilities: a matter of life and death

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 17:25:17 GMT

The Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbed

The fear that so many felt as the death toll rose during the Covid pandemic was magnified for Fiona Walker. “I know from experience they wouldn’t have valued my life,” she says, in a new report on the treatment of people with learning disabilities during the crisis.

The 1.5 million people in the UK with learning disabilities, and their families, had reason for concern. Death rates in England were four to six times higher than average for people with learning disabilities. As is now well established, the pandemic did not create inequalities; it exposed and intensified them. People with learning disabilities die on average 19.5 years earlier than people without, and deaths are almost twice as likely to be classed as avoidable.

Learning the lessons means listening to people with learning disabilities and their family carers. Ms Walker and others were commissioners for the new How We Survive and Thrive report led by Learning Disability England, working with researchers from the University of Birmingham and Manchester Metropolitan University. It describes how families were abandoned by planners in the pandemic, though carers and communities gave welcome support. While care homes were failed, the needs of those living in family homes or community settings were often simply overlooked.

Recommendations include prioritising patients with learning disabilities and finding ways to increase rather than decrease support in a future crisis. But other improvements would help now as well as in the next public health emergency: ensuring people are included on the GP learning disability register, and providing accessible information and reasonable adjustments. Reactions to treatment can be wrongly taken as a refusal of care, when they really point to the need for easier to understand information, or the presence of a carer who can explain to or advocate for the patient. As Mencap has pointed out, such adjustments can be the difference between life and death.

While many carers and health workers may provide remarkable support and treatment, professionals are not immune from society’s prejudices. The shocking imposition of “do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation” decisions on people with learning disabilities in the pandemic may have partially reflected initial advice from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice). It said that patients should be assessed as scoring high for “frailty” – potentially affecting whether they received critical care – if they needed support with personal care, whatever the reason. Nice had to withdraw it. Testimony from patients with learning disabilities and their families suggests dangerous assumptions about patients’ quality of life also played a role. Those will be overcome only through sustained training and accountability.

Alarmingly, however, families and campaigners fear that progress made in recent decades is now being undone. Alongside cuts to social care packages and local support come profound challenges in healthcare. Important initiatives such as the Learning from Lives and Deaths scheme, examining the care received by people with learning disabilities and autism before their deaths, and mandatory training for healthcare staff on treating such patients, face growing funding pressures. The number of learning-disability nurses has fallen by a third since 2009 and student numbers are collapsing. That must be reversed. Learning disabilities should not mean a shorter life.

Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.

The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.

British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.

On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.

Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.

But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.

One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”

A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.

In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.

Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.

The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.

British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.

EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.

The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.

after newsletter promotion

EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.

Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.

Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.

Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.

Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.

Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.

UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.

The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.

This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.

The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.

The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

Steve Borthwick is urging his England players to act smarter and recognise the vital importance of keeping 15 players on the field before a pivotal month for the national team. Borthwick’s side have been shown 14 yellow cards and one red in 2026 to date and, partly as a consequence, have lost five of their past seven Tests.

Borthwick is also concerned that different refereeing interpretations in the domestic Prem are not helping England at international level, with the latest complication being a mid‑season law change preventing so-called “hip-drop” tackles. His experienced prop Ellis Genge has called the timing of the alteration “berserk” but also fully accepts England must improve their disciplinary record in their autumn Nations Championship fixtures.

All national coaches were invited to a meeting with officials on Sunday to discover how exactly the November games will be refereed but Borthwick has already identified two key areas where England need to be watchful. “From my point of view there are some aspects we need to bridge from club rugby to Test rugby,” he said.

“One would be the contact area. That’s telling us straight away there’s a situation we need to bridge. When you look at the teams we are playing against in the next few weeks there is a big breakdown challenge coming.”

Borthwick is also highlighting defensive steel – “We need to ensure we make it very, very difficult for the opposition to score” – which the head coach also believes is not being aided by the four-try bonus-point system in the Prem. He would prefer the adoption of the French system where teams must score three tries more than their opponents to secure an extra point.

“My view on the bonus-point structure is that it shouldn’t be the way it is,” he said. “I think the evidence says it should follow the Top 14, which makes defence important right until the 80th minute. I think that’s not necessarily always the case [in the Prem]. Nobody’s to blame or at fault, that’s just the way it’s structured.”

As for his side’s tactical discipline, Borthwick has also changed his tune since July when he dubbed the media “the negativity committee” after the 31-24 win against Argentina in Santiago del Estero when he was asked about England’s concession of four yellow cards in the second half. “The best players are smart and the best players adjust,” said Borthwick, who invited the referee Christophe Ridley to address his players last week.

“It’s pretty obvious there have been times over the last six to eight months when we haven’t dealt with moments the way we want to. At the 2023 World Cup this team had excellent habits … really it’s been the autumn of 2025 into this year’s Six Nations that cost us.

“Quite frankly we spend too much time defending. The way the interpretations are right now there is likely to be a decision that goes against you which gives an entry into the 22. As soon as you are there, we can all see the number of cards. We spent too much time there … we want to get the ball back faster.”

Forget maxxing your life. 2027 must be the year we relax – and start minning

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 16:00:15 GMT

Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, minning means doing them less, if at all

Public service announcement: fellow citizens, we have maxxmaxxinged. It has been close for a while, but now we have gone over the edge – reached, and passed, maximum maxxing. The tipping point was a week in which we saw reports of Namemaxxing. If you can’t decide between two baby names, pick them both. Suggestions included blending Maeve and Avery to create Mavery, or Leo and Giovanni to make Leovanni – Futupid. Then Dictionary. com revealed its word of the year and, yes, you guessed it: maxxing. It’s fully exhausting, in every way, but mainly in that -maxx has been fully exhausted. For the good of us all, 2027 has to be the year of minning. (The second “n” is important, otherwise pits may be deluged.)

Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile – surely nobody who ever set out to funmaxx achieved it (see: New Year’s Eve), not even Dua Lipa. Minning is much more noble: it’s about making the world, rather than only yourself, better. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, it means doing them less, if at all.

Andy Burnham could have leapt ahead of this trend when he unveiled his crackdown on headphone dodgers by declaring that he was loudcastminning. Other plagues against society with the potential to be similarly addressed are slow walking (dawdleminning), noisy eating (chewminning), not indicating when driving (mindreadminning), and absent-mindedly checking your phone mid-conversation (scrollminning). And let’s not forget dropping litter (binminning), turning up to a friend’s without warning (pop-inminning) and being over competitive (winminning.) Overall, this movement is about being as good a human being as possible (sinminning) but it’s also an opportunity to cut out habits such as drinking too many spirits (ginminning) and even negative familial relationships (kinminning).

Back in the days when all of this was fields and we only used one x in “max”, it was clear that max volume is too loud, max capacity too crowded, and max power too draining. Somewhere along the way we lost sight of that. Let’s take a deep breath, and enjoy the relief of leaning into minning. First person to suggest they’re doing maxxminning will be taken to the tower and made an example of.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 15:00:14 GMT

A great picture can have an immediate and visceral effect on a viewer, as if bypassing thought. But a huge amount of thinking goes into selecting and sourcing them, and researching their backstories

Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?

Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.

Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion.

Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”

The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.

That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”

Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?

“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”

For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”

By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.

Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.

One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.

Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”

Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”

The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.

As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.

The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”

Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”

The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.

The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”

Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”

The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”

Life is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to rest

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:00:19 GMT

The simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasures

Making sense of it is a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday life

There is a particular Buddhist story that reassured me I had found the right path.

The story goes that Prince Siddhartha Gautama was deep in spiritual practice – arduous, unforgiving practice. He had tried everything from breath-holding to extreme fasting. But none of it brought the freedom from suffering he sought.

As is sometimes the case in those moments, he was graced with a memory. He remembered being a child, sitting under the shade of a rose apple tree while his father worked nearby. As he sat there, free from preoccupation, his mind settled and his experience became infused with a deep sense of pleasure and ease.

This memory gestured at what later became a fundamental Buddhist idea: put simply, extreme self-denial is not the path to freedom. More radically, could it be that a certain kind of pleasure – a more refined pleasure – might help point the way?

I’ve always been intrigued by pleasure, its limits but also its invitation. The pleasure Siddhartha remembered was not wily or sneaky, waiting to trick him into attachment, but rather carried him towards freedom of heart.

Admittedly, the Buddha distinguished this kind of pleasure from sensual pleasures, which can become tangled with craving, acquisition and a mistaken belief that happiness lies in getting more.

But the point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure, but to lean into it when it naturally arises.

As humans, we are strangely adept at trying to elicit and extract pleasure, to plan for it and prolong it, but not so good at receiving it when it is right in front of us.

Stress can diminish our sensitivity to pleasure. Psychologists use the term “anhedonia” to describe the diminished capacity to anticipate or experience pleasure, a phenomenon associated with a range of mental health conditions.

As a teenager, I had a free-spirited friend who wholeheartedly called out, “I love bed!” before she went to sleep. We could hear her down the corridor.

I loved bed too; we all did. But would we admit it?

She noticed the sheets, the relief of placing a tired body down, the privilege of a pillow. Boy, she knew how to receive pleasure when it was being offered.

The Buddha observed that all experience is associated with a tonal quality – pleasant, painful or neutral. In Buddhism, we call this vedanā, or feeling tone. And then there is all the manhandling we do with feeling: judging it, willing it to stay, tweaking it.

When working with mindfulness students who are having a hard time, I often do a pleasure check.

I ask, sometimes provocatively, “What are you doing in your free time?” Then: “Are you able to read a good novel? Could you go for a massage or a meandering walk in the sun?” What I am really asking is: can you be with pleasure intentionally, even in the midst of suffering?

These conversations also make it plain that access to pleasure is not enjoyed equally. The time, safety and space necessary to notice and receive pleasure are impacted by our social and material circumstances. But when pleasure does arise amid turbulence, allowing it to register can offer the nervous system a chance to rest, even for a moment.

We feel this viscerally: a slower breath, a softening, a release. And if we are quiet, we might notice our minds relishing it – “How terrific, I love this.” Or as American novelist Kurt Vonnegut put it, “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”

Can we let pleasure simply hold our attention without trying to prolong it?

Pleasure arrives with different inflections. Some forms leave us aching for more. Others are more sublime, spiritual even – the kind the Buddha spoke of: the mind that gathers and settles. The simplicity of the breathing body. The sweetness of simply existing.

I once had a teacher who started meditation sessions with, “It feels good to be in the body.” It was a low bar for pleasure, but somehow I felt it.

Then there is the pleasure of living a life of non-harm, of treating ourselves and others with dignity, love and respect. Subtler still is the pleasure of laying down the burden, even for a moment, of having to be and do.

I remember marvelling that in my mother’s final weeks, days in the hospital could still brim with pleasure. Among the many unpleasant experiences, there was the sweetness of laughter, a leg massage, a feeling of togetherness, and a daughter’s recognition of the comfort and familiarity of being with her mum.

Each evening, I would think how strange it was that there was so much pleasure in despair.

And here receptivity was key. I suspect without it, I might have seen only what was painful and missed the pleasure braided through.

Every time I sit to meditate, I consciously luxuriate in the pleasure of breathing.

Of course, pleasure dissipates, and unpleasant and neutral sensations arrive too. Yet in Buddhist practice, these too are met with the same receptive attention: “Oh, this is unpleasant, and it will change.” Sometimes there is even a kind of pleasure in this honesty.

And, for the record, I still love bed.

Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at the Nan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulness

Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:00:16 GMT

The presenter recalls being a ‘weird little nerd’, almost becoming a scientist – and the most revealing costume she’s worn for work

Born in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She ­graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has p­resented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, is out now.

This is me at the age of four. It was my career ambition to become a witch. My back-up options were spy and nun.

We were living in Canada at the time. Dad was an expert in cold places – glaciers and permanently frozen ground – and he was embarking on a year’s swap with an academic at the University of Ottawa. My mother made the costume for me to go trick or treating with the family across the road. In my basket are sweets and I look very pleased and very proud.

Because of my father’s job, we moved around a lot. I wasn’t naturally good at making friends, because I’m quite shy. New schools could be intimidating, but I always had a safe space when reading books. Whenever I ask my parents what I was like as a child, they say, “We don’t know, because you were always reading a book and not talking to us.” Deep down, I was a secret showoff. I was flamboyant when adopting somebody else’s clothes or character or persona.

Outside school I had Guides, played musical instruments and acted in plays. Nobody there knew I was an A-grade student, so I was able to pass for normal. But at my state school in Nottingham, I couldn’t hide. I was a weird little nerd, and my studiousness marked me out in a way that I didn’t have the social skills to conceal. Even though I was lonely, I soldiered on because of my political views. For example, the pupils were going to have a “wear what you like” day to protest about the teachers who were always going on strike. I disagreed, and thought the teachers should strike, so I went in my school uniform – a horrendously stupid choice as everybody laughed at me.

I always loved history, but my father, being a scientist, wanted me to take a different path. To please him, I chose science subjects for my A-levels. Halfway through, my mum said, “You’re not enjoying this. You need to do what you want to do, which is history.”

At university, I studied ancient and modern history. It was a period in which I went mildly off the rails: staying up late talking to people who were just like me, organising the rag parade, playing in orchestras, rowing and doing all the extracurricular activities. I didn’t work hard until the very end of my three years, as I was too busy having a lovely time.

As soon as I saw the advert for the role of chief curator at Historic Royal Palaces, I thought, “That’s my job!” It was a lengthy recruitment process, with interviews in different palaces, and at one point I got in a tizzy looking for the right entrance at the palace of St James. A sentry was standing in a box, so I said, “Please tell me where the right way is. I’m desperate.” He wasn’t allowed to talk to me, but in the end he took pity and rolled his eyes in the direction I should go.

The role was high-profile and there was an expectation of what someone doing that job would be like. Historically, it had been done by men, always of a certain seniority – people very much in command of themselves. By comparison, I was 29 years old, small and pale. I had bought a long, dark coat, which I thought made me look grown up. But my youth and inexperience eventually became my superpowers, because everybody could see there was something different about the way I was going to do things. I came to realise that my authority is in building a relationship of trust with the person I’m talking to, not making them think that I know more.

My TV career began when BBC Look North came to make a film about Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire, where I was working. We ended up spending the day together, with me showing them how they could tell the story. That night I was struck by how much I enjoyed the experience. I began appearing as an expert “talking head” on various shows, and in 2008 I did a show about Henry VIII. More followed. The world was changing – I wasn’t Simon Schama or David Starkey – and we were ready for more women to talk about history.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

The struggle to look “authoritative” that I’d experienced earlier came up again in my TV career. I would get notes such as, “She needs to wear tailoring. She needs a dark coat.” It felt wrong. I am known for wearing costumes – using whatever it takes to tell a story. Like a primary school teacher, I have no dignity. But that is also the skill that is available to me. The dressing up might be considered frivolous by critics, but clothes tell us about hierarchy and social structures. They are also fun to look at, which is important when making TV.

Each day is different on set, but some are stranger than others. In one of my early shows, I was dressed as a medieval peasant foraging in the woods. My costume was a brown blanket. It was November and really cold, but I didn’t have the confidence to say, “This isn’t working for me.” In the end, I just burst into tears. Crying does work, but it’s better to speak up: I did a programme about the American Revolution once, and said to the producer, “I’d really like to be in the Independence Day procession that goes through Philadelphia on 4 July.” I imagined I’d be in a modest costume with buttons and a hat, maybe playing the cymbals. It turned out I was part of a twirling team and my costume was a skin-tight leotard. The rest of the team were 22-year-old girls. I got changed, but agreed with the cameraman that he would only shoot me from the neck up.

Being recognised is wonderful and terrible, as I’m a showoff but also shy. I’m capable of slipping through the streets of London in my baseball cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skills and clock me. Once a lady recognised me from my teeth alone. I also have a distinctive voice. Someone overheard me speaking in a swimming pool and said, “I know that voice!” I thought, “I’m naked, I’m dripping. I don’t want to engage with you just now, but thank you.”

The story of my life has been “the bookworm shall go to the ball”. I’ve had a wonderful career. But since turning 50, I’ve realised I work too hard. I’m endlessly asking myself, “Do you really love your work? Or is it just the capitalist patriarchy that’s making you think you love your work because that’s good for the economy?”

I don’t have the answers. But that’s the job of the historian. To ask the questions – and, for me, to put on the costumes. So has the girl in the photo grown up at all? Perhaps not.
