The truth about testicles: are we facing spermageddon?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:00:16 GMT

When it comes to fertility, testosterone and reproductive fitness, manosphere misinformation is rife - which can lead to a lot of heartache. Meet the man who wants to change all that

“I think you can tell it’s for a lay audience,” says Michael Carroll, holding up his book, Your Nuts, its cover illustrated with two walnuts in a string bag. The book has arrived in tandem with worldwide concerns about falling birth rates. “Spermaggedon” is a chunky piece of this puzzle, part of a wider debate about whether and why we’re heading for species-icide. Are people deciding not to have kids because of climate anxiety and economic precarity? Or is this an unchosen fertility cliff edge, created by forever chemicals and our lifestyles? This is not a drill, says Carroll, a biologist and reproductive scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University. “There’s compelling evidence to support a historical decline in sperm count and sperm concentration over the last number of decades.” However, it’s just not that simple.

First, it’s not a uniform picture and in some populations sperm counts are going up. The Danish Young Men Study, for instance, showed no drop between 1996 and 2022. In Ireland, a study of 15,000 men between 2008 and 2023 showed a 23% increase in sperm concentration.

Second, it’s not a direct read-across from sperm count or concentration to fertility – those statistics don’t tell you anything about functionality. “If you deposit 300m sperm at the cervix, only a couple of dozen might actually reach the egg,” Carroll explains, and we still don’t know really basic things, like “how the sperm find an egg in the female reproductive tract. We can extrapolate from animal experiments and conduct in vitro experiments, but biologically, we don’t really know.”

Third, “reproductive biology is a very complicated, multi-stepped, timed process requiring two individuals,” and even while we all understand that, any focus on a single issue, whether it’s sperm count or maternal age or generational anxiety, drives us away from an appreciation of that complexity and towards narratives so simplistic as to be basically superstitious. Back in the day, that woo-hoo was all “selfish women are leaving it too late”; now, thanks in part to an overheated manosphere, testicles are centre stage, freighted with notions of masculine destiny being threatened by an effeminate modernity. These aren’t ideal conditions for understanding what is going on.

Carroll grew up in Ireland, the youngest of 12; his unimaginably large family seems salient to his career choices. He brushes off any attempt to psychotherapise him, though, saying this is just how Ireland was in the 60s and 70s (he was born in 1974). “It was very much a theocracy then, and the Catholic church wasn’t in favour of contraception.”

He did his PhD in Newcastle, looking at how sperm fertilise eggs in marine animals. Then, after a postdoc at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Dallas, Texas, looking at stem cells, he trained as a clinical embryologist, working in IVF, before returning to academia to teach reproductive science and reproductive biology, while researching the impact of lifestyle and environmental exposure.

Although Carroll, who is married, has three children from a previous relationship and a stepdaughter, he is familiar with the pain of infertility, from his experience working in IVF.

“It’s a great job, being an embryologist. You’re working at the very beginnings of life, patients really put their trust into you to handle their gametes, the sperm and eggs, and to culture their embryos and get them to a stage where you can give them a family. It comes with great joy. But you also have to be prepared sometimes to break devastating news.”

Some types of azoospermia – where no sperm is produced in the ejaculate – have no cure or treatment. It can be caused by anabolic steroid use, which is sometimes reparable when you stop taking them, but sometimes not. “Don’t take health advice from social media!” Carroll says, and writes, often.

The global fertility picture, though, can’t just be blamed on TikTok. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman will have in her lifetime. In 1963, it was 5.3; by 2024, it was 2.2. Most European nations are well below replacement rate (UK, 1.6; Spain, 1.1) and the only reason the world population isn’t falling is that people are living longer and infant mortality rates have dropped. Carroll keeps the economics front of mind: “some estimates put the total cost of raising a child at $280,000 [£209,000]. I don’t know anybody now who could afford to have 12 children.” Plus there are other social factors, including climate change anxiety. Older maternal age is plainly a factor, though paternal age should be considered more than it is. From 40 to 45 is considered advanced paternal age, and “older men tend to have higher levels of DNA damage or mutations, so there’s a higher prevalence of neuropsychiatric disorders in their offspring – bipolar will be one, schizophrenia will be another”.

But what researchers are starting to call the “disappointment gap” – between the size of family people want and the one they have – is often driven by brute biological realities for both men and women, and where sperm is concerned, individual choices don’t cover it. In 2005, the epidemiologist Christopher Wild coined the expression “exposome”: the combination of environmental and lifestyle factors an individual would be exposed to throughout their life. Pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, plastics, sunshine, processed foods, “everything matters,” says Carroll. “The best way to examine a drop in any biological marker would be prospective surveillance studies, where you follow populations over time.” The Danish data came from military recruits; the Irish sperm research, which was a retrospective study, took place in a fertility clinic.

If longitudinal research yields a frustratingly mixed picture, the understanding of sperm itself is maddeningly partial. We can measure numbers, but that doesn’t tell us anything about function.

For sheer talismanic potency, though, sperm and testosterone are in a class of their own, drawing in social constructs of masculinity and meaning, which collide with these unexplained or only partially understood declines to produce narratives that are unscientific and often work directly against the science. In tandem with that, unwanted childlessness is rising sharply; infertility in broad terms is about 30% down to the woman, 30% down to the man and 30% unexplained. And for men, conventionally the silent partner in this discourse, a diagnosis of low fertility or infertility engenders “feelings of shame, demasculinisation, questioning their own identity and self-worth,” says Carroll. Whether as an embryologist or academic, he just wants people, with or without testicles, to understand what’s going on.

Seeing sperm as magic, and its absence a curse, isn’t a new thing. In 1889, Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard, a professor of experimental medicine, mashed up the testicles of dogs and guinea pigs, extracted the juice, injected himself with it and reported “a radical change … I had regained at least all the strength I possessed a good many years ago” (he was 72 at the time). This unleashed an industry of quacks, flogging “Brown-Séquard Elixir” or, more commonly in the US, the “Elixir of life”. To be fair to Brown-Séquard, the literature at the time on what testicles may or may not be capable of was very undeveloped, and he was like the Withnail of medical research, gamely experimenting on himself throughout his life, once covering himself in varnish to discover the properties of skin (he was found unconscious and had to be cleaned with alcohol), another time giving himself cholera by eating the vomit of a patient, to see if he could cure it with opium (he was found unconscious again and had to be resuscitated).

What concerns Carroll is the revival of that quackery, this time attached to testosterone. “What’s being promoted, especially by podcasters and social media influencers, is that testosterone is a quick hack to make you feel better and more invigorated, it’s a new elixir.” There is an ambient association of testosterone with “masculinity, aggression and competition, but behaviour is complex and it is too simple to put it down to the level of a hormone released from an endocrine gland”. A lack of vigour is more likely to be down to poor sleep or diet, and testosterone replacement therapy won’t put a dent in that, but it will along the way do the exact opposite of what you took it for. “It’s a very sensitive pathway of signals, the brain telling the testicles to produce testosterone. It’s called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Some testosterone will be released to do its thing around the body; more is produced in the testicles. And that’s important for spermatogenesis” – or sperm production and development. If you take supplementary testosterone, he says, “it’s telling the brain to shut down your factory downstairs because we have enough testosterone now, thank you. It’s a negative feedback loop, spermatogenesis is affected, and then there’s poor sperm or no sperm output because of that”.

It’s so pronounced with bodybuilders, who use testosterone replacement therapy to build muscle, that they get testicular atrophy, where their testicles shrink from underuse. It even has a name: “The Mossman-Pacey paradox,” Carroll writes, “whereby men enhance their visual cues of reproductive fitness while reducing their actual ability to reproduce.” Finasteride, a medicine that arrests and sometimes reverses male-pattern baldness by blocking the hormone DHT, has the top-line impact of boosting testosterone (because testosterone converts into DHT so, unconverted, it stays in the bloodstream). But libido, erectile function and mood track the androgen environment in general – so blocking DHT, like taking synthetic testosterone, is another signal to the brain to shut down the factory.

Almost more from a geopolitical than a spermatozoic point of view, it’s sobering to see testosterone make it into US defence policy, with Pete Hegseth announcing over the summer the “High-T Department of War”, mandating that all servicemen over 30 have their testosterone tested, to maximise mental and physical readiness, strength and warrior ethos. It’s not even the stupidest thing to come out of the Department of War recently, but it’s a stark illustration of manosphere misinformation working its way up to policy, flooding the knowledge environment.

And the problem with that is, it causes a lot of heartache. “A lot of men think that if they’re producing semen and they can get an erection, their bits are working,” Carroll says. “They don’t realise what’s going on within the testes, what can affect the quality of the sperm, what can reduce their capacity to reproduce. They don’t even start to look for the information until they’re trying to start a family and there’s a problem.”

Smoking is strongly associated with lower semen volume, lower sperm count, and increased DNA damage. Obesity has been linked to reduced testosterone levels and lower sperm count, but not all studies concur on this, and most obese men are fertile (Carroll is careful to stress this in his book, possibly to ward off anyone thinking they can rely on BMI as a contraceptive). The most solid correlation is between obesity and infertility rather than low sperm count, which also has the most obvious mechanical causation – fat cells produce an enzyme, aromatase, which can convert testosterone to oestrogen. This can directly impair the function of testicular cells. Human bodies are amazing, though sometimes in annoying ways.

More broadly, it’d be good for everyone to “know how it works”, Carroll says. “Plenty of lads go to the gym and they’ll know a lot about muscle physiology and contraction and nutrition, and they’ll be able to use that knowledge to make informed decisions to get the physique or fitness level they want. It should be the same with reproductive health. If you know your testicles need to be two to four degrees lower than body temperature, and prolonged high temperatures can damage sperm production; if you know the risks of STIs, which can cause infertility not just in males but in females as well; if you know that taking Finasteride or TRT can have an impact; this will all help you make informed decisions and ask the right questions.”

Fundamentally, Carroll wrote Your Nuts to broach the isolation of infertility. World Health Organization estimates that around 17.5% of the global adult population will experience infertility at some stage. People (like me) rail against the asymmetry of the discourse, that women’s health and choices are endlessly analysed and policed while men and their nuts slip under the radar, but it’s a painful and alienating experience, being the one that nobody talks about. “We’re in an infodemic era,” says Carroll, “and a lot of that information is not correct. I just want to tell people what we know, and more importantly, what we don’t know.”

Your Nuts: The Science of How They Work and What it Means for Your Fertility by Michael Carroll is published by FiachPress (£22.99)

What does Olivia Colman’s hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 14:00:13 GMT

In Wicker, the love interest is a man made of plaited twigs. In romantasy, women are getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Is this bad news for heterosexual men?

Apologies if this is too personal, but is there anything in your home that turns you on? A sleek standard lamp, say, or a sexy piece of kitchen kit? I’m casting an eye around here and wondering. I used to have the hots for my furry heated throw when it was sleek and glossy, but it’s so matted and grubby now, it gives me the ick. I still fancy the big kitchen cupboard, though. It is steely blue and so capacious, and its generous spice rack gives me a frisson every time I look inside.

I’m prompted to ask by the release of Wicker, the loopy erotic fable in which Olivia Colman’s fisherwoman enjoys a mutually supportive, sexually satisfying partnership with Alexander Skarsgård, whom the basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) has woven from wicker. I haven’t seen it yet, but the trailer is joyful and the premise is sending people – mostly women – wild.

The internet is full of horny comments about Skarsgård who, the fisherwoman’s neighbours gossip, is “strong as a tree and just as hard” (he’s certainly very pleasingly woven; a real statement piece). I also enjoyed an article in New York magazine, entitled What Would Happen If You Had Sex With a Wicker Dick?, in which an exceptionally game gynaecologist addresses this question with utmost seriousness, tackling splinters, lubrication and condom advisability, while also declaring, disarmingly: “But what do I know about wicker? Nothing.”

Unfortunately, I feel obliged to spoil everyone’s fun by wondering: what does it mean? Why has a film whose romantic (erotic) hero is plaited twigs sparked such enthusiasm? Have we all become basket cases? Because this wicker husband is no outlier: non-human romantic heroes have been wildly popular for a while.

At the more human-shaped end of things, romantasy has exploded (there’s wild excitement for romantasy queen Sarah J Maas’s latest), revealing a seemingly infinite appetite for stories about humans getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Sentient object smut gets even wilder: I took an online quiz, guessing which objects of desire came from a real cultural product and which were made up, and completely flunked. There’s real erotica, I learned, about a front door, coronavirus, a garden rake, a coffee mug and Clippy the Microsoft Word paperclip (which does have very come-hither eyes).

So are humans sick of each other – and are women in particular sick of men? Depressing cautionary tales about everything from men’s reluctance to commit, to manosphere-enabled and excused misogyny have fuelled a climate of reported heterofatalism: exhausted disillusionment with the unequal burdens and trials of heterosexual relationships. Wicker features some pretty on-the-nose heteropessimism: married women have to wear giant thunking collars and the men mostly seem to be boorish lumps. So why not choose wicker? You don’t need to mankeep a woven spouse and they won’t add much to the domestic load – at most they need a quick wipe with a damp cloth and some furniture polish.

But hang on. Skarsgård may be part 70s coffee table, sure, but he’s all man: he’s man-shaped, fixes stuff, wears tweedy trousers and, of course, has a penis. Even the more out-there object erotica novels “overwhelmingly pair human women with male creatures and objects”, according to New York magazine. Unsurprising, maybe, when the latest ONS data indicates 93.7% of UK women identify as heterosexual. Reports of heterofatality may be exaggerated.

If anything, I see Wicker-mania and its ilk as indicative of a yearning escapism, a desire for life to be lighter, sexier and sillier. When everything is horrible, why not imagine, and enjoy, a world where – unlike this one – anything’s possible, including mutually satisfying relationships, gender equality and sex with macaroni cheese (also real, yes)?

Speaking of escapism, back to cheerier matters. If nothing at home is igniting your loins, what would you make a sexual partner out of other than flesh and blood? Wicker seems way too scratchy. I came up with a shortlist of cashmere and cake, but neither seem sufficiently sturdy.

Hmm, maybe Christmas cake, specifically, would work? It’s extremely durable and delicious, and if your fruity lover starts getting difficult, you could always keep them in check by biting a warning chunk off their edge. Yes, this could give Stir-up Sunday a whole new meaning.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 13:00:13 GMT

One man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political funding system

In the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to a Super Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.

The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwing Utah senator Mike Lee.

One man was involved at every stage, and his name is on the paperwork for the charity that raised the money, the non-profit that passed it on, the Super Pac that the non-profit donated to and the campaign this money eventually supported.

His name is Thomas Datwyler, and his businesses are mostly headquartered in a rented address in Hudson, Wisconsin, a town of 15,000 near the border with Minnesota. Datwyler operates at an industrial scale, acting as treasurer of more than 350 federal political committees in the current election cycle, including 115 congressional campaigns and 100 Super Pacs, and as an officer of more than two dozen non-profits.

The extent of Datwyler’s activities over several political cycles raises questions about the attitude of Republican campaigns and candidates to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections, and the evolution of so-called “dark money” electoral funding.

Across the 2024 and 2026 cycles, Super Pacs whose books Datwyler also keeps have spent more than $2m supporting 14 candidates that are also his clients, or attacking their opponents, according to FEC filings. In several of those races the money reached the Super Pac through charities and social welfare groups for which he is a treasurer.

Datwyler-tied groups have been funded by donors connected to the rightwing megadonor Leonard Leo, along with the Conservative Partnership Institute and the personal foundation of the Claremont Institute’s board chair, the Thomas Klingenstein Fund, among others.

Money raised from these conservative donors has gone into organisations that Datwyler runs the books for, and those organisations have passed money on to Super Pacs that spent in Republican primaries. Non-profit tax filings do not show which donors’ funds made up any particular onward transfer.

Along the way, the same firms are paid by both the campaigns and the groups that are legally required to be independent of campaigns in order to maintain their tax-exempt status. In Florida’s 19th district, a campaign and the supposedly independent Super Pac backing it share 14 vendors, according to FEC filings.

Federal law prohibits coordination between Pacs and campaign committees, but proving it is challenging. The FEC is a reluctant cop, and while Datwyler has attracted significant controversy and state-level investigations, what he does may not be illegal.

“Somebody in Datwyler’s position is well aware of where all the cracks and crevices in the system are, how to sort of exploit the rules in a way that maximises his clients’ ability to secretly influence elections,” says Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the non-profit Campaign Legal Center.

“There’s a reason why the same handful of people – and Datwyler’s probably the chief among them – tend to come up in connection with these dark money operations. It’s because they have the knowhow of how to do it. And they’re willing to be the public face on each of these entities.

“The actual donors providing the money don’t want to be publicly outed as the source of the outside money pouring into the race.”

Datwyler wrote to the Guardian that “AxCapital [where he is CEO] is grateful that so many clients entrust our team to facilitate their participation in the democratic process. As an industry leader, we have strict internal firewalls, strong safeguards, and robust policies to ensure full compliance with all laws, regulations, and requirements.”

The Green Dragon entities exemplify a pattern that recurs across Datwyler’s network.

The Green Dragon Coalition is a 501(c)4 social welfare non-profit, and one of three entities registered in Delaware in 2023 with sequential IRS employer numbers, all listing the same address in Hudson, Wisconsin. The other two were the Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3 charity, and the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, a Super Pac.

Datwyler is treasurer of all three, and is the only officer that any of the organizations pay: the Green Dragon Coalition paid him $25,012 during the 2024 cycle and the Green Dragon Society paid him $29,066.

This is just a fraction of the compensation Datwyler has received across various arms of the political operation he works on. Tax filings indicate that he received at least $487,545 in the 2023-2024 cycle from non-profits. FEC filings indicate that during the last two election cycles at least $793,470 flowed to Datwyler directly, or to two Delaware-registered consultancies, 10Six Consulting and Same Day Processing, that share a Wisconsin address with the vast majority of his political and charity organizations.

Meanwhile, AxCapital, where Datwyler is CEO, brought in $4.9m across both cycles. AxCapital was created in a 2022 merger of HenryAlan and Datwyler’s 9Seven Consulting.

The Green Dragon Coalition’s $445,000 “educational” grant to the Constitutional Conservatives Fund in 2024 is recorded in the Pac’s FEC receipts in five payments between 15 March and 21 June 2024. In turn, the Pac spent $447,347 supporting Jenkins. Datwyler was also treasurer of Colby Jenkins for Congress, a role he had held since October 2023, and of the candidate’s joint fundraising committee. Datwyler is therefore keeping the books for the charity, the social welfare group, the Super Pac attacking the incumbent and the campaign it was attacking her on behalf of.

The Green Dragon Coalition’s 2024 revenue was $917,002, of which $750,000 – or about 82% – came from the Concord Fund, the Leonard Leo-network group formerly called the Judicial Crisis Network. The Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3, also took $250,000 from Purple Action, a 501(c)4 whose officers include tech mogul and former Trump administration “crypto czar” David Sacks, and $200,000 from the Conservative Partnership Institute, and $90,000 each from “dark money” vectors DonorsTrust and Fidelity’s donor-advised fund. The Thomas D Klingenstein Fund gave the 501(c)3 $75,000 in 2023, before the 2024 payments to the Super Pac.

Lawson Bader, the president and CEO of DonorsTrust, said the organisation was “unfamiliar with the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, and the fact that the Green Dragon Coalition has an affiliated 501(c)4”. Grants from donor-advised funds to a 501(c)3 “cannot be used for political purposes”, he said, adding that DonorsTrust “would reconsider future grant recommendations made to organizations that violate the rules governing charitable activities”.

A Fidelity Charitable spokesperson said: “Use of Fidelity Charitable grants for political contributions or campaign activities is prohibited. The terms all non-profits receive when grant funds are issued to them include explicit language to that effect.”

These are not the only money flows from major conservative funders through Datwyler-connected entities.

In 2024 American Majority Action, a 501(c)4 founded by conservative activist Ned Ryun, gave Integrity Minnesota, for which Datwyler served as treasurer, $250,000 for “voter registration and activation plans”. (A 2020 Campaign for Accountability complaint asked the IRS and two state agencies to investigate whether Ryun’s groups spent more than half their money on politics, which would violate IRS laws governing 501(c)4 groups. Campaign for Accountability communications director Michael Clauw told the Guardian that the IRS did not respond to the complaint or take any action.)

American Majority Action did not respond to a request for comment.

Integrity Minnesota also received $50,000 that year from Restoration of America, which the Chicago Sun-Times reported in October 2024 was part of “a sprawling empire of organizations pushing far-right agendas and election denialism”, funded by at least $150m from shipping-supplies billionaire Richard Uihlein.

The Guardian contacted Restoration of America for comment.

And a separate Datwyler vehicle, Aurora Venture, received $300,000 from Ardleigh Impact Corp, a Delaware 501(c)4 with one director, no employees and no website, registered to the Springfield, Virginia, home of Staci Goede, a former Republican State Leadership Committee finance chief who is the treasurer of 26 federal political committees this cycle.

The Daily Beast reported on 16 May 2024 that Ardleigh had moved more than $2.5m to Republican Super Pacs within months of being formed, raising the suspicion that it may be a straw donor.

The Guardian contacted Goede for comment.

The money pipeline functions such that none of these organizations are named as donors in the FEC filings of the Super Pacs.

The Guardian contacted the Concord Fund, Thomas Klingenstein and the Conservative Partnership Institute for comment, and emailed Purple Action at an address that returned the message undelivered. None responded.

This cycle, the Green Dragon Coalition has put a further $177,500 into the same Super Pac in seven payments since 5 December 2025, the most recent on 21 April 2026. The Pac’s independent expenditures so far this cycle total $15,000 in support of Barry Moore, the Alabama congressman currently running to replace Tommy Tuberville, who is departing the US Senate to run for the Alabama governor’s seat.

The Guardian contacted Barry Moore for comment.

Elsewhere, the Pac’s expenditures have gone to organizations connected to Datwyler’s associates.

Its payments to L4 Consulting LLC total $164,809 across 13 installments between 2 January and 5 June 2026, with the disbursements booked as “PAC strategy consulting” and “fundraising consulting”. L4 is run by Dan Hauser, who is president of both Green Dragon entities and takes no salary from either.

Hauser was reported in October 2025 to have been a paid senior adviser to the Utah senator Mike Lee, another Datwyler client, during the same period. In the 2024 cycle, L4 took $207,560 from the same Super Pac. Green Dragon’s charity separately paid L4 $128,033 for “event production”.

The Guardian contacted Hauser for comment.

Ghosh, the campaign finance reformer, pointed out that while non-profits have to disclose donors to the IRS, with the exception of private foundations and some political non-profits, they do not have to disclose them to the public.

“So if the entire object is to conceal the sources of the money, the [501](c)4 on its own can accomplish that objective. The only thing the [501](c)3 layer adds is that [501](c)3 donations are tax deductible for the donor,” he said.

Ghosh added: “But that’s a little riskier because if they are using the [501](c)3 to first obtain a tax deduction and then that money is being used to influence elections, that’s one of the few things that federal tax law does prohibit.”

Either way, he said that “that’s a transparency nightmare. It becomes this problematic daisy chain where the [501](c)3 is sending money to the [501](c)4, theoretically not to support its political advocacy. But again, who can say exactly whether that’s happening or not? These are opaque entities. They are black boxes.”

Alyssa Bowen, executive director of True North Research, put the same structure more bluntly. “It’s like dark money made darker,” she said. “It’s almost like he’s running science experiments to find out all the ways you can conceal who’s donating.”

She said the charity layer carried a second advantage for the giver. “The Pacs are legally required to disclose your donors, but you’re not [required to do so] for a 501(c)3 or [501(c)]4. And then there’s also the tax benefits – donors receive tax benefits for donating to a 501(c)3,” she said. “So it’s twofold for these donors that are trying to make sure that they’re not held accountable for some of the more political spending that they do.”

A similar pattern is visible across four other 2026 races. In each, Datwyler is treasurer of the campaign and of the Super Pac spending in that race, and in each he held both roles before the spending began.

The Love America Uphold Freedom Pac spent $248,091 for Catalina Lauf in Florida’s 19th district between 13 and 24 July 2026, which is all the independent spending it has ever made. It is registered at Datwyler’s own address, and amended its registration on 11 July to add the domain LAUFPAC. com, two days before the advertising started.

It shares 14 vendors with Lauf’s campaign, seven of them substantive digital firms, over overlapping periods – which engages the FEC’s common-vendor conduct standard independently of who the treasurer is.

The Guardian contacted the Lauf campaign for comment.

On shared vendors, Ghosh said this is “more pressing than just having a treasurer in common. The use of vendors in common for things like media production, placement – that’s exactly the kind of spending that would be the subject of prohibited coordination. If the vendors they’re using are actually taking what they learn from their work for the campaign clients and then utilising that information or passing that information to their Super Pac clients, that’s exactly what the law prohibits.”

The Defending Conservative Values Pac was registered on 9 May 2026 and spent $485,213 against Blake Moore, the incumbent Karianne Lisonbee is challenging, between 29 May and 20 June – again, 100% of its spending, and again in Utah’s second district. The Show Me Valor Pac was registered six weeks after Taylor Burks’ campaign, with Datwyler as treasurer, and spent $166,051 supporting him. The American Honor Pac spent $162,800 for David Flippo in Nevada’s second district; Datwyler is its treasurer, custodian of records and only named officer, and its entire 2026 income – $155,000 – came from Stephen Flippo.

The American Liberty Foundation is simultaneously the name of a 501(c)3, a 501(c)4 and a Super Pac, all with Datwyler as treasurer, the first two presided over by Raymond Yonkura, Jim Jordan’s chief of staff for nearly a decade. The Super Pac spent $294,021 for Jenny Costa Honeycutt in South Carolina’s first district in June 2026, funded by $355,000 from the social welfare arm, $250,000 from the Geo Group’s Pac and $250,000 from a group called Voice of the Children of Israel.

What those campaigns knew is the open question for True North’s Bowen. “It’s concerning that all of these organisations and entities are using him, because what do they know about his past?” Bowen said, referring to Datwyler. “Is that why they’re using him – or are they totally unaware?”

She was skeptical that one person could service so many committees properly. “It feels far-fetched that he could be doing a good job,” she said.

In the current electoral cycle, Datwyler has already attracted controversy.

The Delaware Republican party reportedly claims he went unresponsive and then left in January 2026 amid five straight months of negative federal cash balances, missing a filing deadline and drawing an FEC warning of “civil money penalties, an audit or legal enforcement action”; he says he resigned because the party had not paid him.

In Alabama he is the sole officer of a Pac registered to a rented mailbox that has reportedly drawn legal threats over its attack mailers. A former state senator, Dell Hill, reportedly said in April that he had launched the Pac, whose registration names only Datwyler. Datwyler reportedly said he was “strictly the accountant doing the books” and had “nothing to do with producing the ads”.

after newsletter promotion

One of the Republican incumbents it targeted, the state representative Matt Simpson, lost his primary in May.

In a telephone conversation, Simpson said of Datwyler: “If he found loopholes to try to exploit for his purposes, then that’s the nature of the business that we’re in. You can’t lie, though. That’s the problem that I have with it.”

He gave the Guardian a copy of a later mailer in which the Pac said a false claim about Simpson’s positions “was a printing error”.

The Guardian contacted Phillip Pettus, another incumbent the Pac targeted, for comment.

A Texas campaign Datwyler keeps books for drew a watchdog complaint in May 2026, and Andy Ogles, whose campaign he still runs the books for, confirmed in 2024 that, at that time, the FBI was investigating his campaign finances.

The complaint has not moved because the FEC needs four votes to open an investigation and has had only two commissioners since October 2025. Donald Trump’s two nominees have sat with the Senate rules committee since 11 February with no further action.

In May this year, the Campaign Legal Center asked the commission to investigate Datwyler again, over a $250,000 payment to one of his Super Pacs from the private prison company Geo Group, ICE’s largest contractor.

Datwyler has not been charged with any offence, and several of the investigations closed without findings. His firm’s general counsel has called the allegations against him “baseless attacks”.

The incidents are part of a longer pattern of scandal and regulatory scrutiny.

To date, Datwyler has been named as a respondent in 24 complaints before the FEC. Two ended in penalties, both for conduct that predated his appointment as treasurer. The other 22 were dismissed or closed without a penalty, at least three of them after commissioners deadlocked 3-3.

In January 2023 the FEC fined Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign $15,080 for failing to promptly report contributions totalling $147,601 received between 14 and 30 April 2022, before the 3 May Ohio primary.

Datwyler’s successor as Mandel’s campaign treasurer, Elizabeth Curtis, wrote to the FEC about “the stunning number of inexplicable reporting errors made by Mr Datwyler … ignoring the FEC and potentially incurring significant fines without notifying the Committee”.

The Guardian contacted Curtis for comment via a consultancy website contact form.

In 2023, the FEC fined four campaigns for failing to file required notices of late contributions in the 2022 elections while Datwyler was their treasurer: Mandel’s Senate campaign ($15,080) and the House campaigns of Rodney Davis ($5,820), Ann Wagner ($3,560) and Joe Kent ($3,304), for a total of $27,764. Fines against the campaigns of Rich McCormick and Kyle Sinclair also named Datwyler as treasurer, for failures that predated his appointment.

Those were not the only cases. A Guardian review of FEC enforcement records found 13 cases in which a committee was penalised for failures that occurred, at least in part, while Datwyler was its treasurer, with penalties totalling $110,791. The largest came in April 2024, when Rodney Davis’s campaign agreed to pay $43,475, in a settlement Datwyler signed, after it failed to refund $479,783.82 in general-election contributions within the permitted time once Davis had lost his 2022 primary.

The largest penalties to name Datwyler concerned reporting from before he took over.

In March 2024, Mike Braun’s Senate campaign agreed to pay a $159,000 civil penalty over improperly reported loans from the 2018 race. The FEC’s file on the matter records that Datwyler became the campaign’s treasurer on 29 January 2019, after the period in question, and that the campaign blamed its former treasurer for the errors. Commissioners deadlocked 3-3 on a separate allegation, that the campaign had misreported receipts and disbursements.

A representative for Datwyler reportedly said he “served as treasurer at the time the issue was corrected, reviewed, and resolved, not at the time of the underlying activity”.

In July 2022 Jim Jordan’s campaign agreed to pay $60,000 for failing to accurately disclose $1.2m in receipts and disbursements in five reports covering late 2018 to mid-2020. The FEC’s referral lists Datwyler as its treasurer from 15 July 2020, and the campaign told the commission he had “identified hundreds of errors” in its earlier accounting and filed corrected reports.

He was the shared treasurer of Joe Kent’s 2022 congressional campaign and of a Super Pac backing it – an arrangement the Guardian examined in February 2025, when campaign finance experts questioned the campaign’s routing of more than $1m through a company they described as a possible shell.

In December 2021 Mike Dowling, a former FirstEnergy executive defending himself in a shareholder lawsuit over the $60m scheme that secured passage of Ohio’s HB6 energy bailout, subpoenaed two dark-money groups at the centre of that scandal: Partners for Progress and Generation Now, the latter of which had pleaded guilty to racketeering that February.

He asked for their communications with a list of people and organisations that included Liberty Ohio Inc, a non-profit for which Datwyler was treasurer, as well as Datwyler himself and the group’s secretary, Scott Guthrie. The same list named Ohio’s governor and lieutenant governor and every current and former member of the state legislature. Neither Datwyler nor Liberty Ohio was served with a subpoena or was a party to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit settled in August 2022, with $180m paid to FirstEnergy by insurers to resolve the derivative claims, less $36m in court-awarded legal fees. The defendants admitted no liability or wrongdoing.

Both Datwyler and Guthrie were working at the time on Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign, with Datwyler as its treasurer and Guthrie as its manager. Mandel subsequently lost the 2022 Republican primary to JD Vance, who was subsequently elected Senator for Ohio, and then vice-president as Donald Trump’s running mate.

Committees for which Datwyler served as treasurer spent more than $7m across the race – more than $5.4m of it from the USA Freedom Fund, a Super Pac registered to his own post office box, which put $831,281 behind Mandel and a further $4.6m into attacking his three main rivals: $3m against Mike Gibbons, $1.5m against JD Vance and $36,530 against Jane Timken.

The Guardian can reveal other striking transactions involving Datwyler during that campaign. Between September 2021 and June 2022, Team Josh – the joint fundraising committee for Mandel’s campaign and his leadership Pac – transferred $1.1m in seven installments to the federal account of the Shelby county Republican party, a committee registered not in Ohio but at Datwyler’s post office box in Hudson, Wisconsin. The federal account of a second Ohio county party, Delaware, sent a further $362,458.

Those two transfers were the entire declared income of the Shelby county account, amounting to $1,471,200. It then spent $1,398,811 on independent expenditures supporting Mandel, amounting to 95 cents of every dollar it took in, and wound itself up that December. Datwyler was treasurer of all three committees, and of Mandel’s campaign.

The Guardian contacted Scott Guthrie for comment. An email to Josh Mandel was returned undelivered.

Twice, state authorities have probed Datwyler as opposed to his clients.

The most developed coordination allegation against him is in Tennessee. In 2024, the state’s registry of election finance referred a complaint to the attorney general over the Republican primary in the fourth senate district, where a dark-money Pac spent more than $600,000 to defeat the incumbent, Jon Lundberg. Datwyler was treasurer and officer of that Pac, East Tennessee Conservatives; he was also treasurer of the congressional campaign of Diana Harshbarger, whose son Bobby was the challenger.

The attorney general’s report found that Datwyler had helped Bobby Harshbarger set up his campaign in April, after being introduced by the congresswoman’s chief of staff. According to the report, Datwyler sent him guidance on appointing a treasurer, obtained a tax number for a bank account and opened a fundraising account with Republican donation processor WinRed, and that the Pac he ran then spent heavily against Lundberg.

Investigators could not reach a conclusion, mainly because Datwyler declined, through counsel, to be interviewed or to produce documents. Two registry members said he should be subpoenaed. “The system’s not working the way it needs to on the dark money side,” the registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said, “and I don’t know if we’ve got the tools to do anything for it.” Datwyler’s lawyer, Eric Brown, reportedly said that “news reports confirm that the AG report found no factual or legal basis to support the allegations of improper coordination”.

The registry dismissed the complaint in May 2025 at the request of Ken Yager, the Republican state senator who had filed it. “It’s just one of those where nobody was here to prosecute it,” Lawless said at the time.

The Guardian contacted Bobby Harshbarger for comment.

A second Tennessee complaint went further. Lawyers for the Civic Engagement Forum and Datwyler conceded to the registry that the group had operated as a political campaign committee and should have registered and disclosed its spending, and offered $2,500 to settle. The registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said the offer was not high enough. In July 2025, the registry deferred a decision and ordered the group to register and file its disclosure reports, and in September it accepted a revised offer of a $6,000 penalty and closed the case.

Datwyler reportedly told the attorney general’s investigators that he had no personal knowledge of the Citizen Engagement Forum, a second group named in the complaint.

In April 2024 Emily’s List asked the FEC to investigate an Arizona group with a Democratic-sounding name, the Turn AZ Blue Pac, which had disclosed neither its spending nor its donors and which was listed with Datwyler as its treasurer. Through a lawyer, Datwyler told the commission he “is not, nor has he ever been, the treasurer” of the group, and the FEC’s dismissal report records that he swore he had never heard of it before the complaint. The commission dismissed the case in April 2025.

That July, a Nevada leadership Pac formed to back the Republican Senate candidate Jim Marchant asked the justice department to investigate Datwyler for alleged wire fraud over a $500 cheque written from its account to his compliance firm, AxCapital, after he had stepped down as its treasurer. The complaint, written by the Republican election lawyer Dan Backer, alleged “a long history of running roughshod over federal campaign finance law”. It said Datwyler first described the payment as a bank error made through an online bill-pay system, then said he would refund it; the Pac’s own FEC filings record a $500 “compliance refund” from AxCapital on 22 April 2024. Eric Brown, general counsel of Axiom Strategies, which owns AxCapital, reportedly said the firm faced “baseless attacks” and that the letter was “nothing more than a stunt”. No charges have followed.

Backer told the Guardian this week that he believed the $500 was refunded “only after filing the [justice department] letter”; his letter is dated 26 July 2024. Asked whether the justice department had responded, he said: “Law enforcement agencies generally do not comment on pending investigations.” He said Datwyler had “cost the GOP vast sums of money” and was “just not cut out for this line of work at this level”, and that aggrieved former clients rarely act because “no one ever wants to spend the money or put their reputation out there, to sue or to file an FEC complaint”.

The Guardian also contacted the Tennessee complainant, the state representative Michele Reneau, and Emily’s List for comment. They did not respond.

In Maryland, Datwyler was listed as the treasurer of “Dan Cox for US Congress”, a committee registered in the name of a candidate who had not filed to run. In Ohio’s Mahoning valley, county party chairs of both parties could learn nothing about a group attacking local officials beyond his name on the treasurer designation.

In Texas, a Super Pac Datwyler kept books for reportedly spent almost everything it raised on credit card fees and nothing on campaigning, according to its own FEC filings.

Perhaps most notoriously, George Santos’s campaign named him treasurer in January 2023 and his lawyer told the FEC the appointment was unauthorised – a position the same lawyer later retracted, writing that he had lost confidence in his client’s account.

Santos, the New York Republican who fabricated most of his biography, was expelled from the House in December 2023 and sentenced to more than seven years in April 2025 for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. He served 84 days before Donald Trump commuted the sentence in October.

Datwyler is steadfast in maintaining secrecy on behalf of funders.

Asked in October 2024 about $200,000 that arrived at a Super Pac opposing Sheldon Whitehouse from his Wisconsin address, Datwyler said a Florida couple were the primary funders and declined to name them.

Occasionally, Datwyler’s denials have been undone by his own filings.

Asked in October 2025 about attack mailers in a Utah school board race, he said the address on them “is not associated with us at all”; hours later, the Pac filed state paperwork listing him as its primary officer.

Time after time, however, investigations that reached committees he kept have ended without action against him. Three executives of Navatek, a Hawaii defence contractor, pleaded guilty over schemes that included routing $150,000 of company money through a sham entity, the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers, to 1820 Pac, a Super Pac backing Susan Collins for which Datwyler was treasurer. The Pac told the FEC the contribution was lawful. Commission lawyers later recommended finding that it had failed to refund the money once its source came to light, but the commissioners never voted on that, and in January 2025, with the statute of limitations running out, they dismissed the allegation against the Pac and Datwyler in his official capacity. The Pac’s FEC reports show no refund.

On Datwyler’s overall operation, Saurav Ghosh said: “What you’re describing is both incredibly common and incredibly problematic for our elections.”

Jess Cartner-Morley’s November style essentials: fancy flats, sexy knits and a Christmassy pigeon

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 13:00:12 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Whether it’s a two-in-one coat or a truly delicious handbag, add some fun to getting dressed during the cold, dark months with our expert’s favourites

The best women’s shoes and boots for autumn

The clocks have gone back. The mornings are cold and the evenings are dark. The world seems to be doing its level best to discourage any fashion ambition beyond the need to stay alive and warm enough to function.

But clothes – even in winter – are not just about staying alive. They are about staying alive alive. Alive inside. So this month’s edit is about finding the fun in getting dressed when the weather is trying to discourage you. There is a pink jumper that manages to be both cosy and, well, slutty; a £16 henley that looks considerably more expensive than it is; and a skirt I have been stalking since the summer and can finally report back on. There are also ballet pumps with exactly the right amount of grownup elegance, a sweatshirt that makes a persuasive case for elevating the everyday, and a necklace to bring a bit of sparkle back to the proceedings.

Iris knit

I love a slutty jumper. Are we allowed to say that? I mean it as a compliment. A going-out top you won’t freeze in is perhaps more polite terminology. I want it in the cherry blossom pink, but it is available in lots of other nice colours.

There is something so classy about a henley. Like, when a character in a film is wearing a henley, you know it’s there to tell you this person has a good soul. When done with finesse – a superfine rib, delicate buttons – there is something quite sensual about it, in an old-timey kind of way. Anyway, this M&S version is amazing value.

Polène Cyme bag

Polène handbags are exquisite, which is why there are queues outside the Paris stores when new bags arrive. If you get a chance to swing by the Regent Street store in London, you will see what I mean.

Pigeon tree bauble

Forget robins and turtledoves. Pigeons are the spirit animal of 2026.

Silk blend lace detail skirt

Wear a skirt. This is not a drill: Miuccia Prada says so. Skirts are so back, baby. I spotted this one, with its snazzy lace insert, back in the summer, when M&S womenswear head Lisa Illis was wearing it in the showroom, but it wasn’t yet on sale. I’ve been stalking it ever since; it’s now arrived, and I can confirm it is excellent.

Gathered back sweatshirt

The White Company strapline is “everyday elegance”, which feels like a policy we can all get behind. It has long been a go-to for chic home bits, but the new-ish clothing director Sheila McKain (ex of Jaeger and Donna Karan) is doing excellent womenswear too. The drawstrings at the waist here are great – I never like how a sweatshirt hem hits at the hip – and the gathering elevates it out of the ordinary.

Lapis and blue sapphire necklace

Necklaces are having a moment again. I do find that a lot of pendant necklaces look a bit … babyish? Cutesy? Anyway, this gold-plated one is fab. Here in blues, but also comes in greens (aventurine and onyx) and reds (jasper and garnet).

Pointed leather ballet flat

I don’t like ballet pumps with bows on. So much chicer without. Massimo Dutti makes great shoes; I know I am repeating myself here, but I don’t think enough people know about the brand. These have an almond-shaped toe and a high narrow vamp, both of which give an elegant line. Available in black or burgundy.

Wool coat

One coat, two personalities. A gorgeous, perfectly simple black coat with a luxuriously deep detachable faux-fur collar to dress it up for evening.

Stainless steel tray, cup and spoon

I feel like if I were an architect at a chic Milan studio, this is how I would drink my coffee.

The UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 12:33:55 GMT

Companies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptions

In 2022, a prodigiously talented young artist named Louis Petit was preparing to return to the UK, having been effectively exiled in the Netherlands as a teenager so he could access the medical cannabis he needed to control his epilepsy. Six years earlier, Louis, then 12, had been diagnosed with a rare form of the neurological disease when medical cannabis was still illegal in the UK.

But in Rotterdam, where it was legal, doctors helped him discover that a medical cannabis oil called Bedrolite, in combination with the right mix of anti-epileptic treatment, could slow and eventually stop his seizures. This was something his neurologists in the UK had previously considered impossible.

By the time Louis won a place at City and Guilds of London Art School in 2022, the UK government had legalised medicinal cannabis, pressed by parents needing the drug to treat their epileptic children – most notably Charlotte Caldwell and Hannah Deacon.

Louis assumed his troubles were behind him. “It seems naive now, but I think both me and my mum thought Britain would welcome me back, saying, ‘Thank God you’re better’,” Louis told me. But Louis has never been able to get a prescription for medical cannabis through the NHS. Instead, like almost everyone who needs the drug in this country, his only access has come through the expensive private sector. And now the producer of Bedrolite, a Dutch company, Bedrocan, has declared bankruptcy.

This means there is a high chance that, in the near future, the drug that keeps Louis well will stop being available privately, in a huge blow to all patients who rely on it. If this was people with diabetes facing a shortage of insulin, or people with high blood pressure running out of beta blockers, politicians would be falling over themselves to be seen trying to secure the long-term supply. But because this is epilepsy and cannabis – a medicine that has been stigmatised by a 50-year “war on drugs” – successive governments have avoided the issue, allowing this current crisis to develop, despite patients warning for years that they can’t be just abandoned to the private market.

When the then home secretary, Sajid Javid, legalised medicinal cannabis in 2018, he stood up in parliament and promised patients who needed cannabis medication that their arduous fight was finally coming to an end. “Having been moved by heartbreaking cases involving sick children,” Javid said, “it was important to me that we took swift action to help those who can benefit from medicinal cannabis.”

But these benefits reached a fraction of those who needed help. Since the first few patients received their prescriptions on the NHS, the vast majority of others – including Louis – have been met with a wall of refusal from the healthcare system, with doctors’ requests for public funding to prescribe cannabis medication rarely granted in practice.

Until 2025, there were fewer than five prescriptions for unlicensed cannabis-based products such as Bedrolite given out across the entire NHS. In the absence of an accessible NHS route, the private market has become the only option for treatment for most patients, costing them anything up to £4,000 a month for their medicine.

The result of medicinal cannabis being handed over wholesale to the private sector is that cannabis has quietly become one of the new growth sectors in Britain, with many cannabis companies getting rich from the boom. Remote online prescriptions, 48-hour door-to-door delivery and targeted advertisements on social media have all helped grow the private customer base.

But while private suppliers offer customer-friendly products such as cannabis vape pens and gummies on prescription, Bedrolite is a cannabis oil that was modified specially for children with drug-resistant epilepsy, and can’t be replaced with general cannabis. There is a much larger market for presenting cannabis as the new must-have wellness treatment for the on-the-go millennial suffering from anxiety, sleep issues or chronic pain medicine than there is for trying to treat acute but rare ailments such as complex epilepsy or multiple sclerosis.

And there is little commercial incentive for private companies to spend huge amounts of money on the expensive, large-scale, clinical, randomised control trials that are needed to get more cannabis medication licensed and mainstreamed on the NHS. Successive governments washed their hands of this issue once legalisation eased the immediate pressure from families with sick loved ones who were campaigning against an outright ban.

This dynamic leaves us in the paradoxical position whereby medical cannabis has become one of Britain’s new growth industries at exactly the same time that the most vulnerable patients, who desperately need the medication, cannot access it.

“It’s been one shock after another since we came home,” said Louis’s mother, Emma. “If his neurologists’ funding request to NHS England had been approved last year, his Bedrolite supply would be guaranteed. There is enough stock in the Netherlands to last into 2028. But it’s not available to those without NHS prescriptions.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Initially, it was feared that the drug would stop being on sale in the UK before Christmas, but last week one UK drug manufacturer, Target Healthcare, told families it will secure a six-month stockpile of Bedrolite, offering temporary relief. However, what happens in six months’ time is anyone’s guess.

The possible consequences of epileptic patients such as Louis suffering a forced withdrawal from the medication they use to control their seizures could be severe. The UK government needs to intervene and negotiate with Bedrolite’s manufacturer to secure the supply for all patients who need it in Britain.

But beyond this emergency, the UK government needs to stop ignoring the medical cannabis industry and put in place the necessary investment and regulatory frameworks for it to become an accepted prescription on the NHS.

Even before the recent bankruptcy of Bedrocan, families and campaigners have been insisting that patients shouldn’t be forced to live at the mercy of the volatile private market, all because politicians are too scared of the negative headlines that might come from mainstreaming a still-stigmatised drug such as cannabis on the NHS.

“Health shouldn’t be an issue of whether you are wealthy enough to afford it or even be able to access it,” Louis said to me as we parted. We will see over the next couple of months if the politicians in charge of this country agree.

Dr Kojo Koram is professor of law and political economy at Loughborough University and the author of The Next Fix: The Winners and Losers in the Future of Drugs

Ciara Mageean, European 1500m gold medallist with Ireland, dies aged 34

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 12:31:01 GMT

Mageean won 2024 European 1500m title in Rome

Athlete described as ‘an inspiration to so many’

The Irish middle-distance runner Ciara Mageean, who won European gold and competed at two Olympic Games, has died aged 34, her family have announced.

The athlete, from Portaferry in Northern Ireland, died at 6.30am on Sunday. In a post on social media, her family said she was surrounded by her loved ones, adding: “A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.”

Mageean was one of the most high‑profile athletes in Ireland, specialising in the 1500m event. She represented Ireland at the 2016 Rio Olympics and 2020 Tokyo Games, as well as holding a slew of Irish records.

She became the first individual Irish European champion since Sonia O’Sullivan when she won gold at the 2024 championships in Rome. Mageean was unable to compete at the 2024 Olympics because of an achilles injury. The following year, she announced she had been diagnosed with cancer. She went on to marry her partner, Thomas Moran, in October only weeks before her death.

Micheál Martin, the Taoiseach, said he was deeply saddened at her passing. “My heartfelt sympathies go to her husband Thomas, all her family and friends,” he said. The Tánaiste, Simon Harris, described the news as heartbreaking. He said: “She was a European champion, two-time Olympian, a proud Irish athlete and an extraordinary person.”

Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said Mageean demonstrated “extraordinary talent, determination and dedication”, adding: “I am deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Ciara Mageean, and I want to extend my heartfelt condolences to her husband Tommy, her parents, family, friends and everyone who loved her.

“Ciara’s achievements in athletics brought immense pride to her local community and to people right across Ireland. From representing Ireland at two Olympic Games to winning European championship gold in Rome in 2024, Ciara demonstrated extraordinary talent, determination and dedication.

“However, beyond the medals, records and sporting accolades, Ciara will be remembered for her warmth, courage and tremendous strength of character. Throughout her illness, she showed a remarkable spirit and an incredible ability to find hope and joy in life, even in the most difficult circumstances. Her courage touched countless people and will leave a lasting legacy.

“For a community like Portaferry, this loss will be deeply felt. Ciara was one of our own, and the pride she brought to her community and beyond will never be forgotten. At this incredibly difficult time, I hope her family and loved ones can take some comfort from knowing just how deeply she was admired, respected and loved by so many people.”

The deputy first minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, said: “I am so sorry to hear of the death of Ciara Mageean, at the age of 34 years. An outstanding athlete and ambassador for her sport, Ciara was born in Portaferry, County Down, and represented Northern Ireland and predominantly Ireland on the world stage.

“Ciara had outstanding success, and was an inspiration to many. She spoke with such honesty and bravery about the health battles she subsequently faced. I know so many from right across Northern Ireland were deeply proud and inspired by Ciara. My deepest condolences to her family, teammates and friends, and her husband to whom she had so recently married.”

Like many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote back

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 12:00:12 GMT

The novelist receives passionate AI-written emails almost every day – but when he decided to take up one sender’s offer to find him new readers, the story took a darker turn

There’s no humble way to say it: I get a lot of fan mail. Almost every day, multi-paragraph emails arrive from passionate and well-informed readers in Barcelona and Frankfurt, Chicago and Warsaw. They have appealing names like Bella Monroe, Thalina Rose and Tricia Claxton. Some of them are straightforward enthusiasts while others are more irreverent, like the one who signs off her messages “warm chaos”. Some love the “deadpan genius” of my novels while others admire my nonfiction’s “moral courage”. What they all have in common, though, is that they are entirely fake and trying to con me out of money. They promise to promote my work at their city-wide book clubs or spread the word among their reading communities, if only I transfer a few hundred dollars to cover costs.

In the age of generative AI, scam emails have achieved a new level of personalisation. Most writers I know are receiving a steady stream of emails like this. The messages are often sophisticated enough to bypass a spam filter and reach our inboxes, leaving us no option but to read them and ask the painful question: would any real, living person feel this strongly about my work? Or, as one writer friend put it, the reason I know they’re fake is because they’ve actually read all my books.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

What makes it worse is that the AIs that help write these scams really have read all our books. Last year, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn in compensation to the thousands of authors whose copyrighted work they’d used to train their AI, Claude. In July, a group of publishers filed a lawsuit against Google for utilising “one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history” in order to train their AI, Gemini. So when writers receive these AI-assisted scam messages, we know we are being manipulated by a version of ourselves.

A few months ago, for example, I received a gushing email from Ottessa Moshfegh. The bestselling, Booker-shortlisted author of My Year of Rest and Relaxation – to my mind one of the most potent voices in contemporary fiction – was taking time away from producing her inimitable prose to write me a fan letter. I thanked her for getting in touch. We got chatting and I asked about her work-in-progress. She said that her new novel was “preoccupied with interior life: how emotions register, how they fail to, and what that absence or excess does to identity over time”. I thought we were making a real connection when she said that, really, the best way to understand her work was to explore her Amazon page. Sigh. Never meet your heroes. Other writers have received similar messages from fake Donna Tartt and fake Sally Rooney. It must be strange for the real Moshfegh, Rooney and Tartt to know that their novels have been harvested by tech corporations in order to create the ghost versions of themselves who now haunt the inboxes of their peers.

The correct response to all this is, of course, to simply report the email, block the sender and move on. But there is a part of me that fantasises about dramatically unmasking the scammer, revealing the villain beneath. So when I received an email from the founder of the Berlin Book Club, I decided to see how far I could get. I agreed that I did need help reaching new audiences. I was willing to pay for her connections and expertise. Soon we started discussing payment methods. She wanted me to use CashApp or make a direct bank transfer but I was insistent that I could only send hard cash. We went back and forth for a couple of days. I impressed on her that I had, at that very moment, 500 US dollars in crisp notes in an unmarked envelope and that I lived quite near the post office. She finally relented and gave me a physical address. Neither of us commented on how unusual it was for the founder of the Berlin Book Club to have a postal address in the Philippines. I went on Google Maps and was able to find the street in question, a rural two-lane road with palm trees, a junk shop, an evangelical church and a large building hidden behind high white walls.

The Philippines – along with Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia – is one of the countries most affected by organised crime networks running industrial-scale “scam farms”. Last year, authorities raided a facility in Bamban, north of Manila, freeing nearly 700 people who had been trapped there and forced to work as scammers. Inside the building, it resembled a hybrid between a call centre and a prison, rows upon rows of computers and green screens, and tiny dorms with bunk beds. About half of the workers were Filipino, while the others had been trafficked from China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, Indonesia and Rwanda, their documentation withheld. The bosses, meanwhile, splashed around in the swimming pool next door. When another nearby compound was raided, they found it had its own brothel, karaoke suite and torture room. Across south-east Asia, these scam compounds are a multi-billion dollar industry, run largely by Chinese crime syndicates who routinely use violence and sexual abuse to keep workers in line. With the enormous sums of stolen money flowing through the industry, some compounds are the size of small towns or, perhaps more accurately, labour camps – with thousands of workers.

The scammers are encouraged to make use of the latest technology, not just generative AI but also face masking apps, so that they can conduct video calls wearing whatever face suits the task. The big focus is on “pig butchering”: long-term romance scams where people are tricked into falling in love with a wealthy, glamorous foreigner who then advises them to invest in fake cryptocurrency. When a large scam compound in Cambodia was seized by the Thai army, they discovered that its facilities resembled a TV studio. There were costumes, wigs and different sets for filming different scams. There was a fake Brazilian police station and a replica Vietnamese bank. Scammers were trained to keep their targets on the hook for months, even years, inventing private and personalised narrative worlds through which they could drain all of the victim’s money. In an interview with the BBC, one former scam compound manager sounded not unlike a novelist when he described the process. “[It’s] all about exploiting emotion,” he said. “You create a dream.”

For my part, I did not send any cash to the Philippines. Instead I shared the details I’d received with the country’s cybercrime agency. Although, in the words of Winston Casio, the spokesman for the presidential anti-organised crime commission in the Philippines, the ongoing problem is that the criminals have “the financial capability to corrupt just about anybody in public office. The amount of money they have is their potent tool against law enforcement.” When authorities shut down the Bamban compound, for example, they discovered that it was being run by Alice Guo, the local mayor. Similarly, the idea that AI companies might go out of their way to halt the criminal misuse of their technology seems just as doubtful – and for exactly the same reason. It’s making them fantastically rich.

All of which is to say that my fantasy of unmasking the villain was just that, a fantasy. At least now, when I receive fake fan mail, I can attempt to understand the probable reality behind the quirky name and upbeat tone. On the other side of the screen, there is someone frightened and far from home, sitting in a sound-insulated booth with a dozen phones splayed out on their desk – while behind them their manager walks by, a taser at his hip.

A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 12:00:10 GMT

From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous

Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.

After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.

I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.

Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in the DC Comics Suicide Squad to your local polling place. That’s all we need, John Cena checking your ID before you vote.

It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.

My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.

During a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recent Trump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maher agrees with me.

Here in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, is still popular enough that his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.

According to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)

The Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department is suing to invalidate the results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).

I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?

Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangers won’t involve Leslie Nielsen.

In an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina are shutting polling places in blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.

When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.

It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.

I get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.

Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with my root beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.

As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.

This is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.

I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.

Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates from various Republican buttocks.

Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist
