GB’s Harriet Dart wins maiden WTA title at 30 with Guangzhou Open triumph

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:20:14 GMT

Briton beats 18-year-old Austrian Lilli Tagger 4-6, 6-3, 6-4

Dart, a qualifier, was competing in her first WTA final

Harriet Dart won her first WTA title after the Briton came from a set down to defeat Lilli Tagger in the final of the Guangzhou Open in China.

Dart, who saved three match points in her semi-final against Sun Xinran to reach her first tour‑level final, edged a thrilling match against the 18‑year‑old Austrian 4-6, 6-3, 6-4.

The British No 5, a qualifier for the tournament, dropped serve in the opening game and had to save a break point in her next service game before finally getting on the board against the fourth seed. The 30‑year‑old from Hampstead broke back for 4-4 but Tagger, who won the 2025 junior French Open, hit straight back before wrapping up the first set.

Dart took the first break point of the second set for 5-3 on her way to levelling the match.

In a tense deciding set, a run of five consecutive breaks of serve ended when a gutsy Dart saved two break points to hold for 5-3. In the next game she brought up two champion­ship points, but a big serve from ­Tagger saved the first before Dart hit a mid‑court forehand into the net on the second.

However, Dart wiped that miss from her mind to serve out the match to 15, falling on her back in delight when victory was sealed with an unreturned serve.

Dart, who has been working with the former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli, said on court: “I’ll try not to get too emotional. A big thank you to my team this week. It’s ­amazing to play in front of such a big crowd. It’s been so much fun here and I really appreciate it and hope to be back next year.

“This week shows that even when I’m down – and people think I’m down and out – I’m still able to overcome it. Today was a really tough match. I have no doubt Lilli will go on and win multiple titles. To come through a week like this means a lot.”

Tonga’s gripping win over Samoa a victory for Pasifika pride at Rugby League World Cup

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:05:18 GMT

Tonga defeat Samoa 20-18 in raucous atmosphere

England exit tournament on points difference

Sometimes sport does live up to the hype. Any suggestion that there was little riding on this result was evidently nonsense, when weeks of anticipation evolved into a mass display of national pride, the desire to get one over on their Pasifika cousins far greater than wanting to avoid Australia in the semi-finals. Tonga and Samoa flags had flown from cars for several days across the eastern seaboard and five hours before kick-off the streets of Parramatta were throng with huge groups of both nationalities celebrating their cultural bond.

Both teams were basically through to the final four, yet still produced an exhilarating derby that confirmed England’s exit from the Rugby League World Cup on points difference. Fans who’d paid sums previously unheard of for international rugby league tickets on the black market and resale sites will consider it money well spent. Those who got theirs for $20 will consider it the buy of the year.

Any game would struggle to live up to the pre-match activities that had the CommBank crowd at fever pitch. But Brian To’o’s electrifying early darts and bullocking runs by Tongan props Jason Taumalolo and Addin Fonua-Blake laid platforms for both sides to attack. From there, Samoa looked uncertain in good ball situations while Tonga consistently threatened, Tolutau Koula denied a try by the video referee as the returning Isaiya Katoa linking their attacks beautifully from halfback. But it would take a magnificent side-stepping solo run by Robert Toia down the right centre channel to open the scoring at the predominantly Tongan end 27 minutes in.

Captain Jarome Luai tried to fire Samoa up with a ferocious hit on Spencer Leniu and it was his booming kick that was fumbled by Tonga, Stephen Crichton manufacturing something from nothing to send Brian To’o in for their first points. Toia got the first after the break, finishing a fluid move on the left, Katoa extending the lead to 14-4. Samoa had to strike next and did with a repeat move, Luai’s high kick to the right, a fumble and a wonderful overhead pass, this time by Chanel Harris-Tavita, laid up To’o for his second. Harris-Tavita pulled a hamstring hitting a post with the conversion attempt and hobbled away, his World Cup done. Samoa weren’t going quietly, though. Lehi Hopoate knocked the ball out of Salesi Foketi’s hands as he plunged over the line, the teams exchanging massive hits as the fans swapped hymns.

Samoa, finalists four years ago, were not fading away. Slick handling down the left sent in Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow untouched, but replacement kicker Ronald Volkman made it zero from three for Samoa from the tee and they still trailed. He made up for it a couple of minutes later, bouncing off tackles to complete a dazzling team move and finally put Samoa ahead. His kick made it 18-14 with 10 minutes to play.

Luai’s attempts to keep his team calm fell on ears deafened by the racket from the frenzied stands. Instead, Addin Fonua-Blake blasted through tired tacklers to level and Katoa’s conversion put Tonga back in front. There were times when Tonga’s veteran forwards Tyson Frizell – who’d previously played in World Cups for Wales and Australia – and captain Taumalolo looked exhausted but they went to the well one more time to produce heroic defensive efforts. And when Sua Fa’alogo’s toe touched the touchline and his try was ruled out two minutes from time, Samoa’s race was run. They will face the Kangaroos across Sydney on Sunday, while Tonga take on the Kiwis in Newcastle in Saturday’s semi-final.

Twenty years ago last week, Tonga beat Samoa in front of a couple of thousand neutrals in Leeds. It’s now the biggest fixture in international rugby league, with a ground record of 29,411 rejoicing in the occasion. World Cup organisers, the Australia Rugby League Commission, will have been thrilled with the sell-out event, thousands of Lebanese adding to the atmosphere. Their extraordinary 24-20 golden point win over France in the second game of a triple-header being the game of the tournament until this one, both proving dead rubbers can be a corkers. Somehow the ARLC has found itself both host and promoter of the world’s biggest Pasifika party. Peter V’landys and Co will now be figuring out how to put on a repeat event every year.

‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:00:10 GMT

Former president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wing

That could have been awkward. Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.

“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,” he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”

It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have actively shrugged off their party labels, eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.

Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems that Democrats do.

“Yes, we can!” chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence of an Obama 2008 campaign that now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.

With days to go before midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump’s second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign’s closing days.

America’s first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump’s autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.

“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said in Georgia. “It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it.”

For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign’s closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.

David Litt, a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: “What you’re seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you’re a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters.”

The former president possesses a rare currency in modern US politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.

“Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days,” he continued. “The other thing is he continues to live in Trump’s head rent-free. Donald Trump is out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he’s relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can’t help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president.”

That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obama observed that Trump’s gold-encrusted renovations have left the White House looking as if “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.

The comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.

Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf, accused Obama of snobbery and said: “Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I’m not that choosy.” He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion “deteriorated”.

Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager, even staged a photo-op outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging “the Martha’s Vineyard set” to sample the chain’s multi-page menu.

To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”

For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. “This is a party that spent years complaining, ‘Oh, you’re not allowed to say anything offensive any more,’” he said. “It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can’t cross.”

In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama’s remarks as elite condescension toward working people.

He said: “They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You’ve got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There’s no accountability. You’re reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we’re bombing more places.”

Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-president Bill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly, who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.

In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obama opened his presidential centre in Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.

Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama’s legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.

Norman Solomon, a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: “It’s like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it’s not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama’s record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody’s lifetime – it does not look so great.

“Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity.”

Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama’s tactical value is undeniable. “Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. In Michigan, where there’s been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it’s helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what’s at stake.”

Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.

Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign, said: “Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it’s strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.

“But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement’s momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn’t radical – it’s mainstream. It’s an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become.”

Geevarghese also highlighted Obama’s ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. “Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition’s ‘othering’ – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream.”

Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories with Zohran Mamdani in New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.

Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the DSA, said: “Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are.”

Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength. Nina Turner, a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: “President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement.”

“He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base,” she added. “Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has ‘that thing.’ He’s a force.”

“The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn’t make a whole lot of change,” said Turner. “People were hopeful, though, and it’s the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations.”

Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:00:09 GMT

With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement

The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.

It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.

Yet as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, potentially faces up to 10 years in prison, another narrative has now taken hold. A miscarriage of justice has taken place, according to messages pumped out across his own media platforms and the ecosystem of self-styled “citizen journalists”. Some carried wild commentary during the trial, including from Robinson himself, who wondered aloud about a “Muslim” member of the jury.

Other voices have since joined in, including Reform UK members and Rupert Lowe, the leader of the Restore Britain party and Nigel Farage’s main rival for hard-right voters. “Tommy Robinson has been found guilty – it is my view that the system has, again, treated him unfairly. We live in dark times,” tweeted Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth.

Evidence at Southwark crown court heard how Robinson used what the prosecution described as “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” against Daily Mail reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after they reported on his alleged role influencing the 2024 Southport riots.

They were forced to employ security or leave their homes, while a statement from Young’s daughter told of encounters outside the family address with men believed to have been sent by Robinson, a self-styled champion of women’s safety.

Robinson also admitted “paying” for the personal number of the editor of the Daily Mail, Ted Verity, who was left a message in which Robinson threatened to make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”.

While Robinson will learn his fate on 16 December, there are now wider implications for Britain’s far right. If he goes to jail again, the far right will be deprived of its most effective and – arguably – most charismatic leader, with little or no apparent replacement.

The obvious heir apparent is anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, AKA Danny Tommo, the leader of the Patriot Platform movement that has brought groups of masked men on to the streets of Dover and other towns this year. He, however, is in custody ahead of a trial over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the Channel. He has denied wrongdoing.

“With the Robinson conviction and Thomas being away there is definitely a leadership void in the anti-migrant space, with no obvious significant figure who can step in,” said Joe Mulhall, director of research at Hope Not Hate, which has closely monitored the recent targeting of asylum accommodation and Robinson’s own rallies.

“It’s a really disparate scene made up of lots of little groupuscules, and I think the most likely thing we will see are lots of ad hoc actions being taken by various self-styled ‘patriot groups’. That can be harder to monitor and police, but this conviction is clearly a big blow for the movement nationally.”

The wind has also been taken out of the sails of the anti-migrant movement by other police arrests, including in connection with vandalism attacks targeting houses in multiple occupation (HMOs).

Of continuing concern to observers of the far right is the role of Elon Musk, who Robinson once again thanked for bankrolling his legal expenses after the multibillionaire owner of X was credited with supporting the activist’s terror charges acquittal last year.

One day alone at Southwark court cost £20,000, Robinson told supporters, a drop in the ocean to Musk. Perhaps not surprisingly, others on the far right have been eyeing up that aid.

Question marks now hover over a supposed pivot by Robinson and others around him towards encouraging a voter registration drive by their supporters, though Mulhall points out that Robinson had already appeared to be struggling with this year’s takeoff of protests.

“Patriot Platform suddenly emerged and you could see him [Robinson] scrambling to try to keep up with a support base who had already become quite impatient with what they viewed as his money-making grift,” Mulhall said. Over recent weeks, Robinson’s X feed has been taken up with reposting old footage of him confronting journalists and others in a bid to reinforce his direct action credentials.

One figure who is looking over his shoulder at Robinson, however, is Farage. The Reform UK leader responded with sarcasm when asked about the conviction, and he has clearly changed his party’s policy on permitting members who support Robinson.

Divisions could reignite between figures such as Richard Tice, vocal in the past about not wanting to have anything to do with Robinson and “his lot”, and Reform members embracing the narrative that he has become a martyr.

Meanwhile, Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison, in the worst case, although sentencing guidelines provide a wide range of flexibility to Mr Justice Cavanagh, who will first consider culpability.

A specialist criminal law barrister told the Guardian that at least two “high culpability” factors could be considered. Robinson telling journalists he was coming to get them could amount to “conduct intended to maximise fear or distress”, while hiring an investigator suggested a “high degree of planning and/or sophisticated offence”.

“In terms of harm, I suspect it will be seen in the most serious category, particularly as at least one victim moved house as a result,” the barrister said. “When it comes to the type of sentence, Robinson’s problems are that his track record of previous offences raises questions about the prospect of rehabilitation. There is also a lack of strong personal mitigation and he presents an ongoing risk, namely to journalists who say something he disagrees with.

“The judge might decide that, given the current prison overcrowding crisis, a suspended sentence will suffice. If it’s suspended for the full three years in line with guidelines, it could well have a greater impact on reining in his behaviour.”

This article was amended on 1 November 2026 to correctly refer to the 2024 Southport riots; an earlier version had described these as the Southend riots.

‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each other

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:00:08 GMT

As deadpan spoof documentarian Philomena Cunk returns with a new series on cinema, her creators discuss meeting J-Lo, their worst ever jobs – and why artificial intelligence is like mad cow disease

She has tackled Britain, conquered the world and even grappled with life itself. Now Philomena Cunk is back on our screens – looking as miserable and confused as ever – to take on her biggest subject yet: cinema.

Cinema, the iconically stupid presenter explains, is not just mankind’s greatest achievement but also a world where “men can be heroes, women can get off with heroes, and nobody ever goes to the toilet – unless you’re watching a specialist film from Japan”. So if you’ve ever wanted to know why “Citizen Ken” always has carrots in his pockets, where the word auteur comes from (“They felt they oughta get all the credit”) or how Benedict Cumberbatch reacts to the hardest-hitting questions of his career (such as “Who are you?”), this is quite literally the only place you’ll ever find the answers.

It has been 13 years since Diane Morgan and Charlie Brooker’s comic creation hit our screens, growing from an amusing segment on Brooker’s show Weekly Wipe into one of the most beloved figures on TV. To celebrate this new three-part series we’ve brought Morgan and Brooker together to chat about everything from defecating robots to dinner dates with Kanye West, and what it feels like to imagine a blue horse (there’s weirdly quite a lot about this).

It’s a busy time for them both. Brooker is preparing for the launch of Blackmere, his deadpan detective show due on Netflix early next year, which he says will be in the vein of Airplane! and The Naked Gun. “The title will end up annoying me and that’s all my own fault,” he says. “It’s how Americans say ‘Black Mirror’ and I thought: that’s actually a really good name for a policeman.” As for Morgan, she is on a roll at the moment: her sitcom Ann Droid, about a robotic care assistant, garnered rave reviews, and she recently survived five episodes of Prime Video’s Last One Laughing. “People thought Cunk would be good training for that because she never laughs,” she says. “What they don’t realise is that I do crack up during the interviews, they just cut those bits out.”

When we meet, Morgan has also just gone viral for chatting to J-Lo at the Stella McCartney show in Paris. So, before we get to anything else, what on earth were they chatting about?

Diane Morgan Well she’d just done a film with Brett Goldstein, so I told her that I used to do standup with him and that I enjoyed the film. Charlie Brooker Is that the best you could do? DM Well it’s something isn’t it? What should I have said? Asked her what she’s doing later?

Who’s the most unlikely person you’ve been in conversation with, Charlie? CB Oh, I know the answer to this! It’s Kanye West. It was a couple of years ago. I actually had dinner with him. I don’t know if this is an anecdote for public consumption, really, but … it was quite a bizarre and sad occasion. I ended up thinking: “He’s not well.”

Why did you meet up? CB He wanted to meet because he’d seen a Black Mirror episode and liked it very much … DM Was it one of the earlier funny ones? CB [Deliberately ignoring her] I can tell you which one it was. It was called Metalhead. It’s got your mate Maxine Peake in it and a robot dog. DM Honestly, how dead inside would you have to be to get a robot dog instead of a lovely little rescue dog? CB But a robot pet wouldn’t die! That’s the reason I don’t have a pet in London, because I get very sad pre-emptively imagining that pet getting squashed. DM When you say you “imagine” it, what do you mean? Because you told me once that you had that thing where you can’t see images in your mind [aphantasia]. So if I say: “Picture a blue horse”, everyone else pictures it but you can’t. CB I think I can picture things. It’s just not like on telly where they have a flashback. DM It is for me. It’s full surround sound, and so much detail. CB [Closing his eyes] If I think of a blue horse, I don’t see it … It’s more like my brain is describing it to me. DM That’s fascinating, isn’t it? The man who wrote Black Mirror can’t picture a blue horse! Whereas mine’s got reins on, it’s got facial expressions, it’s going … [Morgan blows an enormous raspberry while circling her head round in a convincingly horse-like manner]. CB OK, what’s it doing right now? Is it lifting its tail? Can you see its bum? DM Well I can now. Now you’ve said that.

This is actually exactly the kind of material my editor asked for in this piece. CB Did they say: “Can it be mainly about their psychic projections of horses?” DM It is interesting, though. Have you been diagnosed with that or … CB Diagnosed with what? DM No imagination. CB Critics might say I have, yes. DM Do you have dreams? CB I definitely see things in dreams and imagine that they’re real. Once I had a dream where a little circle appeared to signal a reel change, like when you’re watching an old film on TV. And the dream itself was about teachers at the school who were assassinating people. So fuck you with your “you can’t see anything in your mind’s eye” nonsense. I think our brains all have different operating systems, like Windows or Mac OS or Linux. DM There’s actually a man who got to 40-odd and discovered he only had half a brain. CB Was his name Jacob Rees-Mogg? DM He was actually an accountant. And he’d been living totally fine with half a brain. They were like, how can this be? Because you think of all the areas of the brain, like, the hippocampus and, er, the other areas of the brain … I just think that’s incredible. That basically you don’t really need a brain. I actually think your brain’s more like an aerial. So we are actually in the cloud and we’re being livestreamed to the receptors in our skulls. And when you die, your body dies, but your consciousness just goes back to the cloud. CB That’s beautiful, actually. What’s the point of that, though? DM Well, what’s the point of anything? Don’t go pulling at that thread! Right, come on, let’s start!

Did you have any idea Philomena Cunk would be such an enduring character? DM No, I was told by people on the programme that I would get a huge backlash because I wasn’t Charlie. They said brace yourself for a lot of shit on social media. Because people just want Charlie. Anything that isn’t Charlie is just people going: “Where’s Charlie, this is fucking shit!” CB And now it’s the other way round!

Was Diane’s audition for Philomena Cunk the first time you met? CB Yeah! Oh, actually, no! Because she’s got an anecdote about me being horrible at the Edinburgh festival. DM Everyone in my family used to read your Guardian column. It started with my dad. He rarely laughed at anything, but he would be crying tears reading your column. And I’d be like: “What’s so funny?” So he’d read a bit of it and we’d all laugh, as a family, together. And then they started printing your photo. CB And that ruined it for you? DM It meant I recognised you at the Edinburgh festival. So I went over and was like: “You’re Charlie Brooker!” And you said: “Yeah, what do you want?” So I said: “I read your column, it’s really funny.” And you said: “So?” CB Surely I was joking. Sometimes when people come up and say: “I really love Black Mirror”, I reply, “What’s wrong with you?” It’s just a joke! DM Looking back, of course it was a joke. But I didn’t know that then. I was mortified. I thought: “He hates me!” and I was crushed. I couldn’t even think about him for years. When the auditions came up for Philomena, I knew I wanted it more than anything … but that Charlie hated me. Whereas actually you didn’t give a shit.

Philomena Cunk was supposed to be a posh character originally, right? CB We used to get people going: “Oh you’re mocking working-class accents,” because of the Barry Shitpeas character. So the idea was to add an airhead, middle-class, yummy-mummy, Chelsea-tractor cupcake blogger to the show. Hence the name Philomena Cunk. DM You’d never get someone called Philomena in Bolton – you’d get your head kicked in. CB I was watching all the audition tapes and wasn’t quite sure who the character was. DM Luckily I’d got the guts up to ask if I could do it in my own accent because I thought that was funnier. CB When I saw you doing it in your flat, fucking depressed, unimpressed-with-everything tone, I was doubled over with laughter. DM Ah, that’s so sweet … you’re forgiven for the Edinburgh thing now. CB The strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever … DM We interviewed Michael Bay for this new series and the crew were a bit terrified of him because they’re big, big fans. But I wasn’t bothered. Because [whispers] I don’t really watch a lot of films. It actually helps that I don’t know or care who these experts are. Actually, I think we confused Michael Bay because I asked him how much he paid for his trainers and he thought I meant actual people who trained him. He said I was asking odd questions. DM I often talk about my mate Paul, though, so that might get confusing.

There are lots of jokes about AI in these new episodes – mainly Cunk challenging experts by saying she’s asked AI. Do either of you use AI? CB I use it when I’m somewhere I don’t know and want to find, say, a good barbecue restaurant that doesn’t serve pork. And then when you turn up it no longer exists. But other than that, no. I would never use it to help write something. DM They’re trying to force it on you, aren’t they? But I won’t even let it do that [Mimics flicking something away]. CB I’m a bit annoyed that there’s new technology and I don’t like it. I think it’s more that I don’t like the people who are making it. Having said that, I think the idea that it’s going to take over the world and destroy us all is a bit far-fetched.

It has started speaking its own language, though, according to reports … CB Yeah, but it’s just been fed on scraps of itself, hasn’t it? It’s a bit like when we started feeding cows on scraps of cow, and in the end they all got mad cow disease. So AI might look like it’s talking in some advanced language but actually all it’s saying is [sticks out tongue and waggles his head]: “Braaaappurgglefluuuurrrk!”

Did you ever think technology would advance this rapidly? CB Not really. Our Alexa recently updated and started speaking in a very human voice, which really freaked my son out. It was like, “Hey, yeah man, we can do that if you like” … a bit uncanny valley. We’ve had to change its voice back to the previous setting. When really what we should be doing is taking it out into the garden and smashing it with a shoe.

Diane, you don’t use AI, but in a way you’ve written quite a pro-AI comedy with Ann Droid? DM Have I? Oh yeah. I suppose I have. [Anxiously] Is that what people are saying? CB It’s what he’s saying, right now! DM It wasn’t supposed to be a statement on anything. It was just supposed to be a funny show about a robot and an old woman. It’s different when it’s your own show. On another person’s show you just say the words and if it’s shit then it’s not your fault. But with this everything rests on you. I remember when I first had the idea. I pitched it to the BBC and then I suddenly thought: “Oh shit, they’re going to make me be the robot aren’t they?” And they did. So I spent a year freaking out about it. Because obviously if you’re on telly pretending to be a robot and it doesn’t go well then it’s going to look really daft isn’t it?

So you went to robot school … DM I did! With a guy called Dan.

What did he teach you? DM Never blink, mainly. He also taught you not to bob your head. To always walk like this [gets up and glides across the room in a chillingly robot-like manner].

Would you fancy robot school, Charlie? CB Well I am quite stiff. I’ve got a very bad back. I’d quite like to be a robot, though. They don’t have to defecate.

Is that something they taught you at robot school? DM No we didn’t cover that.

Did robot school require you to go full method with your character? DM I mean, I practised at home. But I didn’t spend a day as a robot. My job’s not that weird.

What is the weirdest job you’ve ever had? CB I know what Diane is going to say … DM The worming tablets factory? CB Yeah! Did you ever eat them? DM Eat what? A worming tablet? Of course I didn’t. They’re for dogs. And I’m not a dog. Also, I’ve not got worms. You’ve not done horrible jobs like that, have you? CB When I worked at CeX we had a lot of people coming in trying to sell stolen laptops. And a boss who would make us do things, like, one day I had to clear out the back room. DM [Sarcastically] Oh, that sounds terrible. CB It was! It was full of shit and a dead cat!

And look where you both are now! DM I owe it all to Charlie! He totally made everything happen for me. All my subsequent career in comedy is down to him … I owe him everything! CB Ah, that’s lovely. You’ve had to be really nice to me there and it’s all on tape!

Would you like to say anything nice back? CB I’d say that Diane has naturally funny bones. And skin and eyes. She operates on a unique comic frequency – it’s rare to find a performer like that. She’s totally tuned in to the words which means in turn the writing room can tune into her. She elevates everything. Can I be sick now? I don’t like saying nice things.

Cunk on Cinema will air on BBC Two and iPlayer from 12 November.

Why Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunity

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 09:00:07 GMT

The PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. But his EU bridge-building could also resurrect its dreams of independence

Fifty years ago this month, a group of leftwing Scots gathered in the Golden Lion hotel in Stirling for the inaugural conference of a new political party. The “Scottish Labour party” had formally split from Labour at the beginning of 1976, driven by disillusionment over the party’s timid proposals for a new Scottish assembly. They were led by the firebrand MP for South Ayrshire, Jim Sillars, who promised to take Scotland’s Labour tradition back to its roots in both socialism and home rule.

Sillars’ new party was a media sensation in Scotland, and quickly joined by public intellectuals such as Tom Nairn, Hamish Henderson and Neal Ascherson. It offered something new and exciting: a fusion of the two movements that were battling for Scotland’s soul in a decade that had already been defined by electoral clashes between Labour and the Scottish National party.

The party struggled, however, to enthuse the working-class voters on whom Sillars had gambled his future. It did attract a handful of Trotskyist activists from the International Marxist Group, and at the October 1976 conference, Sillars orchestrated a heavy-handed purge of the far left, causing proceedings to degenerate into near-violence. At one point, a member of the party’s national organising committee summoned up Ayrshire’s mining heritage against the “entryist” threat, yelling: “We should get our fucking pit boots on and wade into them!”

Andy Burnham was not quite as forthright earlier this month, when, midway through the SNP’s conference in Aberdeen, he delivered his own speech in Motherwell, offering to cooperate on further devolution within Scotland. The conference itself was far more peaceful, the SNP having already shed its “fundamentalist” wing with the breakaway of Alex Salmond’s Alba party (which Sillars, it’s worth noting, also endorsed). The National Economic Council meeting on Friday between Burnham, John Swinney and the Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, emphasised the shared agenda of three governments seeking to combine devolved power with reindustrialisation – precisely what the SLP was calling for in 1976. But the SLP, which never recovered from its public meltdown in Stirling, made another contribution to the cause that matters intensely to the relationship between Burnham and the SNP.

Keen to make national self-determination palatable to socialists, Sillars’ party sought to remove any hint of separatism from its politics by embracing the new European Economic Community, arguing for “independence in Europe”. With goods, people and services moving freely across borders, independence would no longer mean separation, but simply real equality between self-governing, co-dependent nations.

After the SLP’s collapse, Sillars found his way into the SNP, rising through the ranks to become deputy leader in 1991. “Independence in Europe” came with him. The SNP made some of its first breakthroughs in the 1970s as a Eurosceptic party, distinguishing itself from the three pro-EEC Westminster parties by campaigning against membership in 1975 with the slogan “No voice, no entry”. But by the 1990s, it had completely reversed this position, helped by the new European Union’s growing emphasis on the rights of small nations and minority cultures.

The SNP’s newfound Europeanism reflected and reinforced that of the country it came to govern. It was helped, too, by Scotland’s tendency to define itself against English politics, which became more Eurosceptic over the same period. When the SNP’s success produced a referendum on independence, Europe was one of the central issues. An independent Scotland, voters were told, would be a new state, and would therefore have to reapply to join the EU. Scots voted against independence partly to protect their European passports. Two years later, they voted overwhelmingly to remain in that larger union too.

But England, with 10 times Scotland’s population, swung the result the other way. Scotland was thus asked, over the period of just two years and two votes, to choose between its membership of the UK and of the EU – but in the wrong order. Immediately after the Brexit vote, support for independence briefly surged, but then dropped. Scots realised they did not fancy yet another wrenching break-up. It was only with the arrival of Boris Johnson as prime minister, the conclusion of a hard Brexit, and the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic that “yes” moved into a consistent lead.

Today, yes and no are neck and neck, but many independence campaigners remain concerned about how another referendum campaign might unfold. The fundamental political case for independence has always been that British politics is overwhelmingly Anglocentric, and Scotland’s interests are marginalised. While Brexit has deepened this structural complaint, it has also transformed the economic arguments against independence: if Scotland were to vote for independence and rejoin the EU tomorrow, it would suddenly face a hard border with the rest of the UK, which buys more of Scotland’s exports than every other country in the world put together – including the whole EU.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Some nationalists argue that, under such circumstances, Scotland could be granted the same status as Northern Ireland, which has found a middle ground between European and UK markets. But Northern Ireland has been given special treatment because of the simmering threat of a return to open conflict over the partition of Ireland; Scotland is not a remotely serious candidate for civil war over its borders with England or Europe and would be highly unlikely to be treated with the same sensitivity by the global community.

Scottish nationalism’s problem is also its greatest selling point: it is not motivated by any deep ethnic grievance, and as such its supporters are hard to mobilise into the kind of bloody-minded self-sacrifice that might justify some deeper rupture with England. It is founded, instead, on a modern, peaceful and democratic discontent with Westminster’s gradual abandonment of everything that seemed to make Britain worthwhile: good jobs, functioning public services, international cooperation and a vaguely shared moral compass.

Burnham is therefore a meaningful threat to the SNP, for this is precisely the nostalgic vision of Britain that he promises to restore – with messaging skills that can finally rival the SNP’s and promises of “regional empowerment”. Yet it offers an opportunity as well. It is hard to imagine that Burnham, whether he has three years in power or a decade, will truly be able to resurrect the lost world of dignified work, British industry and social security that he conjures up in his speeches. But it looks increasingly plausible that he may have to rebuild some of Britain’s relationships with Europe as a precondition of his wider agenda. That would repair the one bridge that Scotland truly needs intact for a successful sprint towards independence, should the rest of Burnham’s project falter.

Rory Scothorne is a historian and writer based in Edinburgh

Rampant Salford hint that Beckham’s lofty ambitions are not a pipe dream

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 08:00:07 GMT

The aim of reaching the Championship looks more realistic for a Manchester club in the shadow of City and United

After seven seasons in League Two, Salford City are finally threatening to match the hype brought by their high-profile owners. First it was the Class of ’92 who guided them up through the non-league system into the fourth tier but failed to progress any further. Gary Neville and David Beckham remain, part of a new group that took over in May 2025, with this year beginning to look transformational after securing an eighth straight win, against Exeter, to put them five points clear at the top.

The budget has increased, allowing the club to sign a number of players who will feel they are above League Two standard. Striker Macaulay Langstaff arrived from Millwall; the last time he played at this level, he scored 28 league goals in a season for Notts County. Match-winner Will Aimson spent the past two seasons in the division above with Wigan and has dropped down because of Salford’s project.

In terms of personnel, the most notable change was in the dugout where 48-year-old Peter Cklamovski replaced Karl Robinson, who was sacked after a desperate performance in the playoff final loss to Notts County. Cklamovski’s previous experience came working under Ange Postecoglou before becoming a head coach in his own right in Asia, most recently taking charge of the Malaysia national team. Such was his unknown status, Salford’s chief football adviser Paul Scholes had to Google the Australian before he was appointed.

Off the pitch, Salford reverted to wearing orange, the traditional club colour that was changed by the Class of ’92, who wanted the shirts to reflect their links to Manchester United. The fans voted for it, democracy in action where previously the owners knew best. Beckham has turned Inter Miami into a global brand worth more than £1bn, making pink a key part of its identity. Lionel Messi shirt sales helped the hue travel, with kids across the UK spotted with the famous No 10 on the back. Beckham selected the shade of orange – and the badge was redesigned – but whether Langstaff et al can have the same effect as Messi remains to be seen. “Not many others play in orange, so if you’re going to see that kit around Manchester, you would know it’s not United or City,” says Danny Shepherd of The Future Is Orange podcast.

Attracting new fans is the aim but Salford face competition from much bigger clubs in the region. Even with Manchester City in a crisis and United’s form spiralling, convincing locals to head down to the AIG Stadium is difficult. Cklamovski’s attractive style is a deliberate ploy but the Ammies have the fourth-worst average attendance in League Two. It is optimistic to think they can create a Championship fanbase, even with subsidised away travel.

Cklamovski is making a name for himself with the aggressive attacking football he learned under his mentor. He started with three defeats but since then the Australian has found a pragmatic approach, mixing his playing out from the back ideals with an openness to be more direct when required, which brought a change in fortunes.

“I’d be disappointed if we didn’t go up because of the strength in depth,” says Shepherd. “Last season we had certain linchpin players that if they weren’t available, then we had either a utility player, a youngster or someone whose quality is so much lower that it’s like falling off a cliff. I’m not a rose-tinted spectacles fan, I can’t see how this team cannot get promoted – I think we should win the league at a canter.”

The confidence was not fully apparent in the first half as Salford were sloppy and struggled to create chances, while defensively vulnerable against a resolute Exeter. Goalkeeper Will Norris was booked for rushing out of his area and fouling Sonny Cox, who got his own back by scoring the opener for a side on a fine run themselves, unbeaten in the previous five.

Salford only came to life after the disappointing Luke Molyneux was forced off through injury, replaced by Daniel Udoh in the 55th minute. Energy levels increased and were rewarded by Luke Garbutt’s leveller at the back post after Langstaff’s fine work on the right.

Salford were on top after that and got their reward from the unfamiliar source of former Exeter centre-back Aimson, who sent a shot into the top corner from 25 yards to keep the run going and show this team have character to battle back in difficult circumstances. “We’ve got to stay really focused and diligent,” Cklamovski says. “We’ve got a nice bit of momentum, but don’t look too far forward. Eight wins in a row or 11 unbeaten however you want to look at it, just don’t look back.” He need not worry, there are plenty of people above him looking to the future.

English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 08:00:05 GMT

UK children’s minister Josh MacAlister has travelled to Copenhagen to see what can be learned from Danish system

In a quiet suburb on the outskirts of Copenhagen sits a large white house, set back from the road behind a purple-leaved plum tree. It looks much like the rest of the buildings on the street and there is little outward sign this is Josephine Schneider’s House, considered one of the best children’s homes in the world.

Danish children’s homes are often cited as the gold standard of children’s residential care globally. They are now being studied by the British government as it tries to create a roadmap out of the crisis in which its own children’s home system has become mired.

Last year there were 669 children living in illegal, unregistered children’s homes across England, with councils paying more than £125m of taxpayers’ money to keep them there.

Overall spending on children’s homes soared 96% in five years to over £3.1bn in 2023-24, while standards have dropped, private equity firms are cashing in and a growing number of children are being sent to homes hundreds of miles away.

The situation is dire, the children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, admits. “We now have this shadow system of unregistered, illegal homes, which is certainly not providing therapeutic support and the costs are huge,” he said. “We need big changes, a major shake up, and I spend as many hours as I can a week on children’s social care reform.”

Earlier this week, MacAlister visited Denmark to see how its children’s homes operate and what can be exported back to England, as part of a Department for Education review into how the sector can be improved.

The 140-year-old Josephine Schneider’s House, which houses 12 children and young adults aged six to 23, is starkly different from many British equivalents.

In the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen staffed by the head chef, Rasmus, who cooks the children’s meals, lunch boxes and after-school snacks – pizza rolls are a particular favourite. He works with the children himself, encouraging them to help make the food and come grocery shopping.

The rest of the staff are all degree-level professionals in social pedagogy, a discipline focusing on psychology, child development and ethics, and they strive to recreate a traditional family home by cooking, eating and socialising with the children.

“We don’t have an in-house therapist but everything we do is therapeutic,” said Mads Sørensen, deputy director of the home.

One member of staff sleeps in the house at night and wakes the children up each day at 7am. “We ask them how they like to be woken up, to help them feel safe and create that predictability, make their nervous system calm a bit,” Sørensen said.

Many of the children here have suffered physical, emotional and social neglect, and issues such as self-harm, insomnia and eating disorders are common.

Unlike children’s homes in England, where many children report being isolated and cut off from family and friends, here children are encouraged to have friends stay at the weekends and holidays, there are regular parents evenings, including a Christmas banquet.

Each child also has a team of two to three staff members working with them on their education and wellbeing. In a semi-independent flat on the top floor live the older residents, aged 17 and above, who have their own living area and kitchen as they start to transition into adulthood.

The young people buy their own food and do their own chores, under the guidance of staff, preparing them for independent life beyond the home. They are allowed to stay in the home up until the age of 23, and encouraged to return for regular visits beyond that age.

This is a far cry from children’s homes in England, which teenagers must leave as soon as they turn 18, part of the cliff-edge loss of support that is causing the early deaths of care leavers.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

MacAlister said he may change this. “Getting rid of the really binary date of birth point to decide where you live is something I’m really persuaded by,” he said. “I hear of children being forced to move when they turn 18, even if they’re in the middle of sitting their A-levels. We have to move away from that.”

He also wants to import some of the culture from Danish children’s homes, particularly their focus on personal growth and maintaining family relationships.

“A lot of residential care in England is actually about adults containing their own anxiety and concerns about teenagers, and that’s a really poor model,” MacAlister said. “The first question is always ‘how do we protect ourselves from risk?’ which is not what we should be asking first. It’s very different here in Denmark.”

The quality of staff is crucial, and something at the heart of the ongoing review, which is being led by Emmanuel Akpan-Inwang, the director of Lighthouse Pedagogy Trust, which runs a children’s home in Sutton based on pedagogy principles.

“What’s interesting about Denmark is working in a children’s home is a career that people really want to do,” he said. “It’s competitive. Homes are able to select really great people. They support and train them. They stay in the sector for long periods of time.

“But we can’t simply lift and shift the system to England. The Danes have spent more than 40 years developing it. But we can learn from it.”

At Josephine Schneider’s House, many staff members have been there 10 years or longer. In the UK, about 53% of children’s home staff have worked in the sector for three years or less. Poor pay, working conditions and a lack of training force many to leave the sector early.

But underpinning Danish children’s homes is extensive state funding – a third of homes are publicly owned, 42% are not-for-profit and 27% are private profit.

By contrast, in England, 83% of children’s homes places are now privately run, with some operators recording profit margins of more than 20%.

The government has passed laws giving itself the power to intervene and cap profits by private providers but has yet to use it, with MacAlister saying they need to wait for a new “market oversight body” to provide full transparency of exactly how much money is being made before they can push ahead.

The government of Wales is moving more quickly, and will ban all for-profit providers in children’s social care by 2030. But MacAlister said it would not be easy to replicate this in England, where numbers are much bigger.

“We need to massively boost local authorities so they can take back control of the whole purchasing process, curb demand by making sure more children can live in foster homes or kinship arrangements, and shape a system on our terms, not one that is driven by profit,” MacAlister said.

I’m sick of smug celebrities on the podcast circuit. No wonder there’s a fuss when someone speaks the truth

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:00:04 GMT

It was so refreshing to hear Aaron Sorkin admit he was bad at parts of directing after his movie flop. If only others could be as frank

By most accounts, Aaron Sorkin’s new film The Social Reckoning, a follow-up to his 2010 smash-hit The Social Network, is a flop. The film critic Mark Kermode’s response to seeing it was that Sorkin, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest living screenwriters, is “not a great director”.

It seems that Sorkin agrees. Because Sorkin is very famous, he has had to do the rounds talking about the film in the media, which led to his appearance on the Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast earlier this week, in which he addressed these kinds of criticisms head on. “I’m very worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts that you can’t learn,” he said. “In addition to having absorbed none of the science of filmmaking, I have – and this is a problem in a visual medium – I have no visual sensibility at all, it turns out.”

It’s not the first time a director has made a confession in this vein. Sam Raimi, for instance, memorably told the Nerdist podcast in 2014 that the reason Spider-Man 3 sucked is that he “messed up plenty” because he “didn’t really believe in all the characters”. But someone like Sorkin, a man with five Primetime Emmy wins and four Academy Award nominations, can afford to fess up to some failings. And it’s a pretty funny thing to say, as he does on this podcast, immediately after the host waxes lyrical about all his glittering career highlights and staggering creative ability.

On the one hand, I think the world would be a better place if more people admitted that they are not that good at their jobs. I’d have loved it if the guy I hired to hang some pictures in my last flat, and who positioned several of them as if they were trying to escape through the ceiling and then merrily gouged a hole in one wall before claiming the wall itself was made of some substance previously unknown to masonry, had just held his hands up and said: “Look. My bad. I am not very good at this.”

But it got me thinking about the whole podcast circuit. Podcasts, and the increasingly widespread “video podcast”, have become a cornerstone of the film publicity world. There are the big hitters such as the A24 Podcast and The Big Picture, but there are also endless podcasts you’ve never even heard of, where figures from the entertainment world have to engage in hours of conversation every time they have a new project out. Unlike the old requirement for a celebrity to commit to a couple of broadsheet interviews or a 10-minute slot for some late-night arts programme, the new demand for hours of sprawling chat just ends up being undignified for all involved.

I’ve interviewed actors and directors, and while most of them are media-trained and polite enough to seem engaged in talking about their work, it cannot be fun for them to meander around the houses again and again on the same subject. Making people talk about the same thing over and over is quite literally the basis of certain forms of torture.

I hate to think of the kinds of things I might claim about my own work if I was subjected to hours of repetitive chatter about it. Do we really need to hear actors and directors do so much extemporaneous talk about what they do? Especially when so few of them – mea culpas of this Sorkin kind excepted – are saying anything other than “yeah it was a great experience, I love movies and this new movie of mine in particular”?

I understand that the publicity circuit is a built-in part of making creative work in our digital age. People have to hear about the film for people to buy tickets to the film. The microphones are not going away. But I think that if we must have them, let’s have more strange admissions of incompetence or, even better, straight-up lies, to enliven the conversation.

The only person who seems to be squeezing some personal enjoyment from the media merry-go-round is Robert Pattinson, who once claimed he watched a clown die in a car explosion in an interview for the Today show while promoting Water for Elephants in 2011.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

So, more power to Sorkin, but next time maybe claim that you, I don’t know, secretly run a Facebook group for fans of the 1996 chimp comedy Dunston Checks In. Have a little fun with it.

Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist
