‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:00:04 GMT

There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis?

The home of 85-year-old Uta Frith does not exactly look like the latest front in the culture wars. Located in a serenely quiet corner of north-west London, it suggests a life still well lived, a set of deep interests and an idyllic kind of retirement. There are so many books that some are reachable only using a very tall ladder. The four hours I spend talking to her – and her husband Chris, an expert in schizophrenia – are an absolute pleasure. There is no sense of outrage or upset: even when I ask her about the stream of hostile and abusive emails she has recently received, she is relaxed and phlegmatic. “I tend to cope by just deleting them,” she says. “I don’t dwell on it.”

“It” is a reference to the controversy kicked up by her recently expressed views on a subject that sits at the heart of Frith’s academic career: what it is to be autistic, and who should or shouldn’t qualify for a diagnosis. Back in March, Dame Uta Frith – she was honoured with the title seven years ago – gave an interview to TES magazine (formerly the Times Educational Supplement) scattered with stark pronouncements. Among them was a claim that the so-called autistic spectrum has “gone on being more and more accommodating”, to the point that it “has come to its collapse”. Then, in August, she published a piece in the academic journal Psychological Medicine claiming autism was in dire danger of being turned from a “precise, clinical” term into a “vague, culturally amplified identity category”.

What she said has inevitably added to the cacophony of political and media noise about rising autism diagnoses. In the UK, there was a 787% increase between 1998 and 2018, with the rise greater for women than men, and the single biggest jump among adults; credible American stats have shown an increase across the whole population of 175% between 2011 and 2022, with the largest rise occurring among 26- to 34 year-olds (in both countries, childhood rates have also leapt up). Once, Frith agreed with the idea of a broad autistic spectrum; now, she has come to the conclusion that many people diagnosed as adults are so different from the autistic people whose condition becomes obvious in their early years and have learning disabilities that most of the former group do not merit the label “autistic” at all.

“Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells me. “And then we have a subgroup of people who used to be called neurotic, who have all sorts of mental issues, including anxiety. And a kind of hypersensitivity.”

Over the summer, Frith did an interview with the Times’s Andrew Billen, in which she expressed opinions about the TV presenter and autism activist Chris Packham – who was diagnosed with what was then known as Asperger’s syndrome when he was 44 – which she says she did not expect to make it into print. “He cannot be autistic in my opinion,” Frith said. “It is just absolutely absurd to me that somebody who can communicate as brilliantly as he does – that is what I call a blatant contraindication.” The day after we meet, Packham is scheduled to pay Frith a visit with a BBC camera crew: as with just about everything she talks about, her feelings on this prospect are characteristically relaxed (I subsequently learn that they got on very well).

I have a 20-year-old autistic son, James, who also has learning disabilities – as well as an amazing talent for music – and now goes to a specialist further education college. When he was diagnosed 17 years ago, understanding and awareness of autism seemed to be moving in roughly the right direction. I could never have anticipated the way it has ballooned into a subject of such controversy, which puts me and millions of others in a worldwide community of people who now follow the news with a mixture of bafflement and dread.

On and on it goes. The word “overdiagnosis” is now common currency, partly because of the bestselling book The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist Suzanne O’Sullivan, which claims that autistic people “with the greatest need are becoming invisible” and that there are questions to be asked about diagnoses that cause “more harm than good”. Donald Trump and his health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr look ahead to the absurd prospect of an autism “cure”. The rightwing press and its favoured politicians – whose loathing of any kind of diversity inevitably triggers a mistrust of neurodiversity – rage about how many neurodivergent young people are on disability benefits. Celebrities constantly lay claim to being on the spectrum. Meanwhile, there are real-world tragedies: Jason Arday, for instance, was not only a black Cambridge professor who ended his own life after relentless coverage of his allegedly specious claims about his life story and achievements. He was also autistic – which statistics show put him at a hugely increased risk of suicide.

In December last year, the then health secretary Wes Streeting commissioned three eminent academics to carry out what the government called an “independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”. The result, published a few weeks ago, traced the increase in autism diagnoses to “socio-cultural changes in awareness [and] recognition”, and the fact that “diagnostic concepts have also broadened”. But in some people’s eyes, its authors had tried to have their cake and eat it. “If present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing … towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis,” they said. The review recommended much closer monitoring of privately run clinics that diagnose autism and ADHD. But it also said “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”.

Frith is at pains to stand well away from all this political and cultural hurly-burly, telling the story of her change of mind as a matter of careful thought and worry that, as so-called high-functioning people cast the popular understanding of autism in their image, the needs of more intensely autistic children and adults are in danger of being forgotten. A few minutes after we have talked about the common idea that autism can be a “superpower”, she says, “I have had emails from parents who say, ‘I no longer call my child autistic. When somebody asks, I say he’s intellectually impaired, and they will say, ‘Oh, all right.’ But if I say he’s autistic, they will expect things that are just … not likely.’”

Frith is one of the tiny cluster of people who came up with the understanding of autism now accepted across most of the world. In 1964, she came to London from Germany, and found her niche at the Institute of Psychiatry, connected to the famous Maudsley hospital. She had planned to study obsessive-compulsive disorder, but her head was turned by new research into what were then known as “psychotic” children.

She vividly remembers her first encounters with such kids, at the UK’s first dedicated school for autistic children, in Ealing, west London. “I was fascinated,” she tells me. “The astounding thing was that they could do things I would not expect children who were then called mentally retarded to do.” Like what? “Jigsaw puzzles, tests that would be given to very young children to measure their intelligence. They did pretty well, sometimes in a way that was completely unconventional – like completing the jigsaw with the picture on the underside.”

Frith ran experiments that showed the autistic minds tended to be more responsive to visual cues than words. In 1989, she also came up with the so-called theory of Weak Central Coherence: the idea that autistic people tend to fixate on detail rather than big, over-arching things such as stories and themes.

While all this was going on, she was also keeping the company of the psychiatrist Lorna Wing (who had an autistic daughter) and the psychologist Judith Gould – who would spend four years in the 1970s transforming the understanding of autism. Focusing on the London borough of Camberwell, they interviewed more than 900 teachers of children under 15 who, at one point or another, had needed either psychiatric treatment or attention from social care services. They then visited and closely observed every one of the 132 children those interviews suggested might be autistic, which eventually led to the conclusion that autism was a much more widespread and complex phenomenon than had been previously thought, best considered a “continuum” – or, as they were to later term it, a “spectrum”, a word intended to conjure up images of how light works, combining different colours into a single beam.

Autism, Wing said, ran “from the most profoundly physically and mentally retarded person … to the most able, highly intelligent person with social impairment in its subtlest form”. But what unified everyone on the spectrum was what she and Gould called the “Triad of Impairments”: problems with social skills, reciprocal (ie give-and-take) language and “social imagination”, most obviously evident in children not understanding the concept of pretending while they play. Though subsequent diagnostic criteria have changed – it is now accepted, for instance, that autism usually involves sensory issues including heightened or lowered sensitivity to sound, light, texture, heat and cold – these ideas are still at the heart of what most people think autism is, along with a tendency to deep obsessions, or what the autism vernacular calls “special interests”.

Frith says when the idea of a spectrum arrived, “I was more than happy. I was always worried about the sort of marginal cases, so that was one good thing. And the other was that we had more people to work with.”

The subsequent story of autism included Wing’s creation (in 1981) of the category known as Asperger syndrome: a term named after the work with a group of “little professors” of the Austrian psychologist Hans Asperger, now understood as a collaborator in the Nazi extermination of disabled children. Wing used the term to describe autistic people without language issues or learning disabilities. In 1994, it was included in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association and now on its fifth edition. But it was taken out in 2013, leaving “autistic spectrum disorder” as a single broad category, now broken down into three levels: “requiring support”, “requiring substantial support” and “requiring very substantial support”.

By then, Wing – who died in 2014 – and her colleagues’ work had led on to the idea of neurodiversity, and the activism of so-called autistic self-advocates. And as all this happened, Frith says she began to feel increasingly uneasy. “I suddenly realised, maybe 15, 20 years ago,” she says, “that I had talked completely differently about autistic people in the past compared with people who didn’t have learning disabilities and had been diagnosed more recently. I’d used completely different language and completely different arguments. And that seemed to me to be a sign of something not being quite right.”

She is sceptical about some concepts that are now taken for granted by many autistic people and autism specialists. A good example is “masking”: people – particularly women and girls – trying to cover up autistic traits through a painstaking process of copying which, in most accounts, after a day at work or school, leaves them feeling exhausted. “It’s a non-scientific concept, if ever there was one,” she says. “It’s completely unfalsifiable: if you could use the idea that you’re masking – ie you don’t have any symptoms to show … ”

But, I counter, people who mask say, “I have got symptoms to show. And I show them when I get home from school or work or when I’m on my own.”

“But that’s entirely subjective. It’s true that they have fatigue and exhaustion. These are the really important things to notice. But why believe that they are caused by masking?”

Because it’s such an effort, I reply.

“We all do that,” she says. “It’s acting, which is exhausting. But what does that have to do with autism?”

Well, I say, the deficits and impairments they’re concealing are stereotypically autistic. But what Frith craves, on this subject and many others, is scientific certainty. “The studies I’ve seen measure masking on a test with items on it like ‘I copy body language’. And I dismiss that as non-scientific because subjective experience is not reliable.” She is keen to emphasise there is usually a tentative element to what she thinks and says. “I’m not certain. I may be wrong. But I think we’re at a point where it’s useful to have a debate.”

Disagreement with Frith’s opinions has inevitably been led by some of those aforementioned self-advocates. Among them is Mary Doherty, an Irish anaesthetist who was diagnosed at 45 and has a son and daughter who are both also on the spectrum. She has memories from her schooldays of trying desperately to mask her differences, and failing. Now she is one of the founders of Autistic Doctors International, which promotes the idea that medics who are on the spectrum “bring a variety of strengths to healthcare, including an array of benefits for autistic patients”.

We spend 90 minutes talking on an outdoor cafe terrace near London’s Victoria station. Throughout the conversation, Doherty constantly stretches and loosens an elasticated hairband: an example, she says, of the “stimming”, or self-stimulatory behaviour, many autistic people use as a way to calm themselves. Frith and others, she says, are effectively averting their eyes from “the harm that’s done by invalidating people’s life experience. If you are autistic, understanding your autistic nature is life-changing. It’s so damaging to deny that to people, particularly people who are already at risk of mental health problems.”

Even if they have a blurry intersection, I suggest, there is a pretty obvious distinction between her kind of autism and more intense, “classic” varieties, which is part of what people are now arguing about. “It’s not a clear division, she retorts. “If you see me on a bad day … ” So does she feel a strong instinctive affinity with, say, an autistic person who is non-verbal and has learning disabilities? “Yes. And that was probably one of the biggest shocks to me in the earliest days of my advocacy journey.”

One big current argument, as she knows, is that when it comes to public services and healthcare, more confident, articulate autistic people will somehow get to the front of the relevant queues much more quickly than more intensely affected people (or their parents and carers). And as a consequence, people with more complex needs will get neglected. Maybe, in fact, that has been happening already.

In thousands of people’s everyday lives, the debate about supposed “overdiagnosis” – and whether certain people are now prioritised over others – is very real, not least at the proverbial school gates. One mother I speak to, who asks to remain anonymous, lives in the south-east with her partner and two children, one of whom is a girl with an intense kind of autism that seems to defy cliched categories: she is bright and intellectually curious, but also has profound sensory issues and difficulty navigating through the world that means she requires constant support at school.

She has recently heard that one in five of the children in her daughter’s year are reckoned to be autistic. “From day one, I just felt my child’s needs were lost and misunderstood because that word now applies to so many children.” A lot of kids, she says, “find modern school life very difficult. And people are seeking a diagnosis so their child is treated as an individual. I don’t blame them for that. But it isn’t helpful to the children who have a classically autistic inability to cope with those environments.”

She has one other concern. “When my daughter got her diagnosis, I would have described her as high-functioning because she was verbal and she could read and write. But that term has shifted very far, even from my child. It now seems to mean children who can do every sort of activity; it’s becoming unrecognisable. And you wonder: how wide can the spectrum be?”

Is there any way out of what feels like a polarised stalemate? One possible solution is offered by Frith’s one-time protege Simon Baron-Cohen, another autism expert who has felt the heat of cultural controversy, thanks to his theory that autism might be a byword for what he used to call “the extreme male brain”, low on empathising, but good at understanding systems and patterns (earlier this year, he said such language was no longer useful).

Baron-Cohen’s working life has been defined by autism since he began working at a trailblazing autism school called Family Tree in north London in the early 1980s. And he has seen plenty of past conflict about who should and shouldn’t be considered for particular diagnostic categories, not least when Asperger syndrome was first talked about.

He now thinks the catch-all term “autistic spectrum disorder” – or “autistic spectrum condition” – is proving to be increasingly problematic. “By removing the diagnosis of Asperger syndrome [from the diagnostic manual] and lumping all forms of autism together,” Baron-Cohen recently wrote, “we have ended up with individuals like Elon Musk calling himself autistic, and a child being called autistic who will never leave home or live independently and who has significant learning and language disabilities … So, in 2013, overnight, the prevalence of autism massively increased, as now both major subgroups of autism were folded together.”

I speak to Baron-Cohen – who is in his rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge – via Zoom. “The term ‘autism’ is too much of a sledgehammer,” he says. “It’s being used to cover too many things. So … I want to see subgroups.

We can call them type one, type two, type three, and we can decide. You know, type one is autism with an intellectual disability and a language delay. Type two is autism without an intellectual disability. But the reason why I’d be happy to see a proliferation of subgroups is the research that now shows most autistic people have at least six diagnoses: autism with ADHD, autism with dyslexia, autism with dyspraxia, autism with anxiety, autism with gastrointestinal pain, autism with or without epilepsy. I just think we need to start being more precise.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

I have one possible objection to that, to do with my son James. Most people who are familiar with the politics of autism will know there is often an awkward tension between articulate self-advocates and parents – like me – who have no choice but to speak on their children’s behalf. And woven through it, for me at least, is a nagging ambivalence. I sometimes worry that ideas of autism being a difference rather than a disability overlook James’s lived experience. On the other hand, because of the broad definition of autism, it’s really helpful for me to be able to say, “You know that thing Chris Packham’s got? This is my son’s version of that.” If we move to subtypes and he’s given the label type one – which is understood as lower functioning – that’s going to other him, and I don’t want that to happen.

“Nobody wants to be othered,” Baron-Cohen replies. “We want to make sure all subgroups are equal in terms of access to resources and cultural esteem. And we must never prejudge what someone is capable of.”

Two days after my chat with him, I go back to where the modern understanding of autism all started: the clump of buildings around the Maudsley, where I meet Francesca Happé, another Frith protege and professor of cognitive neuroscience at King’s College London, who is now pioneering research into how the condition is experienced by older people.

“Uta’s right that the most important things to know, to the extent that you can know anybody’s life trajectory, are about levels of language and speech and general intellectual functioning,” Happé says. “Within autism, they’re the most determinate things.”

But she clearly worries about categorisation and her sense that it may well not reflect people’s psychological complexity. “We tried it with Asperger’s: we had a go at, on the one hand, high-functioning, lots of language and no intellectual impairment, that type of autism – and then all the rest of autism. And it didn’t work – because everything blurs, and because people change.

“I’ve met people where, at first sight, I wouldn’t pick up anything. I meet them on another occasion when they’re more tired, and I can begin to see the mask almost literally slip. There’s a particular woman who came to stay with us, and my children could have diagnosed her within about half an hour when she was out of her comfort zone. You know, if she had a bad day, it was a disastrous day.”

Happé has a tentative solution to the overdiagnosis wars. “I would say there’s an argument for autism spectrum disorder as a medical diagnosis, and it must require support. If you don’t require support, then by all means you can say you have an autistic identity, but you don’t have autism spectrum disorder, because it’s not impairing you. What you need at the ground floor, before you get to the disorder level, is understanding: self-understanding, understanding from other people, reasonable accommodations. That’s level zero.”

Which brings us to perhaps the most important question of all: right now, amid all the hue and cry, what is it like to be autistic, particularly if some people might place you – rightly or wrongly – on the borderline? When I contact the National Autistic Society, they put me in touch with two women who roughly fit that description.

Hina Shaikh’s story is so fascinating, it probably deserves a book. She lives in Bradford and was diagnosed with autism four years ago, when she was 42. She was working in a car dealership, and made a successful sale to a man who turned out to be a social worker. “He just said, ‘I think you might be an undiagnosed autistic adult’, just like that. And I was taken aback: you thought of special needs children who weren’t living normal lives. But he started pointing out everything he had noticed: I didn’t make eye contact, I didn’t shake his hand, I didn’t do small talk. And he noticed how I had organised my desk, how all my pens were lined up.”

As she read up on autism, all this seemed to chime with her past history, and her profound unease about everyday social rituals. After her GP instigated a spell of form-filling, she found the average local wait for an NHS diagnosis was 18 months, and went instead to a private clinic in Shropshire. There, a consultant said, “If I had diagnosed you 15 or 20 years ago we would have called it Asperger’s. Now it’s all under one umbrella called autism. But yes, you are autistic.”

She still receives no support for her autism, but has since changed jobs and is now employed by a neurodiversity-friendly company that allows her to work from home. The big issue she spends her spare time on is the lack of autism awareness in her own community. “After I was diagnosed, I went on YouTube, trying to find something in Urdu that would explain autism to my mum. And there was nothing. In the Asian-Muslim community, with a lot of people, if a child is autistic, you take him or her to an Imam and an amulet or something is going to cure them.”

Her dad, she tells me, left the family home in his 50s (“He was one of those people who should have never got married – he couldn’t deal with family life”) and moved to Manchester. He died of Covid-19 in 2021, and she and her sister were given the keys to his flat, where they found apparent proof that Shaikh’s autism had genetic roots. “That’s when we realised he had special interests: there were 13 bikes there, and toolboxes, and collections of albums we couldn’t even have imagined.” They also found a pile of medical paperwork. “I realised they were his autism diagnosis. He’d been diagnosed in his late 50s, after he left.”

Shaikh likes Baron-Cohen’s idea of new autistic subtypes. “I think maybe they could have changed the name of Asperger’s because of its connotations, but they still needed to keep different criteria and different diagnoses. I’m gonna be very blunt now, but I am not like an autistic child who is having severe meltdowns, and who is really struggling socially and academically.”

Abigail Stow is 28. She was diagnosed in April and lives in Stevenage, where she works in the NHS, “booking, doing counselling appointments, answering emails, stuff like that”. As she grew up, she tells me, “I was very horrendously bullied, and it caused a lot of anxiety and depression, and at one point self-harm.” Even if she displayed some signs of autism, she got no extra help or support at school. Then, when she was 19, her stepdad heard a podcast about girls and autism. When she listened, she heard loud echoes of her own experience. “So I went to my GP, got booked in for an assessment, and they turned around to me and said, ‘You can’t possibly be autistic or ADHD because you’re giving me eye contact and you have a boyfriend, and you’re able to work.’ So I was like, I must just be weird.”

Nonetheless, she carried on reading about autism and became increasingly convinced she had autistic traits. “I was really struggling to hold down work. If places were busy, that really stressed me out. I’d wear noise-cancelling headphones if stuff was too noisy. And I really struggled to make friends and keep them.”

She has an autistic brother who got his diagnosis two years earlier (“School just thought he was an angry kid”) and two special interests: dogs and heavy metal. “When I’m obsessed with something,” she says, “it becomes my whole personality.”

She also freely talks about masking. “Work is very masky. I think people at work would probably describe me as outgoing and bubbly and chatty. And then I come home and I’m like, don’t even talk to me.”

When she was diagnosed – by a private company paid by the NHS – it was an epiphanic experience. “I cried. I could breathe again. It just felt so good, knowing I wasn’t crazy and I wasn’t wasting anyone’s time.”

I wonder how she feels if she sees people on, say, TikTok, laying claim to autism when they seem to show none of the signs? “It really depends. I don’t know … I feel like they’re almost trying to, like, cutify autism – like, ‘Oh, I’m a little bit autistic’ or, ‘I’m neuro-spicy, and I’ve got a touch of the tism.’ It just makes me cringe. But I also appreciate [that there are] some people like that who are autistic as well. It’s complicated.”

Back in north-west London, I ask Uta Frith what she thinks will happen next. “Things come in waves,” she says. “There are sometimes subgroups, then sometimes they’re put together again, and then it splits back up. You always have the splitters and the lumpers, don’t you?”

And we’re still in a lump phase, I suggest. “Yes. And the next one will be a split. It’s the pendulum swing.”

And why does she think that will happen?

“Just because the extension of the spectrum has gone too far. There are too many cases that were not anticipated to appear.”

Mary Doherty stands on the opposite side: she insists that what some people see as overdiagnosis is really just the birth pangs of a proper understanding of how many people are autistic. “Without the self-advocacy movement, when [autism] was just people who were obviously disabled, that picture was incomplete. I think we’re moving towards a much more holistic and complete version of what it means to be autistic.”

Is there a way through this ever more intense conflict? Simon Baron-Cohen has a different belief again: in accepting an extended spectrum, but moving into what he calls “precision diagnosis” and “support for whichever group you’re in. Because I see them as equally needy; it’s just that the needs are different.”

And all the time, yet another quintessentially 21st-century battle rumbles on. “I’d like the polarisation of views to change into a discussion where all sides start with the assumption of goodwill and we can actually talk about things without being afraid,” Francesca Happé says, somewhat optimistically. “But I would like that in all aspects of life.”

Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 05:00:03 GMT

Donald Trump uttered five words this summer that could seal the Republican party’s fate: ‘Pretend I’m on the ticket’

He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.

Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”

That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.

“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”

Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.

The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.

The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.

With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.

Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.

Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.

Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”

The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.

Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.

“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”

This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.

“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”

For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.

But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”

Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.

Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.

Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.

“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”

Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”

This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.

Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.

Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”

While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.

In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)

In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.

Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”

However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”

In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.

Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.

Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.

“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”

A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.

Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”

Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”

Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.

Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”

Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2024 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.

Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”

“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

How to improve your memory: 10 easy, enjoyable expert tips – from reading a book to getting more sleep

The Guardian Sun, 01 Nov 2026 05:00:03 GMT

Relying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall. Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can help

Memory can worsen as we age, but it is often possible to do something about it. Here, memory experts share their advice on how to improve your power of recall.

“Memory is a buildable skill. You can train it, just like learning how to ride a bike or drive,” says Sania Alam, the founder of Futuristic Learning, which provides memory-training education. Alam, based in the US, has coached memory athletes who have broken six Guinness World Records. But the times we are living in are not conducive to maintaining a strong memory. “We are in an age where we are bombarded with information,” says Alam. “At the same time, AI has come in, and social media is growing. All of these things are ageing our brains. You see people at a very young age who are beginning to have memory issues.” How can we tackle this? “My suggestion would be to get your hands on any course that teaches you memory techniques, so that you can start using your own brain instead of relying on gadgets, because these days we can’t even memorise our own number, let alone an emergency contact.”

“The best way to improve your memory is to keep your brain active by learning new things and engaging in cognitively stimulating activities,” says Barbara Sahakian, a professor of psychiatry at the University of Cambridge and co-author of Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. “Find something that you would enjoy, but haven’t tried yet,” she says, suggesting chess, a new language or instrument. In 1995, Sahakian published an article in the British Medical Journal with Martin Orrell, emphasising the need to learn new things to reduce the risk of dementia and Alzheimer’s – in other words “use it or lose it”. “Keeping our brains active through learning and remembering, we drive the neural circuits and keep them functioning better for longer,” she says. “Studies with medical students studying for exams and black-cab taxi drivers learning routes in London have shown that the hippocampus actually increases in volume. So, remember to use your brain through education and other challenging activities, so that you can keep it fit and functioning better for longer.”

Reassuringly, you don’t have to sign up to a complicated course to improve your memory but can simply open a book instead. “Reading something that interests you, whether it is fiction or nonfiction, has a positive effect on the brain, cognition and mood,” says Sahakian. “Several studies have shown that reading can reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia with ageing.”

Another way that tech can disrupt memory is through its impact on our ability to focus. “We are rapidly switching our attention from one thing to the next,” says Sahakian. “This makes it difficult for people to then focus their attention and concentrate when they need to accomplish a goal. Experiments have shown that students who have mobile phones in class do not perform as well in tests; even having a mobile phone that was off next to you acts as a distractor of your attention.”

“We have to use these specific techniques. It’s not magic,” says Katie Kermode, a memory champion from Manchester, who started competing in 2008 and set the world record for remembering names, and numerous other titles since. When trying to memorise something, Kermode advises using the journey technique, which she learned when she was nine to memorise the order of the planets in the solar system. “A thermometer breaks, and the silver Mercury goes everywhere. The goddess Venus clears it all up and puts it into a bag and throws it. It lands on the Earth … It goes on like that, making each planet into an object or a person, and making them into a story, so they link from one to the next,” says Kermode. “In competitions we memorise thousands of digits, which I couldn’t just naturally do by sitting and repeating them to myself. You have to work a little bit, but it really helps you to memorise anything that you want to.”

Similarly, you can create a “memory palace”, which has its roots in the work of the Ancient Greek poet Simonides of Ceos and was more recently popularised by the memory expert Tony Buzan, who died in 2019. “I tend to use ‘memory palace’ when there is a prescribed sequence and ‘journey’,” says Kermode. In everyday life, thinking of a route that you know well and placing things to remember along that route, is really helpful with recalling a shopping list, for example. “You put the first item in your driveway, then the second item could go in your hallway, and you mentally walk through it and try to remember it,” says Kermode. It can be used for remembering a speech or presentation, too. “Each topic of your speech can be in a different location, and if you’ve got sub-points to make within that topic, you can visualise that within the location.”

Kermode is pretty good at recalling dates. “I’ve got techniques for remembering them, where each month has a particular meaning and/or a colour, and then each day of the month has an object,” she says. “But remembering to actually do something on that birthday – that’s a different thing that I struggle with. I would say that is a different part of the brain.”

Kermode uses symbolism to turn abstract concepts into something concrete she can visualise. “If you’ve got something quite abstract to remember,” she says, “like you’re trying to remember a birthday in October, you might turn October into a pumpkin because October is an abstract word but you can use symbolism to make it more real. If you’re trying to remember a number, two looks like a swan, so 2 October could be a swan sitting on a pumpkin.” A lot of people aren’t good at visualising, says Kermode. If this is the case for you, “make it more of a story and involve more people. We even have memory competitors that can’t visualise, and they find ways around it.”

Dr Michael Gruneberg, a former senior lecturer in psychology at Swansea University and founder of Linkword Languages, recommends mnemonics, and specifically acronyms, for revision. “When I was preparing for exams, I would do the reading, so I knew my stuff, then I would pick out about eight points on a topic that I thought might come up and list them, then take the first letter of each to make up a word or a sentence.” A common example is “Richard of York gave battle in vain” for remembering the order of colours in the light spectrum (and the rainbow).

Kermode swears by slides. “For each different subject, like history or geography, have a different slide deck on PowerPoint [or similar], and then each subtopic within that could be its own slide. Choose a background for the slide that represents that topic. It should be related to it, and it should be quite detailed, so you can imagine things happening inside it. For instance, for GCSE biology, one of the topics is platelets. I thought of plates, and I thought of a dinner table. So I had a picture of a dinner table with lots of plates of food, and then all the things that relate to that topic on the slide, including clotted cream as a reminder that platelets clot blood.”

Flashcards can be helpful, says Kermode. “But I think what people miss is using the techniques to help them memorise information in the first place, because flashcards just help you review things at certain intervals. You have to put in the effort to memorise it in the first place.” In a lesson or lecture, Kermode writes down the key points and facts that she wants to remember, and lays them out as a mind map. “So you’re not just writing a list of points, but have your key topic as the central image, and then that branches out to each subtopic.”

Make sure you keep running over whatever it is you want to learn, to ensure it stays in your brain. “If it is a short-term list, then you just need to do it once or twice, and you have probably got it,” says Kermode. “If it is something you want to learn more long-term, then you need to review it regularly because otherwise we naturally forget.” Kermode suggests trying “spaced repetition”, which means practising at increasing intervals. “So the first week, you might go over it a couple of times on the first day, and the same the next day, and then a couple of days later. But then the next week you might be on to once a week, and eventually once a month.”

Gruneberg, who is 86, says to always make a note of appointment times. “There is something called ‘prospective memory’ that does not improve, to say the least. Remembering to do things, when to see the doctor, all sorts of things like that. It becomes much more necessary to write these things down as you get older.”

“I use alarms all the time,” admits Kermode. “We do become reliant on it. You can try to remember it, but also set the alarm just in case. I think triggering your mind to do something at a certain point, you have to use something that you’re going to do. Say you need to go to the hairdresser straight after lunch – you could associate using scissors to get into the fridge.”

Sahakian ensures that she gets at least seven hours’ sleep a night. “You consolidate in your memory what you have learned during the day when you sleep at night. Therefore, it is important to sleep well and not to stay up all night cramming for exams.”

“Sleep is really important for your brain to work in an efficient way, especially if you’re trying to memorise something fast,” agrees Kermode. “If you’re tired, it’s not going to work.” After competing, Kermode often feels exhausted. “There was one competition I won, and I got back home and was trying to get some money out at the ATM, and I couldn’t remember my pin because my brain was frazzled.”

“You face a lot of brain fog when you’ve not slept,” says Alam. “Your mind isn’t working at its top speed, and that is because your body has a circadian rhythm that is designed around sleep. Sleep at the time you need to, so that you can stay sharp.” When trying to commit something to memory, Alam recommends taking regular naps, “so that you can give your brain that time to process the information, put it where it needs to be placed, and then it will be handy when you need it”.

Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:00:46 GMT

We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply

John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say.

Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so.

Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now.

Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out.

More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.

It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity.

Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security.

UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?).

The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers.

And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse.

The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”.

In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.”

The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.

Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy.

after newsletter promotion

There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000.

Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500.

The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell.

There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”.

However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness.

Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.

However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-star

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:00:45 GMT

She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend

I’d been warned about Patrick by friends who’d worked with him at the Royal Shakespeare Company. They said: “Marina, you can’t be you around Patrick Stewart. He’s all about the work. He takes it very seriously and he won’t abide you mucking about and trying to make people corpse.”

We had been cast together on Star Trek: The Next Generation and, because of what I’d heard, I was a bit scared, a bit intimidated. And let’s be honest – Patrick was very serious about the work. But there was a concerted effort by the rest of us to beat it out of him. We were from a younger generation and we wanted to shake up this Englishman who was so typical of his generation – stiff upper lip and a Yorkshireman to boot. You know, the kind of person who was not exactly renowned for showing their emotions. Early on Patrick told us all that we weren’t there to have fun, and you should have seen the looks he got. I’m a cockney: I’ve got a Spurs tattoo and we all looked at him in the same way I look at an Arsenal fan. But we did loosen him up. And – he’s said this himself – I think we actually freed him. We gave him a freedom that he said he’d never really felt before.

Of course it went both ways. We learned so much from him, how could you not? We learned from his professionalism and his absolutely insane talent. He brought gravitas to the role. Star Trek was a bit of a punchline before Patrick came along – it’s not any more. Patrick gave it depth – here was this consummate Shakespearean actor playing the captain of a starship. It just shifted everything.

He had reservations about taking the role, and his friends – who loved him and were looking out for him – told him not to do it. They thought it would be the end of his career, whereas it was probably the best decision in showbusiness at that time. He handled fame with grace. He didn’t flaunt it. Never got too big for his boots. Early on, a review in a paper described him as an “unknown Shakespearean actor” and we blew it up and stuck it on his trailer door. Someone less self-deprecating might not have liked that but he left it up there for years. He knew it was all good fun.

Before meeting Patrick I was just a jobbing actor who did a bit of telly. I’d grown up dirt poor and had a difficult childhood, so we came from very similar backgrounds. I kept my cockney accent because I wanted people to know where I came from. Patrick was the same – not through his voice, but through his demeanour and actions. He was down to earth, a regular bloke. The fact that he supported Huddersfield Town shows you who he is – he didn’t go for Leeds or one of the glamour clubs.

We’d both experienced childhood trauma and came out with our stories after we had finished working together. We never sat down and went into it all. But when people have gone through something like that, there’s something in their demeanour, something that you can see in them, that you feel in them.

A month before Covid hit, my husband died. I was on my own in my house in Los Angeles for a year with just my dogs for company. Patrick was one of the very few people who invited me over for lunch, socially distanced in his garden. It had occurred to him that I was grieving and on my own – and he did something about that. It’s a mark of who he is.

He was always on my side. In one of the Star Trek movies we did there was a scene written for Picard and Data, where Picard tells the story of how his family were burned in a fire. Patrick went to the writers and producers and asked if they could rewrite the scene to have me be in it instead of Brent Spiner. He said that Brent’s character Data was an android, and that he really needed to look into my eyes in order to reach the emotions he needed. So our relationship on screen was a two-way street, which sounds ridiculous saying that out loud! I don’t know how I’ve got the cheek to say that when I’m talking about Patrick Stewart! But we did help each other.

It’s also because of Patrick that I am now in the annals of my football team. When Tottenham played Huddersfield in 2018, we both did interviews about the game and it was officially named in the match day programme as the Star Trek derby. That’s now a part of Tottenham history and, as anyone who knows me will tell you, that means more to me than winning an acting award!

It was the absolute privilege of my life and my career to work with him. We were very, very close and stayed in touch right to the end, even though it became difficult to speak to him on the phone because of his health. He went quickly in the end and it makes me very sad that I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye. To say: “Thank you Patrick. Thanks for everything, mate.”

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:36 GMT

Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paint

Wicker Out now Anyone who has ever fantasised about having a husband made out of wicker (surely a universal dream) will want to get themselves along to this Olivia Colman romantasy about a loner fisher who does exactly that. Nightborn Out now Seidi Haarla gives a wonderfully unhinged performance as a woman convinced there is something wrong with her newborn baby: the hellish crying, her bleeding nipples … surely this child is a monster? Directed by Lance Oppenheim (also on a hot streak with You Can See Everything).

I Love Boosters Out now Shoplifting, teleportation, the consequences of sweatshop labour, designer fashion, workers’ rights and demons who suck out your soul while performing oral sex: here’s a comedy from Boots Riley that has it all. Mad Bloomsbury Charleston Firle, Lewes, 4 November to 11 April Coinciding with the centenary of Virginia Woolf’s essay On Being Ill, this show looks at how the Bloomsbury Group – the likes of Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – dealt with ideas of madness, disability and neurodiversity.

Steve McQueen: Resistance Leeds Art Gallery, 6 November to 25 April Deeply moving documentation of how acts of resistance and rebellion have transformed the UK, all conceived by the brilliant Turner prize-winning artist and Oscar-winning director Steve McQueen.

Ex:Re – Save As Out now With her band Daughter currently between albums, Elena Tonra returns to her Ex:Re solo moniker via this second album of textural alt-rock. Songs such as Sleep creep along with a hint of menace, while opener Radio Station spins off into a trippy road trip anthem.

DIIV – Zirp! Out now American alt-rock curios DIIV return with this AG Cook-produced fifth album. The Big Moon – Forever Out now London quartet the Big Moon return with a sunnier take on their brand of indie rock. Created as an imaginary utopia after a period of upheaval in frontwoman Juliette Jackson’s life, songs such as the buoyant Three Things and Fun offer sweet solace. MC

Provocations Podcast For the numerically challenged, this new series hosted by Nihal Arthanayake is essential listening. Experts break down the big stories in finance, such as changes in lending policies and how technology can affect banking.

Concorde: The Untold Story PBS America, 2 November, 8.40pm Encompassing everything from engineering breakthroughs to espionage and political hand-wringing, this film on the race to build the first supersonic airliner between Europe, the Soviet Union and the US makes for surprisingly engaging viewing. Five Great Reads: Elections, eugenics and high school reunions

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 21:21:44 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend. It’s been a big week around the world, with results of three major elections taking many people by surprise. And away from the news cycle, our journalists have been asking some big questions – about birth, death, cocaine and why on earth anyone wants to go to a high school reunion.

At a time when populist leaders and the far right appear to be on the rise, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s extraordinary victory on Sunday offered more than a glimmer of hope. As Jonathan Watts writes: it “should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections”.

So what do we do? Many analysts have put Lula’s win down to galvanising the streets and social media, and that campaign group – in particular the WhatsApp group ‘“Lula’s Army” – gathered up about 8% of the electorate by voting day. But that’s far from the only mechanism – political messaging, challenging tech giants, standing up for the environment and sheer determination are among some of the big takeaways here.

Notable quote: “Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action.”

How long will it take to read: Just under three minutes.

Further reading: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback; In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely.

You may have noticed it – at the pub, with friends at dinner, or maybe even brazenly, out in the open – people shamelessly snorting cocaine. Journalist Robyn Vinter had been observing the uptick in drug use for some time and wanted to know “how did cocaine conquer Britain?” Here, she lays out some sobering findings.

From the middle class to the far right: “It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” a West Ham pub owner says. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. And the class A drug, once firmly associated with middle classes, has moved around the demographics, including now appearing to be a drug of choice for the far right.

Fuelling crime: The Guardian’s investigation found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019, and Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

How long will it take to read: Three and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: ‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse.

Most people do their best to avoid talking about death. But as of now, science has yet to find a cure for the affliction that comes for us all. So why the social taboo? In the final instalment of the Guardian’s series about death – Memento mori – Meaghan O’Connell documents the journey her mother took after deciding she wanted to donate her body to science. O’Connell wasn’t prepared for what came next but says, “In some ways, it was absolutely perfect”.

Why would you donate your body to science? Demand for medical cadavers far outstrips supply. More than 25,000 Americans donate their bodies for research purposes after their death but, according to Tamara Ostervoss, director of Oregon Health & Science University’s (OHSU) body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice”. For medical students, the ability to practise procedures on the real thing versus a human model is like “the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane”.

The emotional cost: Not knowing exactly what happened to her mother’s body weighed on O’Connell’s mind. But she says going down the donation route also offered an element of simplicity. No being upsold by funeral directors, no grief-stricken decisions about embalming, or what goes on the gravestone. Just a quick phone call and a short physical assessment, then “voilà, off my mom went to fulfil her destiny”, O’Connell says.

Notable quote: “Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath”? – O’Connell, after learning her mother’s body was accepted as a medical cadaver.

A memorial of sorts: After fulfilling her mother’s posthumous wishes, O’Connell was invited to a “body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students from OHSU memorialise body donors and their families. Two students offered their thanks through an aerial yoga routine; others sang Taylor Swift. O’Connell was looking for closure but all this offered was amusement.

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: More from the Guardian’s Memento mori series.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

It may be Greek for “good birth” but the term eugenics has, for the past century at least, been seen as a racist and repulsive movement. But whether you like it or not, eugenics is back in a new guise, this time by companies offering prospective parents the problematic promise of delivering the “best baby”. Jan Grue, who has a form of spinal muscular atrophy, considers the ethical implications.

What is ‘the best’? Adverts on the New York City subway offer embryo scans for every genetic disorder under the sun, eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male pattern baldness. Whether the promises are credible is one thing but a more important one might be: what is “valuable and worthless in a human life?”

Notable quote: “I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.”

How long will it take to read: Eight minutes.

Further reading: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter.

High school reunions are notoriously awkward; just ask Romy and Michele. While some look forward to reconnecting with friends, others see reliving the past as “a potential hellscape”. But can you go in prepared? The Guardian asked a mix of experts and reunion-goers for their advice on tackling one of life’s most fraught social situations.

Should you even go? Psychologist and author Amberley Meredith says it is normal to ruminate over reunions, and you should expect to not be the only one with existential questions about your place in life. If you are on the fence, experts say avoid making a pros and cons list – instead, just focus on the potential positives.

The dos and don’ts: Still feeling nervous before the big day? Etiquette expert Jodie Bache-Mclean says you can come prepared with a few conversation starters and a bit of background on your past classmates, but while “a little homework is helpful; a full social media investigation is not”. What about alcohol? Should you drink to calm your nerves? “A glass of wine may help, four may not!” Bache-Mclean says.

How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes.

Further reading: Why are class reunions so terrifying? And are they even good for us?

Two giants rumble into the weekend after very different EFL Cup shootouts in midweek.
