14 Unforgettable Looks From the New York City Marathon

The New York Times November 01, 2026

N. Y. C. Marathon

Advertisement

Supported by

Newlyweds and a woman celebrating a birthday were among the marathoners, some of whom were extending their Halloween festivities into race day.

By Nadav Gavrielov

Photographs by Lanna Apisukh

For a few hours on Sunday morning, Fort Wadsworth on Staten Island became a microcosm of the world. Tens of thousands of runners from all over the world sprawled out across the start village for the New York City Marathon, making their final preparations for the race — including the final touch-ups on their race outfits.

In the interviews below, which have been edited and condensed, some of the participants shared their thoughts about their style and the day in front of them.

Munich, Germany

Are you going to be running in those outfits?

Carina: Yes, I’m running in my wedding dress.

Maxi: And I’m in a wedding suit. We got married recently. Our wedding outfits.

Carina: From three months ago.

So, it’s efficient; you’re recycling them. Some people put them away and never use them again.

Carina: Normally, you wear a wedding dress only once, but I thought I’d wear it twice.

Maxi: We thought this is the best honeymoon.

How are you enjoying New York on your honeymoon?

Maxi: We just knew from movies and from the TV, and when you’re here, the vibe in the city — it’s not describable.

Are you worried that the outfits are going to get damaged while you’re running?

Carina: No.

Maxi: It’s just all about the experience.

How’s married life?

Maxi: She makes the decisions, and I just do what she says.

San Francisco

Did you see the Statue of Liberty on the ferry?

I did. I took a picture with it.

How did that make you feel?

Majestical, excited, great energy.

Are you going to run the race in the outfit?

Yes.

What if the hat falls off?

I’ll pick it up.

Are you going to hold the torch the whole time?

That’s the plan. But it’ll be vibes-based.

Why didn’t you wear a San Francisco outfit?

Because I’m running the New York marathon.

Which city is better?

San Francisco.

The Bronx

Is it your birthday?

It is my birthday.

How do you feel?

I feel amazing. This has been a literal dream come true.

You have the “it’s my birthday” glasses.

Yes, and I’m going to put these on when we get on the bridge.

What does the sash say?

Birthday girl. It’s gold with a little trim on it. So if you see me, say “Happy birthday.”

Are you going to run with the sash on?

I’m going to run with the sash on the whole 26.

What if it falls?

It’s not going to fall.

Rockville, Maryland

What’s your name?

I’m the drubbler. It’s like dribbling and juggling.

Do you love the Knicks?

Well, I mean, I was rooting for them. I’m actually from Washington, D. C.

Are you going to dribble while running?

Yeah. I’m not going to be able to do the whole thing. I’ll probably go like 18 or 20 miles and then it’ll get dark and I’ll have to stop. There are parts where I don’t juggle because I don’t want to lose them — and safety and stuff like that.

Knicks in five this year?

I don’t know. I guess if they won in seven that would be great, too.

Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Did you use this for your Halloween outfit yesterday?

No, I did not. It’s just for the race.

How long ago did you pick it out?

About a few days ago, since I had a really bad stomach bug leading up to the race so I’m very empty so I am eating my carbo-loading meal while I’m running. Just like the hungry caterpillar.

Is it aerodynamic?

I sure hope so.

Where did you get the inspiration?

It was my favorite book growing up.

Will you have nutrients along the way?

Yes, I have a lot of friends scattered around the course, with some snacks to feed the hungry caterpillar. I’m just going to be munching my way, inching my way toward the finish line one snack after another.

Greenpoint, Brooklyn

When did you do this to your hair?

Last night, it took ages actually.

How long are we talking?

Hours, like eight hours. I didn’t even prepare for today because I was scrambling yesterday.

So you haven’t trained at all, mostly just focused on the hair?

The hair was the main priority today. The second priority is running.

Did you also use it for Halloween?

I was asleep at 12, waking up at 3. So if that’s Halloween, that’s Halloween.

So three hours of sleep?

Something like that.

Atlanta

What is this outfit?

It’s a tux. I ran it two years ago, in my dad’s wedding tux. I wanted to follow it up with something that looked pretty similar.

This is actually a special occasion. It’s my 108th marathon in three years.

That’s a lot of marathons. Have you run every single one in a tux?

Not every single one.

Are the white pants going to get dirty?

Oh, they already are. I stayed awake last night. I never went to sleep because it was Halloween. So I went out to the bars. I went to the haunted house, to the pub, to a party. Now I’m here.

So you didn’t sleep last night?

No, no, I’ve been awake since yesterday morning when I woke up and went to the shakeout run.

Is that concerning?

To who?

Fair enough.

Ter Apel, Netherlands

Are you going to run in the Christmas tree?

Yes, yes, yes.

Is it going to get warm?

I hope not.

Isn’t it a little early for Christmas?

It’s on the corner. Next week there is the Christmas tree in New York, I have heard.

Are you going to go to the Christmas tree?

No, we’re going home Monday.

Udine, Italy

What are you wearing on your head?

It’s a chicken. But for me, it’s a little eagle because it’s our flag. We come from the northeast of Italy. This is the flag of our land: Friuli.

Are you going to run with it?

Absolutely. It’s our 11th time here together. Chicken man.

What if the chicken falls off?

No, no, no. He is the athlete, not me.

Barcelona, Spain

Did you train in this outfit?

No, I found it yesterday.

Are you going to be running in it?

No, I’m going to leave it before the start.

Are you going to try to go back and get it afterward?

I want so much. It’s sad that I should leave it, because it is definitely cool. But I just hope that maybe the next person will find it next year and do it once more.

To pass it onto the next generation?

Yes, absolutely.

Financial District, Manhattan

Where’d you get the clips?

I got the clips from Amazon. I’ve seen a lot through Instagram, so I just got inspired from other runners.

Tell me about the sparkles.

Glitter makes you faster.

What’s the goal for today?

The goal for today is to hug all of my friends and family. I have family coming in from Korea who are here to see me run in this marathon for the first time.

Why stars for the clips?

It’s kind of like a shoot for the moon and stars kind of inspiration.

Frankfurt

Tell me about your outfit.

I got inspired during the London Marathon. I saw a lady wearing exactly that outfit, and that’s why I purchased that. And I thought it looks warm and nice.

Did she also have a bagel tucked into the pocket?

No, she did not.

And you’re double fisting cups of coffee.

Yes, I am.

What would you call what you’re wearing?

It’s my queen outfit.

Connections Coach

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit...

Supported by

By Thomas J. Campanella

Dr. Campanella is a professor of city planning at Cornell University.

The triumphal arch was a Roman innovation conceived to honor those of good deed who “should be lifted up,” wrote Pliny the Elder, “above the rest of mortals.” Only later did it become associated with victorious generals returning from battle, a symbolic city gate through which triumphators passed.

Among the first was the Arch of Titus, built around A. D. 81 to commemorate the victory of Titus and Vespasian in the siege of Jerusalem a decade earlier. Its panels depict spoils taken from the Second Temple in victory — including the curved menorah featured on the national emblem of Israel.

Much later came the Arch of Constantine, from 315, adjacent to the Colosseum on the Via Triumphalis. It was the largest Roman arch, built to honor Constantine’s victory at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge. Over the centuries, the arches of Titus and Constantine became archetypes replicated around the world for a gamut of glorious purposes. Not coincidentally, the words arch and archetype share the same Greek root: Arkhein, to rule, and arkhos, chief. Triumphal arches enact a vision of power. Sometimes that is a vision founded in reality; at others, it is aspirational, even deceptive, a gesture made to tell a false tale about a country’s place in the world. President Trump’s proposed arch is just another chapter in the long history of heroic architecture pressed into the service of ideology.

The scale and symbolism of the triumphal arch continued to evolve, often to honor the fallen rather than generals, or to trumpet the aspirations of new regimes. The copper-sheeted Narva Triumphal Arch in St. Petersburg, Russia, built in 1814 and weathered to a glorious verdigris patina, honored Russia’s defeat of Napoleon in 1812, while the Arc de Triomphe in Paris — begun earlier but finished decades later — represented the opposite side, venerating those who fought and died for France in the Napoleonic Wars and preceding revolution.

But the classical references remained. The English architect John Nash channeled Constantine for his Marble Arch, originally erected at Buckingham Palace, completed in 1833 to honor the British side in the Napoleonic Wars.

As the self-styled legatee of the Roman Empire, it was only appropriate that England looked to ancient Rome for its monuments. The Marble Arch was also a riposte aimed squarely at the Arc de Triomphe, which was styled on the Arch of Titus.

New York reconstituted both archetypical arches, too: Stanford White’s exquisite Washington Arch channeled Titus; John Russell Pope’s Theodore Roosevelt Memorial — the monumental Central Park entrance to the American Museum of Natural History — aped Constantine.

The Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Arch just outside Prospect Park, completed in 1892 and topped by Frederick MacMonnies’s soaring quadriga, brought the triumphal arch back around to honor the fallen.

So did Paul Philippe Cret’s Titus-inspired National Memorial Arch at Valley Forge National Historical Park — dedicated in 1917 “to the officers and private soldiers of the Continental Army.”

Nor were triumphal arches confined to Europe and the Americas. George Wittet’s Gateway of India, completed in 1924 on the Mumbai, then Bombay, waterfront, employed elements of 16th-century Gujarati architecture to mark George V’s arrival in December 1911 — the first time a British monarch visited the subcontinent after nearly 300 years of British presence. Ironically, it would later mark the end of British rule: Through its archway in February 1948, the very last British troops departed newly independent India. “This was where the British landed,” wrote Jan Morris, “and this is where, in the end, they left.”

Arch-bloat seems to know no bounds. The tallest triumphal arch in the world was finished on the eve of World War II in Mexico City, the Monumento a la Revolución. At 220 feet, it rises to over three times the height of the Arch of Constantine.

But its standing almost ended just three years later. In 1941, Albert Speer presented plans to his Führer for a monumental arch that would tower nearly 400 feet over Berlin. Taller than the towers of the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge in New York, it would have been twice the height of the Arc de Triomphe, which could have fit snugly within its cavernous maw. Speer’s gargantua anchored the monumental axis of Hitler’s “World Capital Germania,” the proposed rebuilding of Berlin for the Thousand-Year Reich.

Today, all that remains of the megalomanic arch is a concrete cylinder used to test the load-bearing capacity of the marshy Tempelhof site — the 13,644-ton Schwerbelastungskörper.

But megalomania will endure so long as humans have the run of the planet, and so too will outsize arches rise. In North Korea, Pyongyang’s Arch of Triumph, the second tallest in the world, was erected to commemorate Korean independence after World War II. Inaugurated on Kim Il Sung’s 70th birthday in 1982, it consists of 25,500 granite blocks, each representing a day Dear Leader had lived to that point.

Unless you count the Gateway Arch in St. Louis — a polished-steel vault that celebrates manifest destiny and nods to, rather than embraces, the tradition of triumphal arches — Americans have fallen out of the triumphal arch habit this century. That, of course, may well change if Mr. Trump has his way. Despite opposition from a panoply of architectural and preservation organizations, the United States Triumphal Arch would rise to 250 feet, surpassing the Mexican arch as the world’s tallest. That would make it well over twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial and almost 100 feet taller than the Arc de Triomphe.

One issue with the so-called Arc d’Trump is its proposed location at Memorial Circle, just over the Potomac and on axis with the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Washington is a city of vistas and sightlines; few are more sacred than this one. It was to protect this visual axis that landscape architect Gilmore D. Clarke, then-chair of the U. S. Commission of Fine Arts, convinced President Franklin D. Roosevelt not to build the Pentagon at Arlington Farms, where it would have obliterated the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. The War Department was furious, but had to concede. The Pentagon was built instead well out of the way. But today’s so-called War Department may have revenge of a sort: The Arc d’Trump could be the first in history designed to also serve as a military installation, an aerie for snipers and drones.

But the real issue is that of purpose. What exactly is Mr. Trump’s behemoth meant to celebrate? Our abnegation as a force for good in the world? Our bitter internal divisions? Will it be another desperate display of might by a state in decline, an India Gate on the Potomac? Will it be mostly made in China? In the end, of course, it will be a taxpayer-funded monument to the vainglory of our outer-borough emperor, Donald Trump. After all, the English word “trump” — and thus “triumphal” — is derivative of the French word “triomphe.”

Thomas J. Campanella is a professor of city planning at Cornell University.

Judge Rejects Trump Officials’ Move to Challenge Alaska Senate Election

The New York Times November 01, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

In the latest defeat for the Trump administration, the ruling dismisses a lawsuit that pre-emptively contested the results of a race that includes two candidates named Daniel Sullivan.

By Anna Griffin

A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit that pre-emptively challenged the results in a U. S. Senate race featuring two candidates with the same name — a Republican incumbent and another man who could be a spoiler.

The ruling is the latest in a series of court defeats for the Trump administration, which has been seeking to intervene in state-administered elections.

On Friday, the U. S. District Court in California blocked the administration from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the department’s directives on handling ballots.

Also on Friday, a federal appeals court panel denied a request to order California officials to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claimed had been sent to possible noncitizens.

In Alaska, the Justice Department filed its lawsuit last month at President Trump’s direction, asking the judge to block certification of the state’s U. S. Senate election results if Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses but would have won had votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, gone to the incumbent instead.

In that scenario, the suit also demands an investigation into whether voters who selected the retired teacher actually intended to vote for the senator.

Federal officials have not made clear how an investigation into anonymous ballots would be conducted.

In her Sunday ruling, Chief Judge Sharon Gleason of U. S. District Court in Alaska wrote that she did not see how the federal government’s proposed solution to any confusion would solve the problem if it even existed — or how the approach could work given the right to a secret ballot is a core principle of American democracy.

The federal government, she wrote, “offers no rebuttal to the concerns regarding preservation of the secrecy of voting and provides no explanation of how its request for ballot segregation and a court-ordered investigation by law enforcement officers into certain voters’ intent could be implemented while preserving the secrecy of the ballot.”

Kiersten Pels, a spokeswoman for the Department of Justice, said the administration plans to appeal the dismissal and noted that the judge didn’t not address “the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”

The administration’s lawsuit accuses Daniel J. Sulivan of trying to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.” Daniel J. Sullivan has said he voted for Democrats in the last three presidential races and for Mary Peltola, the current Democratic Senate nominee on the ballot, in her 2022 and 2024 campaigns for Congress.

The suit also notes that he switched his party affiliation from Independent to Republican only when he filed to run, and that his campaign website uses the same dark blue and yellow color scheme as the incumbent’s.

A New York Times investigation revealed that a Democratic operative connected to Ms. Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee enlisted Daniel J. Sullivan to run as part of a broader effort to recruit independent and third-party candidates who might peel votes away from the incumbent.

Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has ordered a criminal investigation into the Peltola campaign even as the state elections division, overseen by his lieutenant governor, also a Republican, fought the Trump administration’s civil lawsuit.

Ms. Peltola and national Democrats have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, and they joined the civil case as additional defendants along with national Democrats, the League of Women Voters and Common Cause, a self-described nonpartisan government watchdog organization.

Daniel S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, promised in an interview with CNN Sunday to support any election results but also suggested, without offering explanation or details, that the election could be “stolen.”

In its defense in the Justice Department’s lawsuit, lawyers with the state of Alaska noted that state courts had already rejected an attempt by the state’s elections agency to take Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot and that the final ballot was designed to differentiate between the two men: It lists the senator as “Dan S. Sullivan” and notes his party affiliation and incumbency, and the other man is “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation included.

Alaska also uses ranked choice voting in state and federal general elections, meaning voters are familiar with the system. Any voter confused by the existence of two Dan Sullivans could simply rank both candidates.

Judge Gleason had already expressed skepticism of the Trump administration’s case in a ruling last month agreeing to a speedy hearing. In that order, she pointed out that the federal lawsuit came after Alaskans had already begun casting ballots for November and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the state Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.

In Sunday’s dismissal ruling, she noted that federal lawyers, in their filings, said they were not attempting to interfere in the time, place and manner of Alaskan elections — matters the U. S. Constitution leaves in the hands of states.

But, Judge Gleason said, the federal government’s proposed answers to any voter confusion were “a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan.

“These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska’s election,” she wrote.

If anything, the judge added, such federal intervention amid an ongoing election would cause the precise sort of voter confusion the administration says it is trying to prevent.

Bayliss Wagner and Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.

Senator Chris Murphy Is ‘Awake and Alert’ After Suffering a Stroke

The New York Times November 01, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Connecticut senator, who has been campaigning for fellow Democrats, has been viewed as a potential candidate for president in 2028.

By Michael Gold

Senator Christopher S. Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, was hospitalized on Saturday after suffering a stroke, according to a statement from his chief of staff.

The chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said that Mr. Murphy, 53, was attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday afternoon and “started experiencing numbness in his arm.” He was taken to a nearby hospital, where doctors diagnosed a stroke.

Mr. Murphy was transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for monitoring and treatment. “The doctors are encouraged by his progress; he is awake and alert; and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” Ms. Herwitt said in her statement.

A spokesman for Mr. Murphy would not provide further details about his condition on Sunday.

Mr. Murphy, who became a senator in 2013 and has been viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, has spent the past several weeks on the campaign trail with Democrats as he tries to help his party take control of Congress in the midterm elections. He had been scheduled to help campaign in New Hampshire on Sunday.

Mr. Murphy is one of several senators to experience significant public health issues in recent years, as the health of politicians has received greater scrutiny. The sudden death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, in July from an aortic dissection, a tear in the body’s main artery, added to those concerns.

At least two of Mr. Murphy’s colleagues have had strokes in recent years. Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, experienced what he said was a “minor stroke” in 2022. Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, had a near-fatal stroke that same year, as he was campaigning for election.

Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky and the former majority leader, was gone from the Capitol and out of public view for more than three months earlier this year after a health incident at his home.

Mr. McConnell has also appeared to experience medical issues at the Capitol and in Kentucky, freezing during appearances and needing to be escorted away by his aides.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Running While Famous: Here Are Some of the Celebrities in the Race

The New York Times November 01, 2026

N. Y. C. Marathon

Advertisement

Supported by

Actors, reality stars and athletes are among those in the mass of runners. The comedian Tracy Morgan is the event’s grand marshal.

By Claire Fahy

As running has exploded in popularity, so has the number of celebrities running the New York City Marathon. Among the 60,000 runners who will cross the start line on Sunday are dozens of actors, reality television stars and famous athletes.

Among the most famous faces on the streets on Sunday are Tracy Morgan, the comedian and former “30 Rock star who is acting as grand marshal, and Jennifer Connelly, the Academy Award-winning actress from “Labyrinth,” and “A Beautiful Mind.” According to a list released by the organizers, there will also be the reliable representatives from Broadway that often feature in the hometown race. This year, the “Mean Girls” star Erika Henningsen and Jordan Litz, currently starring as Fiyero in “Wicked” in London’s West End, will wind their way toward the finish line.

Following the newfound tradition of alums from the “Bachelor” and “Bachelorette” reality dating show franchise participating in the five-borough race, Hannah Ann Sluss, Joe Amabile, Matt James, Blake Horstmann, Zac Clark, Greg Grippo and Andrew Spencer will take on the 26.2 miles.

Mr. Amabile notably underwent brain surgery in August to remove a tumor. He posted a video to Instagram on Aug. 20 of his first run post-operation, writing that “if you’re looking for a little inspiration this morning I just ran 3 and half miles only 15 days after my brain surgery.”

Also racing on Sunday are a number of athletes from other sporting fields. Tiki Barber, the former New York Giants running back, and Justin Britt, a one-time Seattle Seahawks player, will represent the National Football League. James Milner will represent England’s Premier League and Darby Allin will show what an All Elite Wrestling athlete can do in a road race.

Mr. Morgan made his way up Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn in a car early in the race.

We’ll be on the lookout for others as the day progresses.

Claire Fahy reports on New York City and the surrounding area for The Times.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Curtis Malone ran a basketball powerhouse in Washington, D. C., before going to prison for drug dealing. Now he wants back in the game.

Curtis Malone at a tournament in Virginia in April. Credit... Matt Eich for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jacob Stern

Jacob Stern attended more than 20 youth basketball games for this article.

No one thought Curtis Malone would be back, not even Curtis Malone. Not the way things ended. The scandal, the media circus, the prison sentence. He’d said he would start a business or something when he got out — just nothing to do with basketball.

And yet there he was, courtside on a Saturday afternoon in March, watching a gym full of high school boys with N. B. A. aspirations compete for a spot on one of his teams. Well, partly watching; he had people for that. Mostly he was on the move, conferring with coaches, sweet-talking parents, taking call after call from scouts and business partners and guys he’d never even heard of — an unending succession of calls from people who all, in one way or another, needed him. Can you find this kid a school? Can you put in a word with the Wizards? Can you get us into the Georgetown game? His phone rang every five minutes or so. “It’s nonstop,” he told me. “Every day.”

But, god, he’d missed it — the handshaking, the backslapping, the maaan, how you been? of it all. For 20 years, from the 1990s to the 2010s, he was the godfather of the basketball scene in Washington, D. C. His American Athletic Union program, DC Assault, basically the basketball equivalent of a travel soccer team, was not just the undisputed No. 1 program in the area but one of the best in the country. His teams won national championships and sent players to the McDonald’s All-American Games, top colleges and the N. B. A.

Malone, who co-founded Assault in his mid-20s, was the top decision maker, the recruiter in chief and the public face, but he was also more than that. To many of his players, he was a surrogate father. And in the broader basketball world, he was a major power broker. College coaches knew that if they wanted to recruit in the area, one of the country’s richest veins of basketball talent, they had to go through Curtis Malone. One day, he aimed to parlay his ever-expanding network of influence into a career as an N. B. A. agent.

Then the whole thing collapsed. In 2013, federal agents raided Malone’s home and arrested him on drug-trafficking charges. At the same time that he was running DC Assault, it turned out, he was also presiding over a sprawling cocaine and heroin operation, moving millions of dollars’ worth of product each year. His alias, he said, was Whitey.

Through his drug business, Malone had undermined the community that raised him. At the same time, he funneled part of the proceeds into DC Assault to help kids escape the community he was himself destroying. “He’s helping young men,” a D. E. A. agent on the case told Sports Illustrated in 2014, “but at the same time he could be poisoning their parents or relatives.” Malone’s stepdaughter called it “the most dysfunctional Robin Hood story ever.” He was sentenced to 100 months in prison.

In May 2020, Malone came home. Despite having renounced his career in basketball, he started hanging around gyms, and before long, coaches came seeking his counsel. Parents asked when he was bringing DC Assault back. He began to feel “the itch” again. And when he got the opportunity to join a league sponsored by New Balance, he couldn’t resist. In late 2025, after 13 years away, Malone announced that he was restarting DC Assault, with the goal of rebuilding it into a national powerhouse, only clean this time — no drugs, no drug money, no double life.

At the Saturday tryout in March, players were vying for spots on one of the program’s three squads made up mostly of high schoolers — the under-15s, the under-16s and the under-17s. They would start their season in April and compete through midsummer. As the day wound down and the gym emptied out, Malone made a final pitch to one of his top recruiting targets for the under-17s, a sharpshooting 6-foot-4 combo guard named Sean Nix who drove six hours from Charlotte, N. C., to be there. “It’s like choosing Duke and North Carolina when it comes to A. A. U.,” Malone told him. “This is one of the all-time great programs in A. A. U. history.” Nix nodded.

After tryouts, Malone and his coaches treated a group of out-of-towners to lunch at a nearby sports bar. He’d already outfitted them with DC Assault gear and New Balance shoes, and when one boy said goodbye, Malone slipped him a thin stack of $20s — for gas, he said. Nix had skipped lunch to get some extra shots up, but that afternoon his father texted Malone: “We’re IN. Let’s make DC Assault great again.”

“Congratulations, man!” one of the coaches said, clapping Malone on the shoulder. “This [expletive] is back!”

“It ain’t back yet,” Malone answered. To him, back meant more than just … existing. Back meant being the best, and for the moment, still a month out from its first official games, DC Assault was nowhere near that. The world of youth basketball had transformed since Malone went to prison. Shoe companies had consolidated control, so that virtually every major team now played on one of their circuits. Dozens of current and former N. B. A. stars now sponsored their own teams. In the D. C. area, rival programs had supplanted Assault, and the New Balance league wasn’t providing anywhere near the funding that Adidas and Under Armour once had. Nor could Malone supplement the budget anymore with, shall we say, alternative income streams.

That Malone could restore Assault to anything like its former glory was far from certain. How he would react if he couldn’t was an open question. But he wasn’t worried. He would figure things out. He was Curtis Malone! With a little time and a little money, he would re-establish his dominance. “When I get that backing,” he said, “nobody gonna beat me.”

Everybody knows Curtis Malone. He’s the kind of guy who can walk into a restaurant with a 45-minute wait and be seated five minutes later. He never feels self-doubt, he told me, and he has a tendency to speak about himself in the third person, as when he chats up a waiter at his favorite seafood place (“You know you’re talking to Curtis, right?”) or when he utters one of his catchphrases (“Curtis is gonna be fine”). When Malone was a teenager, his father used to refer to his friends as his “associates,” because one boy couldn’t possibly have so many friends, but Malone never saw it that way. At a high school basketball showcase early this year, I watched him greet more than 50 people like family. He shook hands, dispensed hugs, came up behind one man and play-acted like he was dunking on him. How could you not want to be friends with Curtis Malone? When, on occasion, he forgot someone’s name, he flashed his signature mischievous-child grin, and all was forgiven. He calls that “the Malone smile,” and it works just as well now, at 58, as it did when he was a kid shoplifting candy bars from convenience stores.

There is no other private Curtis Malone. He never turns off and hardly ever spends time alone. His ex-wife, Monica Smith, told me that during their nearly 10 years of marriage, they “saw each other in passing,” to the point that she started calling him “the married bachelor.” His current wife, Gail, told me she sometimes feels as though she is raising her husband. “This man thinks life is a party,” she laughed. “He a roadrunner,” his mother said — always has been.

Malone’s earliest role models were drug dealers. Ronald Byrd. Irvin Wallace. Twin Jones. Growing up in Palmer Park, Md., he thought of these men as his godfathers.

Malone’s real father, he told me, was a straight-shooting Alabama disciplinarian. Served four years in the Air Force and worked the rest of his life at a bus terminal in downtown D. C. Out of the house in his pale-blue uniform at 5 a. m. everyday. Plus night shifts a few days a week at a 24-hour store that they all called “the fruit stand.” And what did he have to show for it? A World War II-era starter home and some meager savings.

Malone’s father commanded respect, but his godfathers made life look glamorous, easy. “Byrd, he was just so smooth,” Malone reminisced, and the way he said it, it was as though he could see the man rolling up in his sky-blue Lincoln Mark V. When Malone hung out with these guys, he felt smooth, too. They slipped him cash, kept him well-dressed and handled anyone who threatened him. When they got Chinese food, they ordered the whole menu. They showed him respect, taught him a code: Never steal, never lie, never use.

Of the many children who roamed the neighborhood’s alleyways, Malone was known as one of the first out to play in the morning and one of the last home at night. He spent much of that time playing basketball at the local rec center and over time developed a reputation as a talented point guard. His godfathers took notice, even paying for him to attend basketball camps that his parents couldn’t afford. Byrd and Wallace had been serious athletes before becoming dealers, and Malone thinks that they might have seen something of themselves in him — that they wanted him to succeed where they knew, at some level, they had failed.

And yet Malone couldn’t help thinking: Could dealing really be so bad if these men were doing it? To this day, he maintains that they were “some of the best mentors I could’ve had.”

For a while, Malone took their advice. He went to play basketball at Hampton University, a historically Black research college on the shores of the Chesapeake Bay. He tried to be a regular college kid. But he didn’t get along with the coach and never saw any court time, and he was always short on cash. At a party during his second semester, he met a dealer who went by the name New York C. Being around the hustle, he said, “just always gave me the itch,” and with his basketball career foundering, he finally gave in to it. At first, he sold powder a little cocaine and PCP, but before long he dropped out and scaled up to a full-on crack operation. His street crew back in Prince George’s County hustled on corners. His enforcers stepped in when it became necessary to “tough up the competition or shoot one of your customers.” New York C was his main supplier. Malone learned how to cook the product himself. Before long, he had turned the road he grew up on into a crack strip.

Malone is cleareyed, to a point, about the damage he did. “Crack destroyed Palmer Park and my city,” he writes in his memoir, “Duplicity: Basketball, Drugs and My Double Life,” published last year. (The cover depicts a hand tossing a bag of cocaine into a basketball hoop.) “I’ve known people who’ve stolen from their mother — their children — to get high.” Some of his closest friends were addicts. His sister Beverly drifted in and out of rehab. When he urged her to get help, she told him a dealer was no better than a user. “It hit a nerve,” he told me, “because she was right.” Still, he dealt.

In 1990, Malone was arrested in his father’s front yard and did three months in jail after pleading guilty to drug charges. A few years later, he started DC Assault at a Maryland rec center with a few buddies, among them his best friend Troy Weaver, now a top executive with the N. B. A.’s New Orleans Pelicans. The program started as a single team, mostly neighborhood kids, but things took off fast. Malone had an eye for talent, plus a pre-existing network of relationships. “My recruiting tactic,” he once explained, “was, I’m going to find out what neighborhood the kid is from, and I’m going to see who’s the biggest drug dealer in that area — who got influence. And that’s who I’m going to see.”

Within three years, the team’s starting five included four future McDonald’s All-Americans. College coaches came calling. John Thompson, the head coach at Georgetown, helped land DC Assault a sponsorship offer from Nike, but Sonny Vaccaro of Adidas swooped in with an even better one. They had made it. Serious people wanted things from them. Major corporations jockeyed for the privilege of paying them. And Malone was running the show. “Leadership is everything to me,” he told me. “I just can’t see myself being second or third in charge. If I’m going to go rob a bank, I don’t need nobody to drive the car. I’m going to drive the car too. I’ve got to be my own getaway driver.”

Of Assault’s four future All-Americans, DerMarr Johnson was the best. Malone met him one afternoon in 1995, when a friend called him from a D. C. playground and told him to drop whatever he was doing and come see this kid: 14 years old, 6-foot-7, throwing down dunks and raining in 3s. Johnson joined DC Assault and before long moved in with Malone. As a high school junior, he was the top-ranked underclassman in the country, and in his lone year at the University of Cincinnati, N. B. A. scouts salivated over his “limitless” offensive potential. The Atlanta Hawks picked him sixth in the 2000 N. B. A. draft.

Malone had already established DC Assault as one of the nation’s premier A. A. U. teams, but not until Johnson did he internalize that a top player could be his ticket to the big time, his path to legitimacy. He was the one navigating his players through high school. He was the one driving them to practices, feeding them, sometimes even paying their parents’ rent. Then agents swooped in at the last minute to profit off their success. “If we’re doing all the work,” he thought, “why wouldn’t we reap the benefits?” The same skills that made him a successful drug dealer made him successful with DC Assault, he thought, and they would make him a successful agent too. “It’s all the same thing,” a dealer friend once told him, “crack, PCP or car parts” — or basketball prospects.

DC Assault’s second true superstar was Michael Beasley. When Malone met him in 2002 at age 13, Beasley’s father was in prison, and the son already had his own troubles with the law. Beasley also moved in with Malone — who was living with his wife at the time, Monica Smith — and developed into a top prospect. After a phenomenal freshman year at Kansas State University, he was a lock to be selected in the top three picks in the draft. Malone had lined up an agent, whose firm he planned to join as a partner after draft night. Beasley would provide instant credibility for signing other stars.

After the draft, though, Beasley cut off Malone and the agent and eventually replaced them with an industry veteran. Malone still doesn’t know why. “It was a very, very hurtful time,” he told me, “because we had put so much time into building this kid up, into helping him grow up so his life could change.” (Asked for comment, Beasley said he feels “no malice” toward Malone and regrets losing touch with Smith.)

Malone had shifted his focus away from dealing as he worked to start an agency, but as his dream of legitimacy collapsed, he turned back to drugs. If he couldn’t make it big as an agent, then he would make it big as a dealer. He would still be a leader, just a different kind. He hit up his old contacts, and soon he was moving more and more kilos. He told himself that dealing was only temporary — one more good run, and he would quit. He never did.

In 2012, a heroin dealer who bought from him sold drugs to a confidential informant. The D. E. A. tapped the dealer’s phone, which led them to Malone. For more than a year, officers conducted in-person surveillance, listened in on his calls and watched him from a secret camera installed on a telephone pole outside his house. In August 2013, they arrested him at home, where they found an estimated $150,000 worth of cocaine and heroin.

Malone doesn’t speak much about his prison time, but when he does, he talks about it as though it were a long retreat — “a big weight off my shoulders.” He started playing basketball again and ran every day. He sipped moonshine and studied in the law library. “I tell you what, it wasn’t hard for me,” he said, “and I done seen it be hard for people.” I asked if there were any difficult moments. He said there were not.

Despite all this, despite his history as a dealer and his multiple prison stints and his years of deception, parents still trust him. They call people they respect in the youth basketball community, and those people tell them that Curtis Malone is the real deal. He goes to watch their kids play — travels great distances on winter nights when he surely has a million better places to be — and says all the right things. They believe, above all, that he will deliver for their children. And why shouldn’t they? Look at his résumé! He’ll make sure their baby lands a scholarship, maybe even a lucrative name-image-likeness deal. And that, in the end, is what it’s really all about.

The 2026 season got off to a rickety start. At a Richmond showcase in early April, the DC Assault under-17s went down 19 points in the first half to an Adidas-sponsored team that has produced a handful of N. B. A. players over the past decade, then rallied back and took the lead — only to lose it again in the final seconds. Two weeks later, facing a local rival in D. C., the under-17s coughed up another last-minute lead at the end of regulation, then lost on an overtime buzzer-beater.

Some parents were already beginning to grumble. In the old days, Malone dealt mostly with absentee parents who were grateful for him to keep the kids out of trouble. “We used to pick kids up in the ’hood,” he told me. “The kids used to be hard.” Once, at a tournament in Las Vegas, he intercepted a sex worker on her way to his players’ hotel room. “Now,” he said, “mothers and fathers be carrying these [expletive] shoes and bags.” The parents are never satisfied, never think their child is getting enough minutes, enough shots, enough spotlight.

And the stakes have never been higher. Recent legal developments making it possible for colleges to pay athletes mean even high school recruits who may never go pro are now just a step away from potential multimillion-dollar payouts. A series of noteworthy performances can alter a kid’s life. But the competition has also intensified: The N. C. A. A. has made it easier for college athletes to transfer schools multiple times without losing playing time, which means that high school recruits now compete not just against one another but also against college players.

Although it can feel uncomfortable to acknowledge, elite youth basketball players are both children and commodities. When scouts and analysts speak of “talent pipelines,” the phrase is less than literal but more than metaphoric. Top players really are a sort of natural resource. That, in large part, is why global brands like Nike and Adidas invest millions of dollars in their youth-basketball circuits. A fraction of the kids on those circuits will play for top colleges, and a fraction of those college players will make it to the N. B. A., and a fraction of those N. B. A. players will become N. B. A. stars, and a fraction of those N. B. A. stars will become the kind of high-wattage megastars whose endorsements sell market-moving quantities of sneakers.

DerMarr Johnson had sneaker potential. So did Michael Beasley. And in Beasley’s case, it was the complications arising from that potential — and the blurring of the lines between child and commodity — that in large part caused the collapse of his relationship with Malone.

When Malone went to prison, Beasley spoke affectionately of him despite the falling out. “He’s my father,” Beasley said in a 2014 interview. “All the stuff that I have been through, he’s been there for me.” But more recently, Beasley has struck a different tone. “Curt played a major part in my life,” he said on a podcast last year. “But I paid for that.” He suggested that Malone might have used him — that he demanded payment, once Beasley had made it to the N. B. A., for the support he had given him growing up. If he really was a son to Malone, why should he have to pay? (Malone acknowledges receiving a monthly $5,000 stipend from Beasley from January to September 2009, but he insists he never asked for money.) On another podcast the year before, Beasley was even harsher.

“He really took a liking to y’all,” the host said of Malone. “Loved on y’all like y’all was his.”

“Nah, nah,” Beasley interjected. “We ain’t going to go that far.”

“You don’t think so?” the host asked.

“You got kids?” Beasley asked back.

“Yeah.”

“How old?”

“Fifteen, 10 and 5.”

“When they get older, when they grow up, how much money they going to have to pay you?”

Johnson sees things differently. When a near-fatal car crash derailed his N. B. A. career in 2002, Malone flew to see him in the hospital hours after hearing the news. And in the years that followed, as it became clear that Johnson would never make it big, Malone stuck with him. He might have thought of Johnson as his “ticket,” but Johnson never felt that way. He thought of Malone as a father figure and still does. “I don’t know where I would have been,” Johnson told me. “My whole family sold drugs. The N. B. A. was just something that was on TV.” If Malone could make some money off his talent, all the better. “Use me all you want,” Johnson said.

If Beasley stands for the idea that Malone used his players, then Johnson stands for the idea that he loved them. In reality, both are true. Malone himself has said as much. They were his tickets — whether or not Malone ever asked Beasley for money, he hoped Beasley’s success would advance his own ambitions — and they were his sons. If that seems to verge on contradiction, well, that’s Curtis Malone.

The only time I ever saw Malone get emotional was when I asked him about Beasley’s podcast comments. Eight months had passed since the most recent ones, but they still seemed fresh in Malone’s mind. He leaned in, elbows on the table, and looked me in the eyes, speaking as though directly to Beasley.

“Would you have made it without Curtis?” he asked. “When I got you, you were a troubled kid, ankle monitor at 13 years old. I sent you to four, five different schools. I did. Your mother didn’t. Monica took you to every dentist appointment, every [expletive] doctor’s appointment when your tooth hurt, when you needed stitches.”

“I’ve never done anything to you,” he went on. “I’ve never done anything but love you — unconditionally. I loved you unconditionally.”

The Henrico Sports & Events Center in Glen Allen, Va., delivers basketball at industrial scale, basketball farther than the eye can see, an Amazon fulfillment center’s worth of basketball. Twelve courts under one deific roof. Twelve games happening all at once. Twelve whistles blowing and 12 balls bouncing and 240 sneakers — New Balance, all of them — squeaking across semi-reflective hardwood on this April afternoon. The smell of soft pretzels and beer by the concessions stand. The smell of adolescent sweat everywhere else. Parental sanity at a premium. During one game, police officers intervened to prevent a fully grown man from coming to blows with a gaggle of prepubescent boys who threatened to shoot him. This is an undiluted dose of high-level youth basketball, straight to the veins. This is where the comeback began in earnest.

The team’s goal in Glen Allen was, in a sense, rhetorical: to persuade the A. A. U. world that DC Assault was — or at least would soon be — every bit the juggernaut it once was. Eventually that would mean winning the New Balance circuit championship in July and beating top teams on the vaunted Nike and Adidas circuits. But if Assault couldn’t take care of business at a regional New Balance event, it had no chance of achieving those loftier ambitions.

“The man, the myth, the legend,” an opposing coach said as he dapped up Malone courtside. He was one of the coaches of Showtime Ballers, a team based in Orlando, Fla., that spent a few years in the late 2000s as the Florida outpost of DC Assault but pivoted after Malone “resigned,” as he sometimes euphemistically puts it. “He didn’t know me from a can of pork and beans,” Diana Gillion, one of Showtime’s founders told me about Malone. “He stepped in and just helped us out when we really needed it.” All these years later, Showtime was the DC Assault under-17 team’s first opponent.

The game did not start well. Showtime played fast-paced, hard-nosed basketball, and the Assault players seemed rattled. Stagnant on offense, disengaged on defense. Malone stood on the base line, arms-crossed, impassive. He almost always watches games this way, with an expression like he’s reviewing tax documents. Dunks that unleash delirium on a gym hardly register. Not much excites him, he said, because he has seen it all: “A dunk? OK. Block 10 shots and get 10 rebounds.”

Midway through the second quarter, Assault fired up air balls on back-to-back possessions. At halftime, the team trailed by 9 points, and that deficit was flattering. “Look at this [expletive], man,” an older guy said to Malone. “Go-lly.” He didn’t answer.

But Assault came out for the second half more organized, more energetic. Three minutes in, Showtime’s 9-point lead had evaporated. Malone started to get into it. “It’s a dogfight, baby,” he jawed at a referee. “We need some calls too!”

With the game tied at 61 in the final minute, Showtime stole a careless inbound pass and pulled ahead by 2. Timeout, Assault.

Anxiety emanated. The specter of the recent heartbreakers in Richmond and D. C. loomed. With Assault down 2 and only a few seconds to play, the feeling courtside was: Not again.

The referee blew his whistle. The teams took the court. The inbounder arced a pass to a forward in the far corner. “Shoot it!” someone yelled, but that wasn’t the play. Sean Nix came racing around a screen at the top of the key, caught a pass from the forward just behind the three-point line and, in one fluid motion, rose up for a fade-away jumper. The shot hit the net just as the buzzer sounded. Assault 64, Showtime 63.

The bench stormed the court. Malone — who has seen it all — shook his head and smiled. For a moment, at least, the comeback felt complete.

But only for a moment. There is always more to do.

Malone is still angling to make the jump from A. A. U. impresario to N. B. A. agent. He and his stepdaughter, Sydney Smith, have started an agency, and they’re currently courting investors. If the whole agent thing doesn’t work out, Malone knows he would make a good N. B. A. scout, and he hopes one of his old friends in the N. B. A. could help him land a job. If none of that comes together, Malone and Smith have also started a production company. They have a writer at work adapting “Duplicity” into a movie, and by the end of the year, Malone intends to start writing a second volume, this one focused on “the redemption side.”

But DC Assault, he says, is still his “true calling.” In July, after an impressive season, the under-17s were knocked out in the quarterfinals of the New Balance circuit championship tournament. The under-15s won the whole thing. All in all, a strong showing for a program that was never expected to play again — but not the old dominance. DC Assault still can’t compare to the best team in the area. But just give him another recruiting cycle, Malone says. He has even got former Assault players from France and the Republic of Congo scouting overseas. He showed me a photo of a 7-foot French 10th grader. “They say he’s very, very skilled,” Malone said. “They say he’s like a little Wemby.”

If the under-17 team fell short, that was in part because not long after the tournament in Glen Allen, two starters left to join a rival A. A. U. program, one of them arguably Assault’s most talented player. Malone had done everything he could to keep the kid — reassured the mother, even had the tournament organizers hang a banner with his photo. So much for that. On top of the two departures, another D. C.-area team had tried to poach two of his best under-16 players. And a rival coach had sent one of Malone’s players the video of Beasley criticizing him, along with the message, “Are you sure y’all did your research?”

None of this surprises Malone. He expected other coaches in the area to use his past against him. “They really don’t want me back,” he told me. “They smile at you, shake your hand, stab you in the back.”

In the old days, his opponents would never have gotten away with this. But that, he said, “is the different side of me.” He’s not like that anymore. He regrets what he did — or some of it anyway. He admits that he could have struck “a better balance,” but to have left the hustle behind entirely would have felt, on some level, like renouncing his upbringing. “Duplicity” is dedicated, with intentional ambiguity, “to the game.”

From the beginning, Malone modeled himself on his idols: “I watched Twin or Irvin dole out wads of cash and knew I wanted to be just like them when I grew up,” he writes. “And wasn’t I?” He too handed out cash, but he also helped kids secure scholarships. “I not only emulated my childhood idols,” he continues, “I surpassed them.” For better and for worse, DC Assault was built in their image.

It still is. But Malone is going legitimate. So when his rivals disparage him or poach his players, he simply tries not to worry too much about it. “What I’ve learned is if a kid with me leaves me and goes to another team, and that kid done been on three or four teams already, what you think he going to do again?” he asked rhetorically. “The pattern is what it is, man.”

He could, of course, just as easily be talking about himself. When college basketball didn’t pan out, he turned to dealing. When his agent plans fell apart, he turned to dealing again. If things didn’t work out this time, I asked, would he turn to dealing a third time?

“There’s nothing that I’m doing that’s not going to work out,” he said. “That’s not going to happen. ‘Not work out’ is not even in my vocabulary.”

And the way he said it, how could you not believe him?

Jacob Stern is a writer from Washington, D. C. He has written about lightning-strike survivors, anti-government ranchers and a boxer who killed his opponent in the ring.

Culture War Tensions Roil Beverly Hills School Board Race

The New York Times November 01, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Battles over Israel, antisemitism and race have shaken Beverly Hills in recent years and divided the formerly Democratic enclave.

By Tim Arango

Reporting from Beverly Hills, Calif.

Since the Covid-19 pandemic, school board elections around the country, once sleepy affairs, have been convulsed by America’s political and cultural divides. The teaching of racial justice. Gaza and Israel. Transgender rights.

But very few of these battles have had the same mix of wealth, privilege and celebrity as the one that is going on in Beverly Hills, Calif. And this year, the campaign for two seats on the school board has devolved into an all-out political brawl.

“The ugliness of national politics has come to Beverly Hills,” said Gay Abrams, 70, an activist who has lived in the city for decades and recently organized “No Kings” rallies.

Moles have infiltrated group chats. The police have responded to dozens of calls about stolen campaign signs. One of the candidates has a restraining order against an opponent over allegations of doxxing. And in this heavily Jewish community, feelings about Israel and the definition of antisemitism have been at the forefront.

Beverly Hills, while it has always had plenty of Republicans, for decades voted for Democrats for president, save for Ronald Reagan. That changed in 2024, when the city, which has a population of about 30,000, voted for Donald Trump and became a small red dot on the vast blue map of Los Angeles County.

That same year, two new school board members were elected in Beverly Hills, securing a narrow 3-2 conservative majority.

And then controversies began piling up, starting with a pro-Trump rally at Beverly Hills High School after the 2024 election. Minority students said they were bullied, with pro-Trump students yelling, “Deport all Mexicans,” according to a lawsuit filed by a teacher who said she had been fired for a social media post criticizing the rally.

Over time, tensions boiled over arcane issues like when to allow public comment at board meetings and how the bylaws say the board’s vice president should be elected. Then came the political disputes: whether to display the Israeli flag at schools; the inclusion of Charlie Kirk next to notable Americans such as Martin Luther King Jr. at an elementary school exhibit; and the removal of a Maya Angelou book from the same exhibit.

The school board race is nonpartisan, but the rift involves familiar divisions. The conservative board majority has been supportive of Israel and resistant to recognizing ethnic history. Liberals have pushed for celebrating more diversity and said that criticism of Israel does not equate to antisemitism.

On the conservative side of the school board race is Judy Manouchehri, 46, a lawyer and the incumbent president, as well as an ally, David Cienfuegos, 53, a personal injury attorney who grew up in Mexico and California. On the liberal side are two political newcomers: Jackie Kruger, a 47-year-old lawyer and mother; and Kim Lifschitz, 39, a stay-at-home mother.

The four candidates, along with a fifth entrant who has less traction, are competing for two at-large seats that all voters in the school district will choose.

Ms. Manouchehri, who grew up in Beverly Hills after her family fled Iran following the revolution in 1979, considers herself nonpartisan and said she would prefer to focus on the district’s improvements in test scores. (While some data shows gains in test scores, her opponents have pointed to a decline in Beverly Hills High School’s ranking in the U. S. News & World Report.)

She said she was frustrated by the divisiveness within the Beverly Hills Unified School District.

“It’s something that hurts and is disappointing, and I wake up every day and one of my goals is to try to counter the negativity with facts, data and reasons for the Beverly Hills community to be proud of B. H. U. S. D.,” she said in a recent interview.

She said dust-ups over culture war issues are rare, and exaggerated on social media. Still, she apologized for two episodes that have fueled divisions in the city.

In one, she voted against a resolution establishing cultural heritage months, including Black History Month, asking why the city didn’t celebrate a European heritage month. “Looking back, I don’t think I realized the gravity it held for the community,” she said. (The resolution passed on a 3-to-2 vote.)

“I do regret the hurt that my vote on that resolution caused,” she added.

In another, she said it was a mistake for a school club to host the Israeli American influencer Ben Azoulay, who once served jail time after pleading guilty to a sex crime with a minor. She said Mr. Azoulay slipped through the district’s vetting process.

The controversy over Mr. Azoulay was one of the reasons Ms. Kruger decided to run for school board. The incumbents, she said, are “creating chaos and sowing division and demonstrating that they are only here to serve a very small minority.”

Ms. Kruger fled the Soviet Union in 1980, and she said her parents had sacrificed so she could attend Beverly Hills schools.

On a recent evening, residents supporting her and Ms. Lifschitz packed into her modest white cottage on a tree-lined street of multimillion-dollar homes that pass for a middle-class enclave in Beverly Hills and feel far away from the wide lawns and estates on the other side of town.

Over sandwiches and plates of kebab, parents worked the phones, dialing voters.

Ms. Kruger had spent much of the day in court, for a hearing about continuing the restraining order she had secured against Mr. Cienfuegos, whom she has accused of videotaping her home, posting her address on social media and accusing her son of stealing campaign signs.

“This is our opportunity, overnight, to come back to normalcy,” she said of the board election.

Ms. Lifschitz, 39, said she had decided to run to counter what she saw as an extreme, rightward shift of the district.

“It’s really scary to me to see this, honestly, this MAGA infiltration down to this local level,” she said.

During the campaign, Ms. Lifschitz became engulfed in controversy when, in group chats, she appeared to mock both a picture of one school board member at the Western Wall in Jerusalem and the way another board member introduced Holocaust survivors at an event in a “sing-song-y voice like they were pets in a zoo.” Screenshots were leaked online, and Ms. Lifschitz, who is Jewish, was accused of being an antisemite. (“It was just adults venting,” she said.)

Talk to residents long enough about the political upheaval in their city, and they will point to a deeper clash that goes back decades, when Persians, many of them Jews, fled the Iranian Revolution and settled in Beverly Hills. Persian Jews tend to be more conservative — many support the war on Iran, for example — than the old guard of Beverly Hills, who are predominantly Ashkenazi Jews of European descent.

Many liberal Jews in Beverly Hills believe the school board has focused too much on Israel and point to an effort to have schools display the Israeli flag. (After an uproar, the superintendent backed down, citing safety concerns.)

“I’m Jewish and I was raised in this district and I don’t really want my board focusing on a foreign country and an issue that has nothing to do with my classroom,” said Amy Arebalo, who taught in the district for decades and retired last year. “But this has become the board’s priority.”

On a recent afternoon, Russell Stuart, a conservative incumbent not facing re-election, was at his desk at Beverly Hills Guns, an appointment-only gun dealer located on the fifth floor of an office building on Wilshire Boulevard. Mr. Stuart runs a website, the Beverly Hills Standard, that produces articles generated by artificial intelligence that have attacked his opponents.

He framed the split in Beverly Hills as one largely within the Jewish community. The entire five-member school board, including Mr. Stuart, is Jewish.

“I think that in the city of Beverly Hills there’s definitely a divide between the white Jews and the Persian Jews,” said Mr. Stuart.

“It’s absolutely undeniable how well the Persians have done, in this country and this state and this city,” he added. “And I think that there is a resentment, truly a resentment of how well they’ve done.”

Asked about this divide, Ms. Manouchehri said, “It’s starting to feel that way.”

Across the political divide of Beverly Hills, there is a sense of loss — of the civility and decorum people say once defined public life in the city.

“Everyone is just, it’s sad and tiresome,” said David Lucky, 48, a television producer who has a daughter in third grade.

“I don’t know why,” he continued. “I don’t think anyone knows why. And I don’t know what happens after.”

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

This Republican Wants Voters to Consider a Post-Trump World

The New York Times November 01, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

John E. Sununu, the Republican Senate candidate in New Hampshire, has the president’s endorsement but is keeping him at arm’s length.

By Jess Bidgood

Reporting from Rye, N. H.

Debra Smith arrived at a recent candidates forum hating John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for Senate in New Hampshire.

Here, she thought, was another career politician — a former congressman and one-term senator seeking to reclaim his seat nearly 20 years after he lost it, riding the coattails of his father and his brother, both former governors of the state.

A funny thing happened, though, as Mr. Sununu took questions about health care, housing and transportation policy from Chamber of Commerce types as they picked at caprese sandwiches. Ms. Smith found herself impressed as Mr. Sununu wove facts and experience into his answers, lifting the energy of the room.

“He’s very substantial,” she said.

But before Mr. Sununu left the function room at the Atlantic Grill in Rye, N. H., Ms. Smith, an independent voter, told him she still couldn’t vote for him.

“Because of Trump, I can’t,” she said. “I told him I can’t take the risk.”

Mr. Sununu, 62, has turned his comeback Senate campaign into a test of a tricky premise: that in 2026, it is possible to be both a Republican and independent of President Trump. Selling this idea is critical for any hope of success in a purple state that has never really warmed to the president. And as he trails Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, in the polls, he’s running out of time to convince the Debra Smiths of the world to buy it, particularly in a race that is considered critical to determining the balance of power in the Senate.

He is trying. He once wrote an opinion essay that carried the headline “Trump is a loser.” He has insisted in a television ad that he has never even met the president. He rattles off a laundry list of their policy differences to anyone who will listen. And, perhaps more than any other Republican running for Senate right now, he has asked voters to do something that strains the American political imagination: Consider what happens after Mr. Trump.

“In two years, the president will leave office,” he said on a debate stage last month. “And my question is, where do we go next?”

The unsaid part of his bet is that, deep down, voters want a political future that looks like the past.

New Hampshire Republicans have lost every race for the House and the Senate since the dawn of the Trump era, often by quite a lot, even as they have won office at the state level. But the party saw a ray of hope in the Sununu name, which is synonymous with the flinty, establishment Republicanism that used to be a lot more common in New England. Mr. Sununu’s father, John H. Sununu, served as governor for three two-year terms in the 1980s before serving as chief of staff to President George H. W. Bush.

National Republicans had tried unsuccessfully to convince Chris Sununu, Mr. Sununu’s charismatic younger brother and a former governor, to run for the Senate in 2022 against the incumbent Democrat, Maggie Hassan. By early 2025, they were seeking to lure John E. Sununu into the 2026 race. But when Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the longtime Democratic incumbent, announced she would retire, Chris Sununu coyly hinted he might run for the Senate after all. A person familiar with the recruiting efforts said that national Republicans checked in to gauge how serious he was — nobody wanted two Sununus on the ballot, after all — but Chris ultimately demurred.

Today, the campaign signs dotting the state’s landscape read, simply, “Sununu Senator,” without specifying which one is actually running. Democrats have conducted private polling to see if voters know which family member is on the ballot. They say confusion abounds.

One reporter’s text message meant for John E. Sununu recently made it, instead, to his father.

“You have reached the old ancient former Gov. of New Hampshire,” came the reply, which concluded, “not the young dynamic Sen.”

The current candidate says there is no confusion. “Voters absolutely know who I am,” he said.

Mr. Sununu first ran for Congress 30 years ago and held the seat currently occupied by Mr. Pappas for three terms. He won his Senate seat in 2002, in a strong year for Republicans in the wake of Sept. 11, and lost it to Ms. Shaheen in the wave that accompanied the election of Barack Obama in 2008. (He then pursued a lucrative career working at a lobbying firm and sitting on corporate boards.)

On the campaign trail, he tells war stories from another era. He can be trusted to stand up to Mr. Trump, he says, because he stood up to President George W. Bush, insisting that the reauthorization of the Patriot Act, passed after the Sept. 11 attacks, include more protections for civil liberties. He can be trusted to be bipartisan, he says, because he cosponsored legislation with Hillary Clinton. He was the first Republican to call for the firing of Alberto Gonzales, the attorney general for Mr. Bush. (Mr. Gonzales resigned in 2007 after a standoff with congressional critics over the Justice Department’s handling of terrorism investigations and the firing of U. S. attorneys.)

“I think all of those things reinforce a reputation for independence and for directness and honesty,” he said in an interview.

And did his family name help?

“Sure,” he said, quickly changing the subject to how, in 2024, he endorsed former Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina for president over Mr. Trump.

In February, Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Sununu, saying he would work “tirelessly to advance our America first agenda.”

It was a signal to the party to ignore Mr. Sununu’s primary opponent, another former Republican senator named Scott Brown. But it gave Mr. Pappas his biggest attack line: that, for all his claims of independence, Mr. Sununu is as beholden to Mr. Trump as anyone in a Republican Party that has shown total fealty to the president. Mr. Pappas has also depicted him as squishy on Mr. Trump, saying that Mr. Sununu’s opposition to the war in Iran, for instance, has bloomed only alongside its unpopularity.

Mr. Sununu has tried to keep his focus on his state.

“My focus has been on New Hampshire, on the economy, jobs, affordability, and that message has resonated, and that’s why this is a race that a year ago people didn’t think would be competitive,” Mr. Sununu said.

A New York Times/Siena University poll released in late September found Mr. Pappas with a five-point lead — a sign that Mr. Sununu is running significantly more competitively than the state’s last two Republican Senate nominees. One of them, Corky Messner, lost to Ms. Shaheen by nearly 16 percentage points in 2020; the other, Don Bolduc, lost to Senator Maggie Hassan by 9 points. (In a twist, Mr. Bolduc has endorsed Mr. Pappas.)

In that poll, Mr. Sununu’s favorability rating was slightly higher than Mr. Pappas’s, at 45 percent to 43 percent. And 48 percent of voters said Mr. Sununu would better handle issues related to the cost of living; 46 percent said that about Mr. Pappas.

But 60 percent of voters disapproved of Mr. Trump, and 54 percent said they wanted a candidate who would provide a check on him.

As he spoke to the Seacoast Chamber Alliance late last month, Mr. Sununu seemed, at times, to be inhabiting a kind of Brigadoon where there was no President Trump.

He called for term limits in Congress, lamented the unbalanced state of the federal budget and eagerly parried questions about Social Security, going deep into the weeds.

Mr. Pappas had addressed the group first. When he finished, Jimmy Dykes, an independent voter from the coastal town of Hampton, asked why the congressman had not been more visible in that community. But Mr. Dykes said he was planning to vote for Mr. Pappas, anyway.

He associated Mr. Sununu with the wars that began during his tenure in Congress, those in Iraq and Afghanistan, and said he simply couldn’t trust him to deal with Mr. Trump, who he believes is an “existential threat.”

Mr. Dykes was, however, considering voting for Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who has also stayed well away from Mr. Trump. She used to have the job Mr. Sununu wants but narrowly lost re-election to the Senate the night Mr. Trump was elected in 2016. Now, she appears to be cruising to re-election as governor — becoming one of her party’s bright spots in a difficult year.

Mr. Sununu, for his part, declined to say what he thought the Republican Party should look like after Mr. Trump is gone. But does he want to help shape it?

“Absolutely.”

Bayliss Wagner contributed reporting.

Jess Bidgood is a managing correspondent for The Times and writes the On Politics newsletter, a guide to this pivotal moment in American politics.
